Niggahītamāgamo hoti vā kvaci. Cakkhuṃ udapādi cakkhuudapādi, purimaṃ jātiṃ purimajātiṃ, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahuṃ. Avaṃsirotiādīsu niccaṃ… vavatthitavibhāsattā vādhikārassa, sāmattiyenāgamova, sa ca rassa sarasseva hoti… tassa rassānugatattā.

The niggahīta is sometimes an optional augment. For example: cakkhuṃ udapādi from cakkhu udapādi; purimaṃ jātiṃ from purima jātiṃ; kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahuṃ. In cases like avaṃsira it is obligatory. Because this is a systematic option based on the authority of the rule, it is an augment, and it occurs only after a short vowel, because it follows a short vowel.

39. Lopo.

39. Elision.

Niggahītassa lopo hoti vā kvaci. Kyāhaṃ kimahaṃsāratto saṃratto. Salle kho-gantukāmo gantumanoti, ādīsu niccaṃ.

There is sometimes optional elision of the niggahīta. For example: kyāhaṃ (from kiṃ ahaṃ); saratto (from saṃratto). In cases such as sallekho, gantukāmo, and gantumanoti, it is obligatory.

40. Parasarassa.

40. Of the following vowel.

Niggahītamhā parassa sarassa lopo hoti vā kvaci. Tvaṃ-si tvamasi.

There is sometimes optional elision of a vowel following a niggahīta. For example: tvaṃsi from tvaṃ asi.

41. Vagge vagganto.

41. The last member of the class before a member of that class.

Niggahītassa kho vagge vagganto vā hoti paccāsattyā. Taṅkaroti taṃ karoti, tañcarati taṃ carati, taṇṭhānaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ, tandhanaṃ taṃ dhanaṃ, tampāti taṃ pāti. Niccaṃ padamajjhe gantvā, kvacaññātrapi santiṭṭhati.

Indeed, the niggahīta optionally becomes the final nasal of the consonant class when followed by a consonant of that class, due to proximity. For example: taṅkaroti from taṃ karoti; tañcarati from taṃ carati; taṇṭhānaṃ from taṃ ṭhānaṃ; tandhanaṃ from taṃ dhanaṃ; tampāti from taṃ pāti. Having always occurred in the middle of a word, it sometimes also stands elsewhere.

42. Yevahisu ño.

42. Before 'y', 'eva', and 'hi', 'ñ'.

Ya [M 0.0063] eva hi saddesu niggahītassa vā ño hoti. Yaññadeva, taññeva, tañhi, vātveva? Yaṃ yadeva.

When the sounds 'y', 'eva', or 'hi' follow, the niggahīta optionally becomes 'ñ'. For example: yaññadeva, taññeva, tañhi. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like yaṃ yadeva.

43. Ye saṃssa.

43. Of saṃ, before y.

Saṃsaddassa yaṃ niggahītaṃ tassa vā ño hoti yakāre. Saññamo saṃyamo.

The niggahīta of the word saṃ optionally becomes ñ when followed by the letter y. For example: saññamo; saṃyamo.

44. Mayadā sare.

44. M, y, d before a vowel.

Niggahītassa mayadā honti vā sare kvaci. Tamahaṃ, tayidaṃ, tadalaṃ. Vā tveva? Taṃ ahaṃ.

The niggahīta sometimes optionally becomes m, y, or d when a vowel follows. For example: tamahaṃ, tayidaṃ, tadalaṃ. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like taṃ ahaṃ.

45. Vanataragā cāgamā.

45. And the insertion of v, n, t, r, and g.

Ete mayadā ca āgamā honti sare vā kvaci. Tivaṅgikaṃ, ito nāyati, cinitvā, tasmātiha, nirojaṃ, puthageva, idhamāhu, yathayidaṃ, attadatthaṃ. Vā tveva? Attatthaṃ. ‘Atippago kho tāvā’ti-paṭhamanto pagasaddova.

These consonants, and also m, y, and d, are sometimes optionally inserted between vowels. For example: tivaṅgikaṃ, ito nāyati, cinitvā, tasmātiha, nirojaṃ, puthageva, idhamāhu, yathayidaṃ, attadatthaṃ. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like attatthaṃ. In the phrase ‘Atippago kho tāvā’ti, the initial part is just the word paga.

46. Chā ḷo.

46. After cha, ḷ.

Chasaddā parassa sarassa ḷakāro āgamo hoti vā. Chaḷaṅgaṃ, chaḷāyatanaṃ. Vātveva? Chaabhiññā.

After the word cha, the letter ḷ is optionally inserted before a following vowel. For example: chaḷaṅgaṃ, chaḷāyatanaṃ. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like chaabhiññā.

47. Tadaminādīni.

47. The forms tadaminā and so on.

Tadaminādīni [M 0.0064] sādhūni bhavanti. Taṃ iminā tadaminā, sakiṃ āgāmī sakadāgāmī, ekaṃ idha ahaṃ ekamidāhaṃ, saṃvidhāya avahāro saṃvidāvahāro, vārino vāhako valāhako, jīvanassa mūto jīmūto, chavassa sayanaṃ susānaṃ, uddhaṃ khamassa udukkhalaṃ, pisitāso pisāco, mahiyaṃ ravatīti mayūro, evamaññepi payogato-nugantabbā, paresaṃ pisodarādimivedaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The forms tadaminā and so on are valid. Taṃ iminā becomes tadaminā; sakiṃ āgāmī becomes sakadāgāmī; ekaṃ idha ahaṃ becomes ekamidāhaṃ; saṃvidhāya avahāro becomes saṃvidāvahāro; vārino vāhako becomes valāhako; jīvanassa mūto becomes jīmūto; chavassa sayanaṃ becomes susānaṃ; uddhaṃ khamassa becomes udukkhalaṃ; pisitaṃ aso becomes pisāco; mahiyaṃ ravati iti becomes mayūro. In this way, other forms should be inferred from usage. This should be understood as being like the pisodara class of other grammarians.

48. Tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā.

48. Of the t-class, v, r, and ṇ, before y: the c-class, b, y, and ñ.

Tavaggavaraṇānaṃ kvaci cavaggabayañā honti yathākkamaṃ yakāre. Apuccaṇḍatāya, tacchaṃ, yajjevaṃ, ajjhattaṃ, thaññaṃ, dibbaṃ, payyosanā, pokkharañño. Kvacitveva? Rattyā

The consonants of the t-class, and also v, r, and ṇ, sometimes become, respectively, the consonants of the c-class, b, y, and ñ when followed by the letter y. For example: apuccaṇḍatāya, tacchaṃ, yajjevaṃ, ajjhattaṃ, thaññaṃ, dibbaṃ, payyosanā, pokkharañño. Why 'sometimes'? To allow for forms like rattyā.

49. Vaggalasehi te.

49. After class consonants, l, and s: they.

Vaggalasehi parassa yakārassa kvaci te vaggalasā honti.

After a class consonant, l, or s, a following letter y is sometimes assimilated to that preceding consonant.

Sakkate, paccate, aṭṭate, kuppate, phallate, assate. Kvacitveva? Kyāhaṃ.

For example: sakkate, paccate, aṭṭate, kuppate, phallate, assate. Why 'sometimes'? To allow for forms like kyāhaṃ.

50. Hassa vipallāso.

50. Metathesis of h.

Hassa vipallāso hoti yakāre. Guyhaṃ.

Metathesis of h occurs with a following y. For example: guyhaṃ.

51. Ve vā.

51. Optionally with v.

Hassa vipallāso hoti vā vakāre. Bavhābādho bavhābādho.

Metathesis of h optionally occurs with a following v. For example: bavhābādho.

52. Tathānarānaṃ ṭaṭhaṇalā

52. Of t, th, n, and r: ṭ, ṭh, ṇ, and ḷ.

Tathanarānaṃ [M 0.0065] ṭaṭhaṇalā honti vā. Dukkaṭaṃ, aṭṭhakathā, gahaṇaṃ, paligho, palāyati. Vātveva? Dukkataṃ. Kvacitveva? Sugato.

The consonants t, th, n, and r optionally become ṭ, ṭh, ṇ, and ḷ respectively. For example: dukkaṭaṃ, aṭṭhakathā, gahaṇaṃ, paligho, palāyati. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like dukkataṃ. Why 'sometimes'? To allow for forms like sugato.

53. Saṃyogādi lopo.

53. Elision of the first member of a consonant cluster.

Saṃyogassa yo ādībhūto-vayavo tassa vā kvaci lopo hoti. Pupphaṃ-sā jāyate-gini.

The initial member of a consonant cluster is sometimes optionally elided. For example: pupphaṃ-sā jāyate-gini.

54. Vicchābhikkhaññesu dve.

54. In the distributive and repetitive senses, reduplication.

Vicchāyamābhikkhaññe ca yaṃ vattate, tassa dve rūpāni honti. Kriyāya guṇena dabbena vā bhinne atthe byāpitumicchā vicchā. Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati, gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo, gāme gāme pānīyaṃ, gehe gehe issaro, rasaṃ rasaṃ bhakkhayati, kiriyaṃ kiriyamārabhate.

In the distributive (vicchā) and repetitive (ābhikkhañña) senses, a word is reduplicated. Vicchā is the desire to express pervasion of a distinct meaning through action, quality, or substance. For example: He waters tree by tree (rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati); village by village is delightful (gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo); in village by village there is water (gāme gāme pānīyaṃ); in house by house there is a master (gehe gehe issaro); he eats flavor by flavor (rasaṃ rasaṃ bhakkhayati); he undertakes action by action (kiriyaṃ kiriyamārabhate).

Atthiyevā-nupubbiyepi vicchā mūle mūle thūlā, agge agge sukhumā, yadi hi ettha mūlaggabhedo na siyā, ānupubbiyampi na bhaveyya. Māsakaṃ māsakaṃ imamhā kahāpaṇā bhavanthānaṃ dvinnaṃ dehīti māsakaṃ māsakamiccetasmā vicchāgamyate, saddantarato pana imamhā kahāpaṇāti avadhāraṇaṃ. Pubbaṃ pubbaṃ pupphanti, paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃ paccantītyatrāpi vicchāva. Ime ubho aḍḍhā katarā katarā esaṃ dvinnamaḍḍhatā, sabbe ime aḍḍhā katamā katamā imesaṃ aḍḍhutā ihāpi [M 0.0066] vicchāva. Ābhikkhaññaṃ ponopuññaṃ pacati pacati, papacati papacati, lunāhi lunāhitvevāyaṃ lunāti, bhutvā bhutvā gacchati, paṭapaṭā karoti, paṭapaṭāyati.

Vicchā also occurs in a sequential sense: thick at each root, fine at each tip (mūle mūle thūlā, agge agge sukhumā); for if there were no distinction between root and tip, there would be no sequence. From the phrase, 'From this kahāpaṇa, give a māsaka at a time to the two gentlemen,' the distributive sense (vicchā) is understood from 'a māsaka at a time'; the specification 'from this kahāpaṇa' is a determination from another word. In 'they bloom one after another' (pubbaṃ pubbaṃ pupphanti) and 'they ripen one after another' (paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃ paccanti), there is also vicchā. In 'These two are rich; which of the two is richer?' and 'All these are rich; which among them is richest?', there is also vicchā. Ābhikkhaññaṃ means repetition: he cooks again and again (pacati pacati, papacati papacati); 'cut, cut,' thus he cuts (lunāhi lunāhitvevāyaṃ lunāti); having eaten again and again, he goes (bhutvā bhutvā gacchati); he makes a crackling sound (paṭapaṭā karoti, paṭapaṭāyati).

55. Syādilopo pubbassekassa.

55. Elision of the case ending of the first of two.

Vicchāyamekassa dvitte pubbassa syādilopo hoti. Ekekassa. Kathaṃ matthakamatthakenāti? ‘Syādilopo pubbassā’ti yogavibhāgā, nācātippasaṅgo yogavibhāgā iṭṭhappasiddhīti.

In the distributive sense, when a word is reduplicated, the case ending of the first word is elided. For example: ekekassa. How then is matthakamatthakena formed? By 'splitting the rule' (yogavibhāga) 'elision of the case ending of the first.' There is no over-application, for by splitting the rule the desired form is achieved.

56. Sabbādīnaṃ vītihāre.

56. Of sabba and other pronouns, in the sense of reciprocity.

Sabbādīnaṃ vītihāre dve bhavanti pubbassa syādilopo ca. Aññamaññassa bhojakā, itarītarassa bhojakā.

Of sabba and other pronouns, in the sense of reciprocity, they are reduplicated, and the case ending of the first word is elided. For example: aññamaññassa bhojakā (feeders of one another); itarītarassa bhojakā (feeders of each other).

57. Yāvabodhaṃ sambhame.

57. In agitation, as much as is needed for comprehension.

Turitenāpāyahetupadassanaṃ sambhamo, tasmiṃsati vatthu yāvantehi saddehi so-ttho viññāyate, tāvanto saddā payujjante. Sappo sappo sappo, bujjhassu bujjhassu bujjhassu, bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho.

Agitation (sambhamo) is the swift perception of a cause for alarm. When this is present, a word is used as many times as is needed for the meaning to be understood. For example: Sappo sappo sappo (A snake! A snake! A snake!); bujjhassu bujjhassu bujjhassu (Wake up! Wake up! Wake up!); bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho (The monastic Saṅgha is split! The monastic Saṅgha is split!).

58. Bahulaṃ.

58. Variously.

Ayamadhikāro āsatthaparisamattiyā. Tena nātippasaṅgo iṭṭhappasiddhi ca.

This is a governing rule that extends to the end of the chapter. By it, there is no over-application, and the desired forms are achieved.

Iti moggallāne byākaraṇe vuttiyaṃ

Thus in the commentary on the Moggallāna Grammar.

Paṭhamo kaṇḍo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyo kaṇḍo (syādi)

2. The Second Section (on syā, etc.).

1. Dve [M 0.0067] dve-kānekesu nāmasmā si yo, aṃ yo, nā hi, sa naṃ, smā hi, sa naṃ, smiṃ su.

1. Two each for the singular and plural are affixed after a nominal stem: si, yo; aṃ, yo; nā, hi; sa, naṃ; smā, hi; sa, naṃ; smiṃ, su.

Etesaṃ dve dve honti ekānekatthesu vattamānato nāmasmā. Muni munayo, muniṃ munayo, muninā munīhi, munissa munīnaṃ, munismā munīhi, munissa munīnaṃ, munismiṃ munīsu, evaṃ kumārī kumāriyo, kaññā kaññāyoti. Etāni satta dukāni satta vibhattiyo vibhāgo vibhatīti katvā, ettha siamitī-kārā-kārā “kimaṃ sisu” 2,200 ti saṃketatthā.

For these endings, there are two each, occurring in the singular and plural meanings, after a nominal stem. For example: muni, munayo (sage, sages); muniṃ, munayo (sage, sages); muninā, munīhi (by the sage, by the sages); munissa, munīnaṃ (for/of the sage, for/of the sages); munismā, munīhi (from the sage, from the sages); munissa, munīnaṃ (for/of the sage, for/of the sages); munismiṃ, munīsu (in the sage, in the sages). Similarly: kumārī, kumāriyo (maiden, maidens); kaññā, kaññāyo (girl, girls). These seven pairs constitute the seven cases (vibhatti), so called because a case is a division (vibhāga). Here, in the case of si and aṃ, the long vowels ī and ā serve as indicators, according to the rule 'kimaṃ sisu' (2.200).

2. Kamme dutiyā.

2. The accusative is used for the object.

Karīyati kattu kiriyāyā-bhisambandhīyatīti kammaṃ, tasmiṃ dutiyāvibhatti hotaṃ. Kaṭaṃ karoti, odanaṃ pacati, ādiccaṃ passati.

That which is connected by the agent with an action is the object (kamma); in that sense, the second case ending (accusative) occurs. For example: He makes a mat (kaṭaṃ karoti), he cooks rice (odanaṃ pacati), he sees the sun (ādiccaṃ passati).

‘Odano paccatī’ti odanasaddato kammatā nappatīyate, kiñcarahi? Ākhyātato. ‘Kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīya’nti attheva guṇayuttassa kammatā, icchitepi kammattāva dutiyā siddhā gāvuṃ payo dohati, gomantaṃ gāvaṃ yācati, gāvamavarundhati vajaṃ, māṇavakaṃ maggaṃ pucchati, gomantaṃ gāvaṃ bhikkhate, rukkhamavacināti phalāni, sissaṃ dhammaṃ brūte, sissaṃ dhammamanusāsatīti. Evaṃ anicchitepi ahiṃ laṅghayati, visaṃ bhakkheti. Yaṃnevicchitaṃ nāpi [M 0.0068] anicchitaṃ, tatthāpi dutiyā siddhā. Gāmaṃ gacchanto rukkhamūlamupasappati.

In the phrase 'rice is cooked' (odano paccati), the status of being the object is not understood from the word 'rice'; from what then? From the verb. In 'he makes a mat, large and beautiful,' the status of object indeed belongs to that which is endowed with qualities. Also in the case of verbs that take two objects, the accusative is established for both: 'He milks milk from the cow'; 'He asks the cow-owner for a cow'; 'He confines the cow to the pen'; 'He asks the boy the way'; 'He begs the cow-owner for a cow'; 'He picks fruits from the tree'; 'He speaks the Dhamma to the student'; 'He instructs the student in the Dhamma.' Similarly, also in the case of what is not desired: 'He steps over a snake'; 'He eats poison.' Where there is neither desire nor aversion, there too the accusative is established: 'Going to the village, he approaches the foot of a tree.'

Pathaviṃ adhisessati, gāmamadhitiṭṭhati, rukkhamajjhāsatetiadhisīṭhāsānaṃpayoge-dhikaraṇe kammavacanicchā, vatticchāto hi kārakāni honti. Taṃ yathā-valāhakā vijjotate, valāhakassa vijjotate, valāhako vijjotate, valāhake vijjotate, valāhakena vijjotateti. Evamabhinivisassa vā dhammamabhinivisate dhamme vā.

'He lies upon the earth,' 'he stands over the village,' 'he sits upon the tree.' Thus, with the use of adhi-sī, adhi-ṭhā, and adhi-ās, the locative sense is expressed by the accusative case, for grammatical functions depend on the speaker's intention. For example: 'Lightning flashes from the cloud' (ablative), 'of the cloud' (genitive), 'the cloud flashes' (nominative), 'in the cloud' (locative), or 'by means of the cloud' (instrumental). Similarly, with abhinivisati, one can say either 'he is intent on the Dhamma' (dhammam abhinivisate) or 'in the Dhamma' (dhamme vā).

Tathā upanvajjhāvasassābhojana nivuttivacanassa gāmamupavasati, ga, mamanuvasati, pabbatamadhivasati, gharamāvasati. Abhojananivutti vacanassāti kiṃ? Gāme upavasati, bhojananivuttiṃ karotīti attho. Tappānācārepi kammattāva dutiyā siyā nadimpivati, gāmaṃ carati, evaṃ ‘sace maṃ ālapissatī’tiādīsupi. Vihitāva patidhayoge dutiyā – ‘paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā’ti. Taṃ pati bojjhaṅgā bhāsantūti attho, yadātu dhātunāyutto pati, tadā tenā-yogā sambandhe chaṭṭhīva ‘tassa nappaṭibhātī’ti. Akkhe dibbati, akkhehi dibbati, akkhesu dibbatīti kammakaraṇādhikaraṇavacanicchā.

Similarly, with the verb vasati (to live) preceded by upa, anu, adhi, and ā, when it does not mean 'to fast,' the accusative is used: 'He lives near the village' (gāmam upavasati); 'He lives along the village' (gāmam anuvasati); 'He dwells on the mountain' (pabbatam adhivāsati); 'He inhabits the house' (gharam āvasati). What is the point of stating 'when it does not mean abstention from food'? When it does mean fasting, the locative is used: Gāme upavasati, which means 'he fasts in the village.' The accusative may also be used idiomatically, as in 'he drinks the river' or 'he walks to the village,' and similarly in expressions like 'if he will address me.' The accusative is prescribed in connection with pati as a separate word: 'May the factors of enlightenment occur to you, Cunda.' The meaning is, 'May the factors of enlightenment speak to you.' But when pati is joined with a verbal root, the genitive is used in the sense of relation: 'It does not occur to him.' 'He plays dice' (accusative), 'he plays with dice' (instrumental), 'he plays at dice' (locative)—this shows the speaker's wish to express the sense of object, instrument, or location.

3. Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge.

3. For time and distance in continuous connection.

Kiriyā, guṇa, dabbehi sākallena kāladdhānaṃ sambandho accantasaṃyogo. Tasmiṃ viññāyamāne kālasaddehi addhaaddehi ca dutiyā hoti. Māsamadhīte, māsaṃ kalyāṇi, māsaṃ [M 0.0069] guḷadhānā, kosamadhīte, kosaṃ kuṭilā nadī, kosaṃ pabbato. Acantasaṃyogeti kiṃ? Māsassa dvīhamadhīte, kosassekadese pabbato.

'Continuous connection' is the complete connection of time and distance with an action, quality, or substance. When this is understood, the accusative is used with words denoting time and distance. For example: 'He studies for a month'; 'She is beautiful for a month'; 'Molasses and grain for a month'; 'He studies for a kosa'; 'The river is crooked for a kosa'; 'The mountain stretches for a kosa.' What is the point of specifying 'continuous connection'? To show that when the connection is not continuous, another case is used: 'He studies for two days of the month' (genitive); 'The mountain is in one part of the kosa' (genitive).

Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā, imaṃ rattiṃ cattāro mahārājāti evamādīsu kālavācī hi accantasaṃyogattāva dutiyā siddhā. Vibhattivipallāsenapi vā bahulaṃvidhānā.

In expressions such as 'Having dressed in the morning,' 'At one time the Blessed One,' and 'This night the Four Great Kings,' the accusative is established for words expressing time precisely because of continuous connection. Or, it is because of the frequent provision for the interchange of cases.

Phalappattiyaṃ kiriyāparisamattyapavaggo, tasmiṃ viññāyamāne kāladdhānaṃ kiriyāyāccantasaṃyoge tatiyābhimatā, sāpi karaṇattāva siddhā ‘māsenānuvāko-dhīto, kosenānuvāko-dhīto’ti. Anapavaggetu asādhakatamattākaraṇattābhāve dutiyāva ‘māsamadhīto-nuvāko, na cāne na gahito’ti.

Apavagga means the completion of an action with the attainment of its result. When this is understood, the instrumental case is preferred for words of time and distance in continuous connection with an action, and this is established because of instrumentality. For example: 'The section was learned in a month'; 'The section was learned over a kosa.' But when there is no such completion, because it is not the most effective means and thus lacks instrumentality, only the accusative is used: 'He studied the section for a month, but did not grasp it.'

Kārakamajjhe ye kāladdhānavācino, tato sattamīpañcamiyo abhimatā ‘ajja bhutvā devadatto dvihe bhuñjissati, dvīhā bhuñjissati, atraṭṭho-yamissāso kose lakkhaṃ vijjhati, kosā lakkhaṃ vijjhatī’ti, tāpīha sakasakakārakavacanicchāyeva siddhā.

From words expressing time and distance that are within the scope of a grammatical function, the locative and ablative are preferred. For example: 'Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat in two days' (locative), or 'after two days' (ablative). 'This archer, standing here, shoots the target at a kosa's distance' (locative), or 'from a kosa's distance' (ablative). Here too, these cases are established simply by the speaker's wish to express their respective grammatical functions.

4. Gati bodhāhāra saddatthākammaka bhajjādīnaṃ payojje.

4. In the causative of verbs with the meaning of motion, understanding, eating, making a sound, intransitive verbs, and verbs such as 'to break'.

Gamanatthānaṃ bodhatthānaṃ āhāratthānaṃ saddatthānamakammakānaṃ bhajjādīnañca payojje kattari dutiyā hoti. Sāmatthiyā ca payojakabyāpārena kammatāvassa hotīti patīyate. Gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ, yāpayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ, bodhayati māṇavakaṃ dhammaṃ, vedayati māṇavakaṃ dhammaṃ, bhojayati māṇa-vakaṃ [M 0.0070] modakaṃ, āsayati māṇavakaṃ modakaṃ, ajjhāpayati māṇavakaṃ vedaṃ, pāṭhayati māṇavakaṃ vedaṃ, āsayati devadattaṃ, sāyayati devadattaṃ, aññaṃ bhajjāpeti, aññaṃ koṭṭāpeti, aññaṃ santharāpeti. Etesamevāti kiṃ? Pāceti odanaṃ devadattena yaññadatto. Payojjeti kiṃ? Gacchati devadatto. Yadā carahi gamayati devadattaṃ yaññadatto, tamaparo payojeti, tadā gamayati devadattaṃ yaññadatteneti bhavitabbaṃ … gamayatissā-gamanatthattā.

In the causative, the accusative is used for the original agent of verbs with the meaning of going, understanding, eating, making a sound, intransitive verbs, and verbs such as 'to break.' And it is understood that by the power of the instigating agent's action, the original agent acquires the status of an object. For example: 'He makes the young man go to the village'; 'He makes the young man understand the Dhamma'; 'He feeds the young man sweets'; 'He makes the young man recite the Veda'; 'He makes Devadatta sit'; 'He makes Devadatta lie down'; 'He has another break something'; 'He has another pound something'; 'He has another spread something.' What is the point of specifying 'of these only'? To exclude other verbs, e.g., 'Yaññadatta has Devadatta cook rice' (instrumental). What is the point of specifying 'in the causative'? To exclude the simple verb: 'Devadatta goes' (nominative). But when another causes Yaññadatta, who is causing Devadatta to go, then it should be 'he causes Devadatta to go by means of Yaññadatta,' because the verb gamayati (to cause to go) itself does not have the meaning of going.

5. Harādīnaṃ vā.

5. Optionally for harati and other verbs.

Harādīnaṃ payojje kattari dutiyā hoti vā. Hāreti bhāraṃ devadattaṃ devadatteneti vā, ajjhohāreti sattuṃ devadattaṃ devadatteneti vā, kāreti kaṭaṃ devadattaṃ devadatteneti vā dassayate janaṃ rājaṃ janeneti vā, abhivādayate guruṃ devadattaṃ devadatteneti vā.

In the causative of harati (to carry) and other verbs, the accusative is used for the original agent optionally. For example: 'He has Devadatta carry the burden' or 'has the burden carried by Devadatta'; 'He has Devadatta swallow flour' or 'has flour swallowed by Devadatta'; 'He has Devadatta make a mat' or 'has a mat made by Devadatta'; 'He has the people see the king' or 'has the king seen by the people'; 'He has Devadatta pay respect to the teacher' or 'has respect paid to the teacher by Devadatta.'

6. Na khādādīnaṃ.

6. Not for khādati and other verbs.

Khādādīnaṃ payojje kattari dutiyā na hoti. Khādayati devadattena, ādayati devadattena, avha, payati devadattena, saddāyayati devadattena, kandayati devadattena, nāyayati devadattena.

In the causative of khādati (to eat) and other verbs, the accusative is not used for the original agent. For example: 'He has [it] eaten by Devadatta'; 'He has [it] taken by Devadatta'; 'He has [someone] called by Devadatta'; 'He has a sound made by Devadatta'; 'He has crying done by Devadatta'; 'He has leading done by Devadatta.'

(1) Vahissāniyantuke. Vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattena aniyantuketi kiṃ? Vāha-yati bhāraṃ balībadde.

For `vah` (to carry), when the agent is not the controller. The instrumental is used when the agent is a controller, e.g., 'He has the load carried by Devadatta.' What is the point of specifying 'when not the controller'? To provide for the accusative case when the agent is not a controller, e.g., 'He makes the oxen carry the load'.

(2) Bhakkhissāhiṃ [M 0.0071] sāyaṃ. Bhakkhayati modake devadattena. Ahiṃsāyanti kiṃ? Bhakkhayati balībadde sassaṃ.

For bhakkhati (to eat), when it does not mean 'to destroy,' the instrumental is used for the agent. For example: 'He has sweets eaten by Devadatta.' What is the point of specifying 'when it does not mean destroying'? To show that when it does, the accusative is used: 'He has the crops eaten (destroyed) by the oxen.'

7. Jhādīhi yuttā.

7. In connection with dhi, etc.

Dhīādīhi yuttato dutiyā hoti. Dhiratthu maṃ pūtikāyaṃ, antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nālandaṃ, samādhānamantarena, mucalindamabhito saramiccādi, chaṭṭhiyāpavādo-yaṃ.

The accusative is used in connection with dhi and other words. For example: 'Shame on me, this foul body!'; 'between Rājagaha and Nālanda'; 'without concentration'; 'the lake around Mucalinda,' etc. This is an exception to the genitive case.

8. Lakkhaṇitthambhūtavicchāsvabhinā.

8. With abhi in the senses of a mark, a state, and part-by-part.

Lakkhaṇādīsvatthesvabhinā yuttamhā dutiyā mahāti. Rukkhamabhi vijjotate vijju, sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi, rukkhaṃ rukkhamabhitiṭṭhati.

The accusative is used with what is connected with abhi in the meanings of 'mark,' etc. For example: 'Lightning flashes towards the tree' (mark); 'Devadatta is good towards his mother' (state); 'He stands by tree after tree' (part-by-part).

9. Patiparīhi bhāge ca.

9. With pati and pari, and also in the sense of 'share'.

Patiparīhi yuttamhā lakkhaṇādīsu bhāge catthe dutiyā hoti. Rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate vijju, sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pati, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati tiṭṭhati, yadettha maṃ pati siyā. Rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijju, sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pari, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari tiṭṭhati, yadettha maṃ pari siyā.

The accusative is used with what is connected with pati and pari in the meanings of 'mark,' etc., and also in the meaning of 'share.' For example: 'Lightning flashes towards the tree'; 'Devadatta is good towards his mother'; 'He stands by tree after tree'; 'Whatever share would fall to me here.' Also: 'Lightning flashes around the tree'; 'Devadatta is good towards his mother'; 'He stands by tree after tree'; 'Whatever share would fall to me here.'

10. Anunā.

10. With anu.

Lakkhaṇādīsvatthesvanunā yuttamhā dutiyā hoti. Rukkhamanu vijjotate vijju, saccakiriyamanu vuṭṭhi pāvassi, hetu ca lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, sādhu devadatto mātaramanu, rukkhaṃ rukkhamanu tiṭṭhati, yadettha maṃ anu siyā.

The accusative is used with what is connected with anu in the meanings of 'mark,' etc. For example: 'Lightning flashes along the tree'; 'Rain fell in consequence of the act of truth,' for a cause is also a mark; 'Devadatta is good towards his mother'; 'He stands by tree after tree'; 'Whatever share would fall to me here.'

11. Sahatthe.

11. In the sense of 'with.'

Sahatthe-nunā [M 0.0072] yuttamhā dutiyā hoti. Pabbatamanu senā tiṭṭhati.

The accusative is used with what is connected with anu in the sense of 'with.' For example: 'The army is situated along the mountain.'

12. Hīne.

12. In the sense of 'inferior.'

Hīnatthe-nunā yuttamhā dutiyā hoti. Anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto.

The accusative is used with what is connected with anu in the sense of 'inferior.' For example: 'The wise are inferior to Sāriputta.'

13. Upena.

13. With upa.

Hīnatthe upena yuttamhā dutiyā hoti. Upa sāriputtaṃ paññavantho.

The accusative is used with what is connected with upa in the sense of 'inferior.' For example: 'The wise are inferior to Sāriputta.'

14. Sattamyādhikye.

14. In the sense of 'superiority,' the locative.

Ādhikyatthe upena yuttamhā sattamī hoti. Upa khāriyaṃ doṇo.

The locative is used with what is connected with upa in the sense of 'superiority.' For example: 'A doṇa is less than a khārī.'

15. Sāmitte-dhinā.

15. With adhi in the sense of 'lordship.'

Sāmibhāvatthe-dhinā yuttamhā sattamī hoti. Adhi brahmadatte pañcālā, adhi pañcālesu brahmadatto.

The locative is used with what is connected with adhi in the sense of 'lordship.' For example: 'The Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta' or 'Brahmadatta is lord over the Pañcālas.'

16. Kattukareṇesu tatiyā.

16. The instrumental is used for the agent and instrument.

Kattari karaṇe ca kārake tatiyā hoti. Purisena kataṃ, asinā chindati. Pakatiyā-bhirūpo, gotthena gotamo, sumedho nāma nāmena, jātiyā sattavassikoti bhūdhātussa sambhavā karaṇe eva tatiyā. Evaṃ samena dhāvati visamena [M 0.0073] dhāvati, dvidoṇena dhaññaṃ kiṇāti, pañcakena pasavo kiṇātīti.

The instrumental case is used for the grammatical functions of agent and instrument. For example: 'Done by a man'; 'He cuts with a sword.' Also: 'Handsome by nature'; 'Gotama by clan'; 'Sumedha by name'; 'seven years old by birth'—due to the presence of the root 'bhū' (to be), the instrumental is indeed in the sense of instrument. Similarly: 'He runs evenly'; 'He runs unevenly'; 'He buys grain for two doṇas'; 'He buys cattle for five pieces.'

17. Sahatthena.

17. In the sense of 'with.'

Sahatthena yoge tatiyā siyā. Puttena saha gato, puttena saddhiṃ āgato, tatiyāpi chaṭṭhīva appadhāne eva bhavati.

In connection with saha and its synonyms, the third case is used. For example: 'He went with his son'; 'he came with his son.' The third case, like the sixth, is used with the subordinate noun.

18. Lakkhaṇe.

18. In the sense of a characteristic.

Lakkhaṇe vattamānato tatiyā siyā. Tidaṇḍakena paribbājakamaddakkhī, akkhinā kāṇo, tena hi aṅgena aṅgino vikāro lakkhīyate.

When denoting a characteristic, the third case is used. For example: 'He saw the wandering ascetic by his triple staff'; 'blind in one eye.' For by that limb, a defect in the one who possesses the limb is indicated.

19. Hetumhi.

19. In the sense of cause.

Takkiriyā yogge tatiyā siyā. Annena vasati, vijjāya yaso.

In the sense of cause, the third case is used. For example: 'He lives by means of food'; 'fame because of knowledge.'

20. Pañcamīṇe vā.

20. Or the fifth case in the sense of debt.

Iṇe hetumhi pañcamī hoti vā. Satasmā baddho, satena vā.

In the sense of debt as a cause, the fifth case is used optionally. For example: 'Bound for a debt of a hundred,' or 'by a hundred.'

21. Guṇe.

21. In the sense of a quality.

Paraṅgabhūte hetumhi pañcamī hoti vā. Jaḷattā baddho jaḷattena vā, paññāya mutto, hutvā abhāvatoaniccā, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho.

When the cause is an attribute, the fifth case is used optionally. For example: 'Bound because of dullness,' or 'by dullness'; 'freed by wisdom'; '[formations are] impermanent because they cease to be after having been'; 'from the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness.'

22. Chaṭṭhī [M 0.0074] hetvatthehi.

22. The sixth case with words meaning cause.

Hetvatthavācīhi yoge hetumhi chaṭṭhī siyā. Udarassa hetu, udarassa kāraṇā.

In connection with words expressing the meaning of cause, the sixth case is used for the cause. For example: 'For the sake of the belly'; 'for the reason of the belly.'

23. Sabbādito sabbā.

23. From sabba and so on, all cases.

Hetvatthehi yoge sabbādīhi sabbā vibhattiyo honti. Ko hetu, kaṃ hetuṃ, kena hetunā, kassa hetussa, kasmā hetusmā, kassa hetussa, kasmiṃ hetusmiṃ, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ, kena kāraṇena, kiṃ nimittaṃ, kena nimittena, kiṃ payojanaṃ, kena payojanena iccevamādi. Hetvatthehītveva? Kena kataṃ.

In connection with words meaning cause, all case endings are used with the pronoun sabba and others. For example: 'What is the cause?,' 'for what cause?,' 'by what cause?,' 'of what cause?,' 'from what cause?,' 'of what cause?,' 'in what cause?'; 'what is the reason?,' 'by what reason?'; 'what is the sign?,' 'by what sign?'; 'what is the purpose?,' 'by what purpose?,' and so on. Is this only with words meaning cause? [No, for example:] 'By whom was it done?'

24. Catutthī sampadāne.

24. The fourth case in the sense of the recipient.

Yassa sammā padīyate tasmiṃ catutthī siyā. Saṅghassa dadāti. Ādhāravivakkhāyaṃ sattamīpi siyā saṅghe dehi.

The fourth case is used for one to whom something is properly given. For example: 'He gives to the Sangha' (saṅghassa dadāti). When wishing to express the sense of a location, the seventh case may also be used: 'Give to the Sangha' (saṅghe dehi).

25. Tādatthye.

25. In the sense of 'for that purpose'.

Tasse-daṃ tadatthaṃ, tadatthabhāve jotanīye nāmasmā catutthī siyā. Sītassa paṭighātāya, atthāya hitāya (sukhāya) devamanussānaṃ, nālaṃ dārabharaṇāya, yūpāya dāru, pākāya vajatītvevamādi.

`Tadattham` means 'this is for that.' To express the state of being for that purpose, the fourth case is used after a noun. For example: 'for warding off the cold' (sītassa paṭighātāya); 'for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans' (atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ); 'not adequate for supporting a wife' (nālaṃ dārabharaṇāya); 'wood for a sacrificial post' (yūpāya dāru); 'he goes for the purpose of cooking' (pākāya vajati), and so on.

Kassa sāduṃ na ruccabhi, mā-yasmantānampi saṅghabhedo ruccittha, khamati saṅghassa, bhattamassa nacchādesīti chaṭṭhī sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ, na cevaṃ virodho siyā sadisarūpattā, evaṃvidhesu ca sambandhassa saddikānumatattā[M 0.0075], kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesīti atthamatte paṭhamā.

'To whom is it not pleasing?' (kassa sāduṃ na ruccabhi); 'May schism in the Sangha not be pleasing even to the venerable ones' (māyasmantānampi saṅghabhedo ruccittha); 'It is acceptable to the Sangha' (khamati saṅghassa); 'The meal did not satisfy him' (bhattamassa nacchādesi). Here the sixth case is used when wishing to express relation, and there is no contradiction because of the similarity in form. In such cases, the use of the genitive for relation is approved by grammarians. In 'Whose Dhamma do you approve of?' (kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesi), the nominative is used for the bare meaning.

Evamaññāpi vidhaññayyā, paratopi yathāgamaṃ.

Thus other usages should also be known, and from other sources according to the tradition.

Rañño sataṃ dhāreti, rañño chattaṃ dhāretīti sambandhe chaṭṭhī, evaṃ rañño silāghate, rañño hanute, rañño upatiṭṭhate, rañño sapate, devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino, tassa kujjha mahāvīra, yadihaṃ tassa pakuppeyyaṃ, duhayati disānaṃ megho, yo mittānaṃ na dūbhati, yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati, kyāhaṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi, issayanti samaṇānaṃ titthiyā, dhammena nayamānānaṃ kā usūyā rañño bhāgyamārajjhati, rañño bhāgyamikkhate, tena yācito ayācito vā tassa gāvo paṭisuṇāti, gāvo āsuṇāti, bhagavato paccassosuṃ, hotu patigiṇāti, hotvanugiṇāti, ārocayāmi vo pativedayāmi vo, dhammaṃ te desessāmi, yathā vo bhagavā byākareyya, alaṃ te idha vāsena, kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, arahati mallo mallassāti.

'He owes the king a hundred' (rañño sataṃ dhāreti); 'he holds the king’s umbrella' (rañño chattaṃ dhāreti)—in these, the sixth case denotes relation. Similarly: 'he praises the king' (rañño silāghate); 'he conceals from the king' (rañño hanute); 'he attends upon the king' (rañño upatiṭṭhate); 'he swears to the king' (rañño sapate); 'even the gods envy him, the Such-like One' (devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino); 'be angry with him, O great hero' (tassa kujjha mahāvīra); 'if I were to be angry with him' (yadihaṃ tassa pakuppeyyaṃ); 'the cloud is hostile to the directions' (duhayati disānaṃ megho); 'who is not treacherous to his friends' (yo mittānaṃ na dūbhati); 'who offends an uncorrupted person' (yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati); 'how have I offended the noble sirs?' (kyāhaṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi); 'the sectarians are jealous of the ascetics' (issayanti samaṇānaṃ titthiyā); 'what envy is there for those who are led by the Dhamma?' (dhammena nayamānānaṃ kā usūyā); 'he covets the king’s fortune' (rañño bhāgyamārajjhati); 'he looks upon the king’s fortune' (rañño bhāgyamikkhate); 'whether asked by him or not, he promises him cows' (tena yācito ayācito vā tassa gāvo paṭisuṇāti); 'he listens to him about the cows' (gāvo āsuṇāti); 'they responded to the Blessed One' (bhagavato paccassosuṃ); 'he accepts, saying, “So be it”' (hotu patigiṇāti); 'he approves, saying, “So be it”' (hotvanugiṇāti); 'I announce to you, I declare to you' (ārocayāmi vo pativedayāmi vo); 'I will teach you the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ te desessāmi); 'as the Blessed One would explain to you' (yathā vo bhagavā byākareyya); 'enough of this living here for you' (alaṃ te idha vāsena); 'what use are your matted locks to you, you fool?' (kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha); 'a wrestler is a match for a wrestler' (arahati mallo mallassāti).

Jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññamānoti tādatthya catutthī, tiṇena yo attho tadatthāyapīti attho, “yo ca sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati” tiṇamiva jīvitaṃ maññamānoti savisayāva vibhattiyo. Saggāya gacchatīti tādatthye catutthī, yo hi saggaṃ gacchati tadatthaṃ tassa gamananti, kammavacanicchāyantu dutiyāva saggaṃ gacchatīti.

In 'not considering life to be worth even a blade of grass' (jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññamāno), the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose; the meaning is 'not even for the purpose that grass serves.' In the quote, 'He who considers cold and heat to be no more than grass' (yo ca sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati), and in 'considering life like grass' (tiṇamiva jīvitaṃ maññamāno), the case endings are each used in their proper sphere. In 'he goes for heaven' (saggāya gacchati), the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose, for he who goes to heaven, his going is for that purpose. But when wishing to express it as the object of the action, the second case is used: 'he goes to heaven' (saggaṃ gacchati).

Āyu [M 0.0076] bhoto hotu, ciraṃ jīvitaṃ, bhaddaṃ kalyāṇaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ, kusalaṃ anāmayaṃ, hitaṃ pathyaṃ sukhaṃ sātaṃ bhoto hotu, sādhu sammuti metassa, puttassāvikareyya guyhamatthaṃ, tassa me sakko pāturahosi, tassa pahiṇeyya, bhikkhūnaṃ dutaṃ pāhesi, kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo, ekassa dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā pahoti, upamaṃ te karissāmi, añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi, tassa phāsu, lokassattho, namo te purisājañña, sotthi tassa, alaṃ mallo mallassa, samattho mallo mallassa, tassa hitaṃ, tassa sukhaṃ, svāgataṃ te mahārājāti sabbattha chaṭṭhī sambandhe, evaṃvidhamaññampeva viññeyyaṃ yathāgamaṃ.

'May there be long life for the venerable one' (āyu bhoto hotu); 'long life' (ciraṃ jīvitaṃ); 'may there be good, fortune, benefit, purpose, what is wholesome, health, welfare, what is suitable, happiness, and pleasure for the venerable one' (bhaddaṃ kalyāṇaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ, kusalaṃ anāmayaṃ, hitaṃ pathyaṃ sukhaṃ sātaṃ bhoto hotu); 'may this be well agreed for him' (sādhu sammuti metassa); 'he should reveal the secret matter to his son' (puttassāvikareyya guyhamatthaṃ); 'Sakka appeared to me' (tassa me sakko pāturahosi); 'one should send to him' (tassa pahiṇeyya); 'he sent a messenger to the bhikkhus' (bhikkhūnaṃ dutaṃ pāhesi); 'striving is fitting for ascetics' (kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo); 'it is sufficient for one, two, or three' (ekassa dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā pahoti); 'I will make a comparison for you' (upamaṃ te karissāmi); 'I raise my cupped hands in reverence to you' (añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi); 'may he be comfortable' (tassa phāsu); 'for the welfare of the world' (lokassattho); 'homage to you, O thoroughbred of men' (namo te purisājañña); 'well-being to him' (sotthi tassa); 'a wrestler is a match for a wrestler' (alaṃ mallo mallassa); 'a wrestler is capable against a wrestler' (samattho mallo mallassa); 'welfare for him' (tassa hitaṃ); 'happiness for him' (tassa sukhaṃ); 'welcome to you, O great king' (svāgataṃ te mahārāja). In all these, the sixth case is in the sense of relation. Other such examples should also be understood according to the tradition.

26. Pañcamyavadhismā.

26. The fifth case from a boundary.

Padatthāvadhismā pañcamīvibhatti hoti. Gāmasmā āgacchatu, evaṃ corasmā bhāyati, corasmā uttasati, orasmā tāyati, corasmā rakkhatīti, sace bhāyatha dukkhassa, pamāde bhayadassivā, tasanti daṇḍassāti chaṭṭhī sattamiyopi honteva sambandhādhāravacanicchāyaṃ.

The fifth case ending is used to denote a boundary from which something proceeds. For example: 'Let him come from the village' (gāmasmā āgacchatu). Similarly with verbs of fearing and protecting: 'he fears the thief' (corasmā bhāyati); 'he is terrified of the thief' (corasmā uttasati); 'he protects from the thief' (corasmā tāyati); 'he guards from the thief' (corasmā rakkhati). In 'if you fear suffering' (sace bhāyatha dukkhassa), 'seeing fear in negligence' (pamāde bhayadassivā), and 'they are terrified of the stick' (tasanti daṇḍassā), the sixth and seventh cases also occur when wishing to express relation or location.

Ajjhenā parājeti, paṭipakkhe parājetīti savisayāva vibhattiyo. Sace kevaṭṭassa parajjissāmīti chaṭṭhīpi hoti sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ. Yavehi gāvo vāreti, pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye, kāke rakkhati taṇḍulāti savisayeva pañcamī. Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvīti dutiyāva dissati kammatthe. Upajjhāyā antaradhāyati[M 0.0077], upajjhāyā adhite, kāmato jāyate sokoti savisaye pañcamī.

In 'he is overcome by study' (ajjhenā parājeti) and 'he defeats his opponent' (paṭipakkhe parājeti), the case endings are each in their own sphere. In 'if I am defeated by the fisherman' (sace kevaṭṭassa parajjissāmi), the sixth case also occurs when wishing to express relation. In 'he keeps the cows from the barley' (yavehi gāvo vāreti), 'one should restrain the mind from evil' (pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye), and 'he protects the rice from the crows' (kāke rakkhati taṇḍulā), the fifth case is in its own sphere. In 'the wise one should guard the mind' (cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī), the second case is seen in the sense of the object. In 'he hides from the preceptor' (upajjhāyā antaradhāyati), 'he learns from the preceptor' (upajjhāyā adhite), and 'from desire, sorrow is born' (kāmato jāyate soko), the fifth case is in its own sphere.

Tattheva-ntaradhāyi su, naṭassa suṇoti, padumaṃ tattha jāyethāti sattamīchaṭṭhiyopi honteva savisaye. Himavantā pabhavati gaṅgā, pāṇātipātā viramassu khippaṃ, añño devadattā, bhinno devadattāti savisayeva pañcamī. Evaṃ ārā so āsavakkhayā, itaro devadattā, uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā, pubbo gāmā, pubbeva sambodhā, tato paraṃ, tato aparena samayena, tatuttarinti. Sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ chaṭṭhīpi purato gāmassa, dakkhiṇato gāmassa, upari pabbatassa, heṭṭhā pāsādassāti. Pāsādamāruyha pekkhati pāsādā pekkhati, āsane upavisitvā pekkhati āsanā pekkhatīti avadhivacanicchāyaṃ pañcamī.

'He disappeared right there' (tatthevantaradhāyi su); 'he listens to the actor' (naṭassa suṇoti); 'a lotus might grow there' (padumaṃ tattha jāyetha)—here the seventh and sixth cases also occur, each in its own sphere. 'The Ganges originates from the Himalayas' (himavantā pabhavati gaṅgā); 'abstain quickly from killing living beings' (pāṇātipātā viramassu khippaṃ); 'other than Devadatta' (añño devadattā); 'different from Devadatta' (bhinno devadattā)—in these the fifth case is in its own sphere. Similarly: 'he is far from the destruction of the taints' (ārā so āsavakkhayā); 'other than Devadatta' (itaro devadattā); 'up from the soles of the feet, down from the top of the hair' (uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā); 'east of the village' (pubbo gāmā); 'before enlightenment' (pubbeva sambodhā); 'after that' (tato paraṃ); 'at a later time' (tato aparena samayena); 'beyond that' (tatuttariṃ). When wishing to express relation, the sixth case is also used: 'in front of the village' (purato gāmassa); 'south of the village' (dakkhiṇato gāmassa); 'above the mountain' (upari pabbatassa); 'below the palace' (heṭṭhā pāsādassā). 'Having ascended the palace, he looks' is equivalent to 'he looks from the palace'; 'having sat on the seat, he looks' is equivalent to 'he looks from the seat'—when wishing to express the boundary, the fifth case is used.

Pucchānākhyānesu kuto bhavaṃ? Pātaṭaliputtasmāti. Tathā desakālamānepi pāṭaliputtasmā rājagahaṃ satta yojanāni, sattasu yojanesūti vā. Evaṃ ito tiṇṇaṃ māsāna-maccayenāti, kicchāladdhanti guṇe pañcamī. Kicchena me adhigatanti hetumhi karaṇe vā tatiyā. Evaṃ thokā mutto, thokena muttoti. Thokaṃ calatīti kiriyāvisesane kammani dutiyā.

In questions and answers: 'Where are you from, venerable sir?' (kuto bhavaṃ?) 'From Pāṭaliputta' (pāṭaliputtasmā). Similarly in measuring space and time: 'From Pāṭaliputta to Rājagaha is seven yojanas' (pāṭaliputtasmā rājagahaṃ satta yojanāni), or 'at seven yojanas' (sattasu yojanesu). Similarly: 'after the passing of three months from now' (ito tiṇṇaṃ māsānamaccayena). In 'obtained with difficulty' (kicchā laddhaṃ), the fifth case is in the sense of a quality. In 'by me it was attained with difficulty' (kicchena me adhigataṃ), the third case is in the sense of cause or instrument. Similarly, 'narrowly escaped' (thokā mutto), or 'escaped by a little' (thokena mutto). In 'it moves a little' (thokaṃ calati), the second case is an adverbial accusative.

Dūranti katthayogepi savisayeva pañcamīchaṭṭhiyo siyuṃ, dūraṃ gāmasmā, antikaṃ gāmasmā, dūraṃ gāmassa, antikaṃ gāmassāti, dūranti katthehi tu sabbāva savisaye siyuṃ bādhakābhāvā dūro gāmo, antiko gāmotvevamādi.

In connection with words meaning 'far' and 'near', the fifth and sixth cases are used, each in its own sphere: 'far from the village' (dūraṃ gāmasmā); 'near the village' (antikaṃ gāmasmā); 'far from the village' (dūraṃ gāmassa); 'near the village' (antikaṃ gāmassa). But when these words are used as predicates, all cases may be used in their own sphere as there is no contradiction: 'the village is far' (dūro gāmo); 'the village is near' (antiko gāmo), and so on.

Keci [M 0.0078] panāhu ‘asattavacanahetehi pāṭipadikatthe dutiyātatiyāpañcamīsattamiyo, sattavacanehi tu sabbāva savisaye’ti, te panaññeheva paṭikkhittā. Dūraṃ maggo, antikaṃ maggoti kiriyāvisesanaṃ… bhūdhātussa gammamānattā. Visuddho lobhanīyehi dhammehi, parimutto so dukkhasmā vivicceva kāmehi, gambhīrato ca puthulato ca yojanaṃ, āyāmena yojanaṃ, tato pabhuti, yato sarāmi attānanti savisayeva vibhattiyo.

Some, however, say: 'With words that are not substantives, the second, third, fifth, and seventh cases are used in the meaning of the nominal stem; but with substantives, all cases are used, each in its own sphere.' This view, however, has been rejected by others. In 'the path is far' (dūraṃ maggo) and 'the path is near' (antikaṃ maggo), the usage is adverbial, because the verb root bhū (to be) is understood. 'Purified from alluring things' (visuddho lobhanīyehi dhammehi); 'he is freed from suffering' (parimutto so dukkhasmā); 'secluded from sensual pleasures' (vivicceva kāmehi); 'a yojana in depth and in breadth' (gambhīrato ca puthulato ca yojanaṃ); 'a yojana in length' (āyāmena yojanaṃ); 'from then on' (tato pabhuti); 'since I remember myself' (yato sarāmi attānaṃ)—in these, the case endings are each in their own sphere.

27. Apaparīhi vajjane.

27. With apa and pari in the sense of avoidance.

Vajjane vattamānehi apaparīhi yoge pañcamī hoti. Apa sālāya āyanti vāṇijā, pari sālāya āyanti vāṇijā, sālaṃ vajjetvāti attho. Vajjaneti kiṃ? Rukkhaṃ parivijjotate vijju. Āpāṭaliputtasmā vassi devoti mariyādā-bhividhīsvavadhi visayeva pañcamī, vinā pāṭaliputtena saha veti viseso, evaṃ yāva pāṭaliputtasmā vassi devoti.

In connection with apa and pari when they mean 'avoidance', the fifth case is used. For example: 'Merchants come, avoiding the hall' (apa sālāya āyanti vāṇijā); 'merchants come, avoiding the hall' (pari sālāya āyanti vāṇijā). The meaning is 'having avoided the hall.' Why the specification 'in the sense of avoidance'? [Because when it means something else, another case is used, as in:] 'Lightning flashes around the tree' (rukkhaṃ parivijjotate vijju). In 'it rained up to Pāṭaliputta' (āpāṭaliputtasmā vassi devo), the fifth case is used with the preposition ā in the senses of limit (mariyādā) and inclusion (abhividhi); the distinction is that 'limit' means excluding Pāṭaliputta, while 'inclusion' means including it. It is similar with yāva: 'It rained as far as Pāṭaliputta' (yāva pāṭaliputtasmā vassi devo).

28. Paṭinidhipaṭidānesu patinā.

28. With pati in the senses of substitution and exchange.

Paṭinidhimhi paṭidāne ca vattamānena patinā yoge nāmasmā pañcamī vibhatti hoti. Buddhasmā pati sāriputto, ghatamassa tesasmā pati dadāti, paṭinidhipaṭidānesūti kiṃ? Rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate.

In connection with the word pati when it means substitution or exchange, the fifth case ending is used after a noun. For example: 'Sāriputta in place of the Buddha' (buddhasmā pati sāriputto); 'he gives him ghee in exchange for that' (ghatamassa tesasmā pati dadāti). Why the specification 'in substitution and exchange'? [Because when it means something else, another case is used, as in:] 'Lightning flashes towards the tree' (rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate).

29. Rite dutiyā ca.

29. With rite, and also the second case.

Ritesaddena [M 0.0079] yoge nāmasmā dutiyā hoti pañcamī ca. Rite saddhammaṃ, rite saddhammā.

In connection with the word `rite`, the accusative case is used with a noun, and also the ablative. For example: `rite saddhammaṃ` (without the good Dhamma); `rite saddhammā` (without the good Dhamma).

30. Vinā-ññatra tatiyā ca.

30. With `vinā` and `aññatra`, the instrumental case is also used.

Vinā-ññatrasaddehi yoge nāmasmā tatiyā ca hoti dutiyā pañcamiyo ca. Vinā vātena, vinā vātaṃ, vinā vātasmā, aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena, aññatra dhammaṃ, aññatra dhammā.

In construction with the words `vinā` (without) and `aññatra` (except for), the instrumental, accusative, and ablative cases are used with a noun. For example: `vinā vātena`, `vinā vātaṃ`, `vinā vātasmā` (all meaning 'without wind'); `aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena` (except for one alms-gatherer); `aññatra dhammaṃ`, `aññatra dhammā` (both meaning 'except for the Dhamma').

31. Puthanānāhi.

31. With `putha` and `nānā`.

Etehi yoge tatiyā hoti pañcamī ca. Puthageva janena, puthageva janasmā, janena nānā, janasmā nānā.

In construction with these, the instrumental and ablative cases are used. For example: `puthageva janena` (separate from the people), `puthageva janasmā` (separate from the people); `janena nānā` (different from the people), `janasmā nānā` (different from the people).

32. Sattamyādhāre.

32. The locative case in the sense of location.

Kiriyādhāra bhūta kattu kammānaṃ dhāraṇena yo kiriyāyādhāro tasmiṃ kārake nāmasmā sattamī hoti. Kaṭe nisīdati (devadatto), thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati, ākāse sakunā, bhilesu telaṃ, gaṅgāyaṃ vajo.

The locative case is used for the factor of location, which is the support of an action by containing its agent and object. For example: `Kaṭe nisīdati (devadatto)` (Devadatta sits on a mat); `thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati` (one cooks rice in a pot); `ākāse sakunā` (birds are in the sky); `bhilesu telaṃ` (oil is in cavities); `gaṅgāyaṃ vajo` (a herd is in the Ganges).

33. Nimitte.

33. In the sense of cause.

Nimittatthe sattamī hoti. Ajinamhi haññate dīpi, musāvāde pācitthiyaṃ.

The locative case is used in the sense of a cause or reason. For example: `Ajinamhi haññate dīpi` (a leopard is killed for its hide); `musāvāde pācitthiyaṃ` (for false speech, there is a Pācittiya offense).

34. Yabbhāvobhāvalakkhaṇaṃ.

34. When the state of one thing is the characteristic of another.

Yassa [M 0.0080] bhāvo bhāvantarassa lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, tato sattamī hoti. Gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato. Bhāvoti kiṃ? Yo jaṭāhi so bhuñjati. Bhāvalakkhaṇanti kiṃ? Yo bhuñjati so devadatto, “akāle vassati tassa, tāle tassa na vassatī”ti visayasattamī.

When the state of one thing is the characteristic of another state, the locative case is used for the former. For example: `Gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato` (He went while the cows were being milked); `duddhāsu āgato` (He came when they had been milked). Why the word 'state' (`bhāva`)? Consider: `Yo jaṭāhi so bhuñjati` (He who is distinguished by matted hair, he eats). Why 'characteristic of a state' (`bhāvalakkhaṇa`)? Consider: `Yo bhuñjati so devadatto` (He who is eating is Devadatta). The example, '`akāle vassati tassa, tāle tassa na vassatī`' (It rains for him out of season; it does not rain for him in season), is a locative of sphere.

35. Chaṭṭhī cānādare.

35. And the genitive in the sense of disregard.

Yassa bhāvo bhāvantarassa lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, tato chaṭṭhī bhavati sattamī ca anādare gamyamāne. “Ākoṭayanto so neti, sivirājassa pekkhato”, “maccu gacchati ādāya, pekkhamāne mahājane”.

When the state of one thing is the characteristic of another, the genitive and locative cases are used to express this when disregard is implied. For example: `‘Ākoṭayanto so neti, sivirājassa pekkhato’` (He leads him away, striking him, while King Sivi looks on in disregard); `‘maccu gacchati ādāya, pekkhamāne mahājane’` (Death goes, having taken someone, while the great crowd looks on in disregard).

Gunnaṃ sāmīti sambandhe chaṭṭhī, gosu sāmīti visayasattamī, evaṃ gunnamissaro, gosvissaro, gunnaṃ adhipati, gosu adhipati, gunnaṃ dāyādo, gosu dāhādo, dunnaṃ sakkhi, gosu sakkhi, gunnaṃ patibhū, gosu patibhū, gunnaṃ pasūto, gosu pasūto, kusalā naccagītassa, kusalā naccagīte, āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa, āyutto kaṭakaraṇeti.

`Guṇṇaṃ sāmī` (master of the herd) is genitive in the sense of relation; `gosu sāmī` (master among the cows) is locative in the sense of sphere. Similarly: `guṇṇaṃ issaro` (lord of the herd), `gosvissaro` (lord among the cows); `guṇṇaṃ adhipati` (ruler of the herd), `gosu adhipati` (ruler among the cows); `guṇṇaṃ dāyādo` (heir to the herd), `gosu dāyādo` (heir among the cows); `dunnaṃ sakkhi` (witness for the two), `gosu sakkhi` (witness among the cows); `guṇṇaṃ patibhū` (surety for the herd), `gosu patibhū` (surety among the cows); `guṇṇaṃ pasūto` (produced from the herd), `gosu pasūto` (produced among the cows); `kusalā naccagītassa` (skilled in dance and song), `kusalā naccagīte` (skilled in dance and song); `āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa` (appointed to mat-making), `āyutto kaṭakaraṇe` (appointed in mat-making).

Tathādhāravacanicchāyaṃ sattamī, bhikkhūsu abhivādenti, muddhani dhumbitvā, bāhāsu gahetvā, hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti, pathesu gacchanti, kadalīsu gaje rakkhantīti. Ñāṇasmiṃ pasannoti visayasattamī, ñāṇena pasannoti karaṇe tatiyā, evaṃ ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko ñāṇena ussukkoti.

Similarly, the locative is used when wishing to express location. For example: `bhikkhūsu abhivādenti` (they pay respect to the monks); `muddhani dhumbitvā` (having kissed on the head); `bāhāsu gahetvā` (having taken by the arms); `hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti` (they wander for alms with bowls in hand); `pathesu gacchanti` (they go on the paths); `kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti` (they protect elephants in the plantain groves). `Ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno` (confident in knowledge) is a locative of sphere, whereas `ñāṇena pasanno` (confident by means of knowledge) is an instrumental of means. Similarly, `ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko` (zealous for knowledge) and `ñāṇena ussukko` (zealous through knowledge).

36. Yato niddhāraṇaṃ.

36. Specification from a group.

Jātiguṇakiriyāhi [M 0.0081] samudāyatekadesassa puthakkaraṇaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ. Yato taṃ karīyati, tato chaṭṭhīsattamiyo honti. Sālayo sūkadhaññānaṃ pathyatamā, sālayo sūkadhaññesu pathyatamā, kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā, kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā, gacchataṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo, gacchantesu dhāvanto sīghatamo. Sīlameva sutā seyyoti avadhimhiyeva pañcamī.

Specification is the separation of one part from a group on the basis of class, quality, or action. The genitive and locative cases are used for the group from which the specification is made. For example: `Sālayo sūkadhaññānaṃ pathyatamā` or `sālayo sūkadhaññesu pathyatamā` (rice is the most wholesome of awned grains); `kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā` or `kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā` (the black cow is the most rich in milk of all cows); `gacchataṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo` or `gacchantesu dhāvanto sīghatamo` (of those who are going, the one running is the swiftest). In the phrase `Sīlameva sutā seyyo` (Virtue is indeed better than learning), the ablative is used in the sense of a standard of comparison.

37. Paṭhamātthamatte.

37. The nominative in the sense of the mere stem-meaning.

Nāmassābhidheyyamatte paṭhamāvibhatti hoti. Rukkho. Itthi pumā napuṃsakanti liṅgampi saddatthova, tathā doṇo khārī āḷhakanti parimāṇampi saddatthova, eko dve bahavoti saṅkhyāpi saddatthova.

The nominative case is used to express only the meaning of the nominal stem. For example: `Rukkho` (a tree). Gender—feminine, masculine, and neuter—is also simply the meaning of the word; likewise measure—such as `doṇa`, `khārī`, and `āḷhaka`—is also simply the meaning of the word; and number—such as one, two, and many—is also simply the meaning of the word.

38. Āmantaṇe.

38. In the sense of address.

Sato saddenābhimukhīkaraṇamāmantaṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ visaye paṭhamā vibhatti hoti. Bhopurisa, bhokkatthi, bho napuṃsaka.

Address (`āmantaṇa`) is the act of directing someone who is present towards oneself by means of a word. In this sense, the nominative case is used. For example: `Bho purisa` (O man), `bho katthī` (O braggart), `bho napuṃsaka` (O neuter one).

39. Chaṭṭhī sambandhe.

39. The genitive in the sense of relation.

Kiriyākārakasañjāto assedambhāvahetuko sambandho nāma. Tasmiṃ chaṭṭhī vibhatti hoti. Rañño puriso, sarati rajjassāti sambandhe chaṭṭhī, rajjasambandhiniṃ satiṃ karotīti attho, kammavacanicchārantu dutiyāva sarati rajjaṃ. Tathā rajakassa vatthaṃ [M 0.0082] dadāti, paharato piṭṭhiṃ dadāti, bālo pūrati pāpassa, amacce tāta jānāhi, dhīre atthassa kovide, divasassa tikkhattuṃ, sakiṃ pakkhassa, pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa kumbhantvevamādi.

Relation (`sambandha`) is a connection that is not covered by the other factors of action. The genitive case is used in this sense. For example: `Rañño puriso` (the king’s man). In `sarati rajjassa` (he remembers the kingdom), the genitive is used in the sense of relation, meaning 'he performs the act of remembering related to the kingdom.' However, when wishing to express this as a direct object, the accusative is used: `sarati rajjaṃ`. Similarly: `rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti` (he gives cloth to the washerman); `paharato piṭṭhiṃ dadāti` (he gives his back to the one who is striking); `bālo pūrati pāpassa` (the fool is full of evil); `dhīre atthassa kovide` (the wise one, skilled in the meaning); `divasassa tikkhattuṃ` (three times a day); `sakiṃ pakkhassa` (once a fortnight); `pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa kumbho` (a pot full of gold and silver), and so on.

Kitakappayoge kaktukammesu bahulaṃ sambandhavacanicchāyaṃ chaṭṭhī, sādhu sammato bahujanassa, suppaṭividdhā buddhānaṃ dhammadhātu, dhammassa gutto medhāvī, amataṃ tesaṃ paribhuttaṃ, tassa bhavanti vattāro, avisaṃvādako lokassa, alajjīnaṃ nissāya, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādotvevamādi.

In construction with participles, the genitive is frequently used for the agent and the object when one wishes to express a relation. For example: `sādhu sammato bahujanassa` (well-regarded by the multitude); `suppaṭividdhā buddhānaṃ dhammadhātu` (the Dhamma-element thoroughly penetrated by the Buddhas); `dhammassa gutto medhāvī` (the wise one, guardian of the Dhamma); `amataṃ tesaṃ paribhuttaṃ` (the deathless has been partaken of by them); `tassa bhavanti vattāro` (there are speakers for him); `avisaṃvādako lokassa` (not deceiving the world); `alajjīnaṃ nissāya` (relying on the shameless); `catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo` (the sensitive matter derived from the four great elements), and so on.

Kattukammavacanicchāyantu tatiyā dutiyāyo ca, sañcatto pitarā ahaṃ, sarasi tvaṃ evarūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā, bhagavantaṃ dassanāyatvevamādi.

However, when wishing to express the agent and object directly, the instrumental and accusative cases are used. For example: `sañcatto pitarā ahaṃ` (I was abandoned by my father); `sarasi tvaṃ evarūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā` (do you remember having spoken such words?); `bhagavantaṃ dassanāya` (for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One), and so on.

40. Tulyatthena vā tatiyā.

40. Or the instrumental with words meaning 'equal'.

Tulyatthena yoge chaṭṭhī hoti tatiyā vā, tulyo pitu, tulyo pitarā, sadiso pitu, sadiso pitarā, iha kathaṃ tatiyā na hoti? Ajjunassa tulā natthi, kesavassupamā na ceti, nete tulyatthā, kiñjarahi tulyānamopammatthā.

In construction with words meaning 'equal,' the genitive or the instrumental case is used. For example: `tulyo pitu` or `tulyo pitarā` (equal to the father); `sadiso pitu` or `sadiso pitarā` (similar to the father). Why, then, is the instrumental not used in `Ajjunassa tulā natthi` (There is no equal to Arjuna) and `kesavassa upamā na ca` (and no simile for Kesava)? Because these words (`tulā`, `upamā`) are not adjectives meaning 'equal'; rather, they are nouns meaning 'an equal' and 'a simile'.

41. Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe.

41. After a stem in `-a`, `yo` and `naṃ` become `ā` and `e`.

Akāranthato nāmasmā yonaṃ ṭāṭe honti yathākkamaṃ, ṭakārā sabbadesatthā, buddhā buddhe, atoti kiṃ? Kaññāyo, itthiyo, vadhuyo, idha kasmā na bhavati aggayo. Avidhānasāmatthiyā.

After a nominal stem ending in `-a`, the `yo` endings of the nominative and accusative plural become `ā` and `e` respectively. The letter `ṭ` in the rule indicates total substitution. For example: `buddhā`, `buddhe`. Why the specification 'after `-a`'? To exclude cases like `kaññāyo`, `itthiyo`, `vadhuyo`. Why is `aggayo` not formed here? By the force of another rule.

42. Ninaṃ vā.

42. Optionally `ni`.

Akārantato [M 0.0083] nāmasmā ninaṃ ṭāṭe vā honti yathākkamaṃ. Rūpā, rūpe, rūpāni, atotveva aṭṭhīni.

After a nominal stem ending in `-a`, the endings `ni` and `naṃ` optionally become `ā` and `e` respectively. For example: `rūpā`, `rūpe`, `rūpāni`. Why 'after `-a`'? Consider `aṭṭhīni`.

43. Smāsmiṃnaṃ.

43. The endings `smā` and `smiṃ`.

Akārantato nāmasmā smāsminnaṃ ṭāṭe vā honti yathākkamaṃ. Buddhā buddhasmā, buddhe buddhasmiṃ, atotveva aggismā aggismiṃ.

After a nominal stem in `-a`, the endings `smā` (abl. sg.) and `smiṃ` (loc. sg.) optionally become `ā` and `e` respectively. For example: `buddhā` or `buddhasmā` (from the Buddha); `buddhe` or `buddhasmiṃ` (in the Buddha). Why 'after `-a`'? Consider `aggismā`, `aggismiṃ` (from a stem in `-i`).

44. Sassāya catutthiyā.

44. For the dative, `ssa` becomes `āya`.

Akārantato parassa sassa catutthiyā āyo hoti vā. Buddhāya buddhassa, bhiyyo tādatthyeyevāyamāyo dissate, kvacidevaññattha, atotveva isissa, catutthiyāti kiṃ? Buddhassa mukhaṃ, attatthanti atthasaddena samāso.

After a stem in `-a`, the dative singular ending `ssa` optionally becomes `āya`. For example: `buddhāya` or `buddhassa` (for the Buddha). This `āya` is seen more for the sense of purpose, and rarely otherwise. Why 'after `-a`'? Consider `isissa`. Why 'dative'? Consider `buddhassa mukhaṃ` (the Buddha's face), which is genitive. The word `attatthaṃ` (for one's own sake) is a compound with `attha`.

Sabbāditopi smāsmiṃsānaṃ ṭāṭeāyā honteva… niruttikārānumatattā buddhavacane sandassanavato ca, tatrodamudāharaṇaṃ ‘asmā lokā paramhā ca, ubhayā dhaṃsate naro’, ‘tyāhaṃ mante paratthaddho’, ‘yāyeva kho panatthāya āgaccheyyātho tamevatthaṃ sādhukaṃ manasikareyyātho’ti.

Also after `sabba` and other pronouns, the endings `smā`, `smiṃ`, and `sā` become `ā`, `e`, and `āya` respectively, because it is approved by etymologists and seen in the word of the Buddha. Here is an example: '`asmā lokā paramhā ca, ubhayā dhaṃsate naro`' (A person is ruined by this world and the next, by both); '`tyāhaṃ mante paratthaddho`' (I, stiff with pride in those mantras); '`yāyeva kho panatthāya āgaccheyyātho tamevatthaṃ sādhukaṃ manasikareyyātho`' (For whatever purpose you have come, you should attend carefully to that very purpose).

45. Ghapatekasmiṃ nādīnaṃ yayā.

45. For `ghapa`- and `nadī`-class nouns, in the singular, `yā`.

Ghapato nādīnamekasmiṃ yayā honi yathākkamaṃ. Kaññāya, rattiyā, itthiyā, dhenuyā, vadhuyā, ekasminti kiṃ? Kaññāhi, rattīhi.

After `ghapa`- and `nadī`-class nouns, the singular case endings become `yā`. For example: `kaññāya`, `rattiyā`, `itthiyā`, `dhenuyā`, `vadhuyā`. Why 'in the singular'? To exclude the plural, e.g., `kaññāhi`, `rattīhi`.

46. Ssā vā tetimāmūhi.

46. Optionally `ssā` after `ta`, `eta`, `ima`, `amu`.

Ghapasaññehi [M 0.0084] tetimāmūhi nādīnamekasmiṃssā vā hoti, tassā kataṃ, tassā dīyate, tassā nissaṭaṃ, tassā pariggaho, tassā patiṭṭhitaṃ, tāya vā, evaṃ etissā etāya, imissā imāya, amussā amuyā, etehīti kiṃ? Sabbāya, nādīnaṃ tveva? Sā, ghapatotveva? Tāhi amūhi.

After the `ghapa`- and `nadī`-class pronouns `ta`, `eta`, `ima`, and `amu`, the feminine singular case endings optionally become `ssā`. For example: `tassā kataṃ` (done by her), `tassā dīyate` (is given to her), `tassā nissaṭaṃ` (departed from her), `tassā pariggaho` (her possession), `tassā patiṭṭhitaṃ` (established in her); or alternatively `tāya`. Likewise `etissā` or `etāya`; `imissā` or `imāya`; `amussā` or `amuyā`. Why 'after these pronouns'? To exclude `sabbāya`. Why '`nadī`-class'? To include `sā`. Why '`ghapa`-class'? To exclude `tāhi`, `amūhi`.

47. Naṃmhi nuka dvādīnaṃ sattarasannaṃ.

47. For the seventeen numerals from `dvi` onwards, `nna` in `naṃ`.

Dvādīnaṃ sattarasannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ nuka hoti naṃmhi vibhattamhi, dvinnaṃ catunnaṃ, pañcannaṃ, evaṃ yāva aṭṭhārasannaṃ, ukāro uccāraṇattho, kakāro antāvayavattho, tena naṃmhi na dīgho.

For the seventeen numerals from `dvi` (two) onwards, the augment `nna` is inserted before the genitive plural ending `naṃ`. For example: `dvinnaṃ`, `catunnaṃ`, `pañcannaṃ`, and so on up to `aṭṭhārasannaṃ` (eighteen). The `u` in the sutra is for pronunciation; the `k` indicates it is an affix, and therefore the preceding vowel is not lengthened.

48. Basukatinnaṃ.

48. For `bahu` and `kati`.

Naṃmhi bahuno katissa ca nuka hoti, bahunnaṃ, katinnaṃ.

For `bahu` (many) and `kati` (how many), `nna` is also inserted before the genitive plural ending `naṃ`. For example: `bahunnaṃ`, `katinnaṃ`.

49. Ṇṇaṃṇṇannaṃ tito jhā.

49. After `ti`, which is a `jha`, `ṇṇaṃ` or `ṇṇannaṃ`.

Jhasaññā tito naṃvacanassa ṇṇaṃṇṇannaṃ hoti, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, jhāti kiṃ tissannaṃ.

After `ti` (three), which has the technical name `jha`, the ending `naṃ` becomes `ṇṇaṃ` or `ṇṇannaṃ`. For example: `tiṇṇaṃ`, `tiṇṇannaṃ`. Why the designation `jha`? To exclude `tissannaṃ` (from the feminine form `tisso`).

50. Ubhinnaṃ.

50. `innaṃ` for `ubha`.

Ubhā naṃvacanassa innaṃ hoti, ubhinnaṃ.

For `ubha` (both), the ending `naṃ` becomes `innaṃ`. For example: `ubhinnaṃ`.

51. Suña sassa.

51. `su` for `ssa`.

Nāmasmā sassa suña hoti, buddhassa, dvisakārapāṭhena siddhe lāghavatthamidaṃ.

After a nominal stem, the genitive singular ending `ssa` becomes `su`. For example: `buddhassa`. This rule is for brevity, as the result is achievable by other means.

52. Ssaṃssāssāyesvitare kaññebhimānami.

52. In `ssaṃ`, `ssā`, `ssāya`, `i` for `itara`, `eka`, `añña`, `eta`, `ima`.

Ssamādīsvitarādīnami [M 0.0085] hoti, itarissaṃ, itarissā, ekissaṃ, ekissā, aññissaṃ, aññissā, etissaṃ, etissā, etissāya, imissaṃ, imissā, imissāya, esviti kiṃ? Itarāya, esanti kiṃ? Sabbassaṃ, sabbassā.

In the endings `ssaṃ`, etc., `i` replaces the final vowel of `itara`, etc. For example: `itarissaṃ`, `itarissā`; `ekissaṃ`, `ekissā`; `aññissaṃ`, `aññissā`; `etissaṃ`, `etissā`, `etissāya`; `imissaṃ`, `imissā`, `imissāya`. Why 'in these endings'? To exclude `itarāya`. Why 'for these stems'? To exclude `sabbassaṃ`, `sabbassā`.

53. Tāya vā.

53. Optionally for `tā`.

Ssamādīsu tassā vā i hoti, tissaṃ tassaṃ, tissā tassā, tissāya tassāya, ssaṃssāssāyesvitveva? Tāya.

In the endings `ssaṃ`, etc., `i` optionally replaces the vowel of `tā`. For example: `tissaṃ` or `tassaṃ`; `tissā` or `tassā`; `tissāya` or `tassāya`. Why 'in `ssaṃ`, `ssā`, `ssāya`'? To exclude `tāya`.

54. Tetimāto sassa ssāya.

54. After `tā`, `etā`, `imā`, `ssa` becomes `ssāya`.

Tāetāimāto sassa ssāyo hoti vā. Tassāya tāya, etissāya etāya, imissāya imāya.

After `tā`, `etā`, and `imā`, the genitive singular ending `ssa` optionally becomes `ssāya`. For example: `tassāya` or `tāya`; `etissāya` or `etāya`; `imissāya` or `imāya`.

55. Ratyādīhi ṭo smino.

55. After `ratti`, etc., `o` for `smiṃ`.

Ratyādīhi smino ṭo hoti vā, ratto rattiyaṃ, ādo ādismiṃ.

After `ratti` and other similar words, the locative singular ending `smiṃ` optionally becomes `o`. For example: `ratto` or `rattiyaṃ` (at night); `ādo` or `ādismiṃ` (at the beginning).

56. Suhisubhasso.

56. `o` for `ubha` before `su` and `hi`.

Ubhassa suhisvo hoti. Ubhosu, ubhohi.

For `ubha` (both), its final vowel becomes `o` before the endings `su` (loc. pl.) and `hi` (ins. pl.). For example: `ubhosu`, `ubhohi`.

57. Ltupitādinamā simhi.

57. For agent nouns in `-tu` and for `pitu`, etc., `ā` is the substitute for the nominative singular ending `si`.

Ltuppaccayantānaṃ pitādīnaṃ ca ā hoti simhi. Kattā, pitā. Pitu, mātu, bhāvu, mītu, duhitu, jāmātu, nattu, hotu, potu.

For stems ending in the suffix `-tu` and for `pitu` and others, `ā` is the substitute for the nominative singular ending `si`. For example: `kattā` (doer), `pitā` (father). The group includes: `pitu` (father), `mātu` (mother), `bhātu` (brother), `dhītu` (daughter), `duhitu` (daughter), `jāmātu` (son-in-law), `nattu` (grandson), `hotu` (sacrificer), `potu` (purifier).

58. Ge a ca.

58. And `a` is also a substitute for the vocative singular ending `ga`.

Ltupitādīnaṃ [M 0.0086] a hoti ge ā ca, bho katta, bho kattā, bho pita, bho pitā.

For agent nouns in `-tu` and for `pitu`, etc., `a` and also `ā` are substitutes for the vocative singular ending `ga`. For example: `bho katta`, `bho kattā`; `bho pita`, `bho pitā`.

59. Ayunaṃ vā dīgho.

59. The vowels `a`, `i`, and `u` are optionally lengthened.

A i u iccesaṃ vā dīgho hoti ge pare tiliṅge. Bho purisā, bho purisa, bho aggī, bho aggi, bho bhikkhū, bho bhikkhū.

The final vowels `a`, `i`, and `u` are optionally lengthened when the vocative singular ending `ga` follows, in all three genders. For example: `bho purisā`, `bho purisa`; `bho aggī`, `bho aggi`; `bho bhikkhū`, `bho bhikkhu`.

60. Ghabrahmādite.

60. After `gha`-stems and `brahman`, etc., `e` is the substitute.

Ghato brahmādito ca gasse vā hoti. Bhoti kaññe, bhoti kaññā, bho brahme, bho brahma, bho khatte, bho khatta, bho ise, bho isi, bho sakhe, bho sakha. Sakhi sakhīti itthiyaṃ siddhameva. Ākatigaṇo-yaṃ, evamaññatrāpi.

After a `gha`-stem and after `brahman` and others, `e` is optionally the substitute for the vocative singular ending `ga`. For example: `bhoti kaññe`, `bhoti kaññā`; `bho brahme`, `bho brahma`; `bho khatte`, `bho khatta`; `bho ise`, `bho isi`; `bho sakhe`, `bho sakha`. In the feminine, the forms `sakhi` and `sakhī` are already established. This is an illustrative group, and it should be understood similarly in other cases.

61. Nammādīhi.

61. Not after `ammā` and others.

Ammādīhi gasse na hoti. Bhoti ammā, bhoti annā, bhoti ambā.

After `ammā` and others, `e` is not the substitute for the vocative singular ending `ga`. For example: `bhoti ammā`, `bhoti annā`, `bhoti ambā`.

62. Rasso vā.

62. Shortening is optional.

Ammādīnaṃ ge rasso hoti vā. Bhoti amma, bhoti ammā.

For stems like `ammā` and others, the final vowel is optionally shortened in the vocative singular. For example: `bhoti amma`, `bhoti ammā`.

63. Gho ssaṃ, ssā, ssāyaṃ tiṃsu.

63. For a `gha`-stem, shortening occurs before the three endings `ssaṃ`, `ssā`, and `ssāyaṃ`.

Ssamādīsu gho rasso hoti. Tassaṃ, tassā, tassāya, taṃ, sabhatiṃ, esviti kiṃ? Tāya, sabhāya.

Before the endings `ssaṃ`, etc., a `gha`-stem is shortened. For example: `tassaṃ`, `tassā`, `tassāya`. Why the specification 'in these cases'? To allow for forms like `tāya` and `sabhāya`.

64. Ekavacana yosva-ghonaṃ.

64. For stems not designated `gho`, shortening occurs in the singular case endings and before the plural ending `yo`.

Ekavacane [M 0.0087] yosu ca ghaokārantavajjitā naṃ nāmānaṃ rasso hoti tiliṅge. Itthiṃ, itthiyā, itthiyo, vadhuṃ vadhuyā, vadhuyo, daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍinā, daṇḍino, sayambhuṃ, sayambhunā, sayambhuvo, agho nanti kiṃ? Kaññāya, kaññāyo, oggahaṇamuttaratthaṃ.

In the singular case endings and before `yo`, the final vowel of a noun is shortened in all three genders, except for `gha`-stems and stems ending in `o`. For example: `itthiṃ`, `itthiyā`, `itthiyo`; `vadhuṃ`, `vadhuyā`, `vadhuyo`; `daṇḍiṃ`, `daṇḍinā`, `daṇḍino`; `sayambhuṃ`, `sayambhunā`, `sayambhuvo`. Why the exception 'not `gho`'? To allow for forms like `kaññāya`, `kaññāyo`. The inclusion of `o` is for a subsequent rule.

65. Ge vā.

65. Optionally in the vocative singular.

Aghonaṃ ge vā rasso hoti tiliṅge, itthi, itthī, vadhu, vadhū, daṇḍi, daṇḍī, sayambhu, sayambhū. Aghonaṃtveva? Bhoti kaññā, bho go.

For stems not designated `gho`, the final vowel is optionally shortened in the vocative singular in all three genders. For example: `itthi`, `itthī`; `vadhu`, `vadhū`; `daṇḍi`, `daṇḍī`; `sayambhu`, `sayambhū`. Why 'not designated `gho`'? To exclude forms like `bhoti kaññā` and `bho go`.

66. Sismiṃ nānapuṃsakassa.

66. In the nominative singular, there is no shortening for a non-neuter noun.

Napuṃsakavajjitassa nāmassa sismiṃ rasso na hoti. Itthī, daṇḍī, vadhū, sayambhū. Sisminti kiṃ? Itthiṃ, anapuṃsakassāti kiṃ? Daṇḍi kulaṃ.

For a noun that is not neuter, the final vowel is not shortened in the nominative singular. For example: `itthī`, `daṇḍī`, `vadhū`, `sayambhū`. Why 'in the nominative singular'? To allow shortening in forms like `itthiṃ`. Why 'not neuter'? To allow shortening in forms like `daṇḍi kulaṃ`.

67. Gossāgasihinaṃsu gāvagavā.

67. For the stem `go`, before endings other than `ga`, `si`, `hi`, and `naṃ`, the substitutes are `gāva` and `gava`.

Gasihinaṃvajjitāsu vibhattīsu gosaddassa gāvagavā honti. (Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ), gāvo, gavo, gāvena, gavena, gāvassa, gavassa, gāvasmā, gavasmā, gāve, gave. Agasihinaṃsūti kiṃ? Bho go, go tiṭṭhati, gohi, gonaṃ.

Before case endings other than `ga`, `si`, `hi`, and `naṃ`, the substitutes `gāva` and `gava` occur for the word `go`. For example: (`gāvaṃ`, `gavaṃ`), `gāvo`, `gavo`, `gāvena`, `gavena`, `gāvassa`, `gavassa`, `gāvasmā`, `gavasmā`, `gāve`, `gave`. Why the exception 'other than `ga`, `si`, `hi`, `naṃ`'? To allow for the forms: `bho go`, `go tiṭṭhati`, `gohi`, `gonaṃ`.

68. Sumhi vā.

68. Optionally before `su`.

Gossa sumhi gāvagavā honti vā. Gāvesu, gavesu, gosu.

For the stem `go`, the substitutes `gāva` and `gava` optionally occur before the locative plural ending `su`. For example: `gāvesu`, `gavesu`, `gosu`.

69. Gavaṃ sena.

69. For the genitive singular, `gavaṃ` is a substitute.

Gossa [M 0.0088] se vā gavaṃ hoti saha sena. Gavaṃ, gāvassa, gavassa.

For the stem `go`, `gavaṃ` is an optional substitute for the genitive singular, replacing the stem and the ending `sa`. The resulting forms are `gavaṃ`, `gāvassa`, and `gavassa`.

70. Gunnaṃ ca naṃnā.

70. And `gunnaṃ` is a substitute for the genitive plural.

Naṃvacanena saha gossa gunnaṃ hoti gavaṃca vā. Gunnaṃ, gavaṃ, gonaṃ.

For the stem `go`, `gunnaṃ` and optionally `gavaṃ` are substitutes for the genitive plural, replacing the stem and the ending `naṃ`. The forms are: `gunnaṃ`, `gavaṃ`, and `gonaṃ`.

71. Nāssā.

71. For the instrumental singular ending `nā`, `ā` is the substitute.

Goto nāssa ā hoti vā. Gāvā, gavā, gāvena, gavena.

After the stem `go`, the instrumental singular ending `nā` is optionally substituted by `ā`. The forms are: `gāvā`, `gavā`, `gāvena`, `gavena`.

72. Gāvumhi.

72. The form `gāvuṃ`.

Aṃvacane gossa gāvha vā hoti. Vāvhaṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ. Gossa goṇādeso na kato… saddantarattā.

In the accusative singular, for the stem `go`, there is optionally the substitute `gāvuṃ`. The forms are: `gāvuṃ`, `gāvaṃ`, `gavaṃ`. The substitution `goṇa` is not made for `go` because it is a different word.

73. Yaṃ pīto.

73. `Yaṃ` after a stem designated `pa` or ending in `ī`.

Pasaññīto aṃvacanassa yaṃ vā hoti. Itthiyaṃ, itthiṃ. Pītoti kiṃ? Daṇḍiṃ, rattiṃ.

After a stem designated `pa` or ending in `ī`, the accusative singular ending `aṃ` optionally becomes `yaṃ`. For example: `itthiyaṃ`, `itthiṃ`. Why the specification 'after a stem designated `pa` or ending in `ī`'? To exclude forms like `daṇḍiṃ`, `rattiṃ`.

74. Naṃ jhīto.

74. `Naṃ` after a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`.

Jhasaññīto aṃvacanassa naṃ vā hoti. Daṇḍinaṃ, daṇḍiṃ. Kathaṃ ‘buddhaṃ ādiccabandhuna’nti? Yogavibhāvā. Jhāti kiṃ? Itthiṃ. Īti kiṃ? Aggiṃ.

After a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`, the accusative singular ending `aṃ` optionally becomes `naṃ`. For example: `daṇḍinaṃ`, `daṇḍiṃ`. How is the form `ādiccabandhunaṃ` in the phrase ‘buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ’ explained? By splitting the rule. Why the specification `jha`? To exclude `itthiṃ`. Why the specification `ī`? To exclude `aggiṃ`.

75. Yonaṃ none pume.

75. `No` and `ne` for `yo` in the masculine.

Jhīto [M 0.0089] yonaṃ none vā honti yathākkamaṃ pulliṅge. Daṇḍīno, daṇḍine, daṇḍī, jhīto tveva? Itthiyo, pumeti kiṃ? Daṇḍīni kulāni.

After a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`, the nominative and accusative plural endings (`yo`) optionally become `no` and `ne` respectively in the masculine. The forms are: `daṇḍīno`, `daṇḍine`, `daṇḍī`. Why the specification 'after a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`'? To exclude `itthiyo`. Why 'in the masculine'? To exclude `daṇḍīni kulāni`.

76. No.

76. No.

Jhīto yonaṃ no vā hoti pulliṅge. Daṇḍino tiṭṭhanti, daṇḍino passa, daṇḍī vā.

After a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`, the plural ending `yo` optionally becomes `no` in the masculine. For example: `daṇḍino tiṭṭhanti` (the staff-bearers stand), `daṇḍino passa` (see the staff-bearers), or also `daṇḍī`.

77. Smino ni.

77. `Ni` for `smiṃ`.

Jhīto smiṃvacanassa ni hoti vā, daṇḍini, daṇḍismiṃ, jhīto tveva? Aggismiṃ.

After a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`, the locative singular ending `smiṃ` optionally becomes `ni`. For example: `daṇḍini`, `daṇḍismiṃ`. Why the specification 'after a stem designated `jha` or ending in `ī`'? To exclude forms like `aggismiṃ`.

78. Ambvādīhi.

78. After `ambu` and so on.

Ambuādīhi sminoni hoti vā, phalaṃ patati ambuni, pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ, vātveva? Ambumhi, paṃsumhi.

After `ambu` and similar words, the locative singular ending `smiṃ` optionally becomes `ni`. For example: `phalaṃ patati ambuni`; `pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ`. Why 'optionally'? To allow for forms like `ambumhi` and `paṃsumhi`.

79. Kammādito.

79. After `kamman` and so on.

Kammādito smino ni hoti vā. Kammani kamme. Kamma, camma, vesma, bhasma (asma), brahma, atta, ātuma, ghamma, muddha. Kammāditoti kiṃ? Buddhe.

After `kamma` and similar words, the locative singular ending `smiṃ` optionally becomes `ni`. For example: `kammani`, `kamme`. The group includes: `kamma`, `camma`, `vesma`, `bhasma` (`asma`), `brahma`, `atta`, `ātuma`, `ghamma`, `muddha`. Why the specification 'after `kamma` and so on'? To exclude forms like `buddhe`.

80. Nāsseno.

80. For `nā`, `ena`.

Kammādito nāvacanassa eno vā hoti. Kammena, kammanā, cammena, cammanā, kammāditotveva? Buddhena.

After `kamma` and similar words, the instrumental singular ending `nā` optionally becomes `ena`. For example: `kammena`, `kammanā`; `cammena`, `cammanā`. Why the specification 'after `kamma` and so on'? Consider the form `buddhena`.

81. Jhalā sassa no.

81. After stems designated `jha` or `la`, `ssa` becomes `no`.

Jhalato [M 0.0090] sassa no vā hoti. Aggino aggissa, daṇḍino daṇḍissa, bhikkhuno bhikkhussa, sayambhuno sayambhussa,

After a stem designated `jha` or `la`, the genitive singular ending `ssa` optionally becomes `no`. For example: `aggino`, `aggissa`; `daṇḍino`, `daṇḍissa`; `bhikkhuno`, `bhikkhussa`; `sayambhuno`, `sayambhussa`.

Kathaṃ ‘yo ca sisso mahāmune’ ti? (3) “Ito kvaci sassa ṭānubandho”ti brahmādīsu pāṭhā sassa e ṭānubandho.

How is the form `mahāmune` in the phrase ‘yo ca sisso mahāmune’ explained? By the rule, 'In some cases, `ssa` has the indicatory letter `ṭa`.' Based on the reading for `brahmā` and similar words, the indicatory `ṭa` signifies the substitution of `e` for `ssa`.

82. Nā smāssa.

82. `Nā` for `smā` and `ssa`.

Jhalato smāssa nā hoti vā. Agginā aggismā, daṇḍinā daṇḍismā, bhikkhunā bhikkhusmā, sayambhunā sayambhusmā.
