For example: nīlañca taṃ uppalañca iti nīluppalaṃ (that which is blue and is a lotus, thus 'blue lotus'); chinnañca taṃ paruḷhañca iti chinnaparuḷhaṃ (that which is cut and has grown back); satthī ca sā sāmā ca iti satthisāmā (she who is Satthī and is dark); muni ca so sīho ca iti munisīho (he who is a sage and is a lion, thus 'sage-lion'); sīlam eva dhanaṃ iti sīladhanaṃ (virtue itself is wealth, thus 'the wealth of virtue').

Kvaci [M 0.0122] vākyameva puṇṇo mantāṇiputto, citto gahapati. Kvaci vuttiyeva kaṇhasappo, lohitasāli, visesananti kiṃ? Tacchako sappo, ekattheneti kiṃ? Kāḷamhā añño. Kathaṃ ‘pattajīviko, āpannajīviko, māsajāto’ti? Aññapadatthe bhavissati.

Sometimes only a phrase is used: Puṇṇo mantāṇiputto (Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī); Citto gahapati (Citta the householder). Sometimes only a compound expression is used: kaṇhasappo (black snake); lohitasāli (red rice). Why the term 'modifier'? To exclude tacchako sappo (a carpenter is a snake). Why 'with a single meaning'? To exclude kāḷamhā añño (other than the black one). How then are pattajīviko (one whose livelihood is a bowl), āpannajīviko (one who has attained a livelihood), and māsajāto (one who is a month old) formed? They will be in the sense of another term.

12. Naña.

12. The particle na.

Nañiccetaṃ syādyantaṃ syādyantena sahekatthaṃ hoti, na brāhmaṇo abrāhmaṇo, bahulādhikārato asamatthatthehi, kehici hoti ‘apunageyyā gāthā, anokāsaṃ kāretvā, amūlā mūlaṃ gantvā. Īsaṃkaḷāro, īsaṃpiṅgaloti ‘syādi syādine’ti samāso, vākyameva vātippasaṅgābhāvā.

This particle na, ending in a case suffix, is compounded into a single meaning with another word ending in a case suffix. For example, na brāhmaṇo (not a brahmin) becomes abrāhmaṇo (a non-brahmin). Because of the governing rule 'variously,' it occurs with some syntactically unconnected words, for example: apunageyyā gāthā (verses not to be recited again), anokāsaṃ kāretvā (having made a non-opportunity), amūlā mūlaṃ gantvā (having gone to the root from a non-root). In īsaṃkaḷāro (slightly dark) and īsaṃpiṅgalo (slightly brown), the compounding is by the general rule 'a word with a case suffix with another word with a case suffix.' It is only a phrase when there is no possibility of over-application.

13. Kupādayo niccamasyādividhimhi.

13. Ku, pa, etc., are always compounded outside the domain of case endings.

Kusaddo pādayo ca syādyantena sahekatthā honti niccaṃ syādividhivisayato-ñattha, kucchito brāhmaṇo kubrāhmaṇo, īsakaṃ uṇhaṃ kaduṇhaṃ, panāyako, abhiseko, pakaritvā, pakataṃ, duppuriso, dukkaṭaṃ, supuriso, sukataṃ, abhitthutaṃ, atitthutaṃ, ākaḷāro, ābaddho.

The word ku and the prefixes pa, etc., are always compounded into a single meaning with a word ending in a case suffix, outside the domain of the rules for case endings. For example: a contemptible brahmin is kubrāhmaṇo; slightly warm is kaduṇhaṃ; panāyako (leader); abhiseko (consecration); pakaritvā (having done well); pakataṃ (done well); duppuriso (a bad person); dukkaṭaṃ (a misdeed); supuriso (a good person); sukataṃ (a good deed); abhitthutaṃ (praised); atitthutaṃ (over-praised); ākaḷāro (slightly dark); ābaddho (bound).

(9) “Pādayo gatādyatthe paṭhamāya”. Pagato ācariyo pācariyo, pantevāsī.

(9) The prefixes pa, etc., are compounded with a word in the nominative case in the sense of 'gone,' etc. For example: a teacher who has gone forth (pagato ācariyo) becomes pācariyo; and pantevāsī.

(10) “Accādayo kantādyatthe dutiyāya”. Atikkanto mañcamatimañco, atimālo.

(10) The prefixes ati, etc., are compounded with a word in the accusative case in the sense of 'surpassed,' etc. For example: one who has surpassed the bed (atikkanto mañcaṃ) is atimañco; one who has surpassed a garland is atimālo.

(11) “Avādayo [M 0.0123] kuṭṭhādyatthe tatiyāya”. Avakuṭṭhaṃ kokilāya vanaṃ avakokilaṃ, avamayūraṃ.

(11) The prefixes ava, etc., are compounded with a word in the instrumental case in the sense of 'reviled,' etc. For example: a forest reviled by a cuckoo (avakuṭṭhaṃ kokilāya vanaṃ) is avakokilaṃ; similarly, avamayūraṃ (a forest reviled by peacocks).

(12) “Pariyādayo gilānādyatthe catutthiyā”. Parigilāno ajjhenāya pariyajjheno.

(12) The prefixes pari, etc., are compounded with a word in the dative case in the sense of 'weary,' etc. For example: one weary of study (parigilāno ajjhenāya) is pariyajjheno.

(13) “Nyādayo kantādyatthe pañcamiyā”.

(13) The prefixes ni, etc., are compounded with a word in the ablative case in the sense of 'gone out,' etc.

Nikkhanto kosambiyā nikkosampi, asyādividhimhīti kiṃ? Rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate.

One gone out from Kosambī (nikkhanto kosambiyā) is nikkosambi. Why the condition 'outside the domain of case endings'? To exclude cases like rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate (it shines towards the tree).

14. Cī kriyatthehi.

14. The suffix -cī with words denoting action.

Cīppaccayanto kiriyatthehi syādyantehi sahekattho hoti, malinīkariya.

A word ending in the suffix -cī is compounded into a single meaning with words that denote action and end in a case suffix. For example: malinīkariya (having made something dirty).

15. Bhūsanādarānādaresvalaṃsāsā.

15. The words alaṃ, sa, and asa in the sense of adornment, respect, and disrespect.

Bhūsanādisvatthe svalamādayo saddā kiriyatthehi syādyantehi sahekatthā honti, alaṃkariya, sakkacca, asakkacca. Bhūsanādīsūti kiṃ? Alaṃbhutvā gato, sakkatvā gato, asakkatvā gato, pariyattaṃ sobhanamasobhananti attho.

In the sense of adornment, etc., the words alaṃ, sa, asa, etc., are compounded into a single meaning with words that denote action and end in a case suffix. For example: alaṃkariya (having adorned), sakkacca (respectfully), asakkacca (disrespectfully). Why the condition 'in the sense of adornment, etc.'? To exclude cases like alaṃ bhutvā gato (having had enough, he went), sakkatvā gato (having been able, he went), and asakkatvā gato (having been unable, he went). The meaning is 'sufficiently', 'well', or 'unwell'.

16. Aññe ca.

16. And others.

Aññe ca saddā kiriyatthehi syādyantehi saha bahulamekatthā bhavanti, purobhūya, tirobhūya, tirokariya, urasikariya, manasikariya, majjhekariya, tuṇhībhūya.

And other words are variously compounded into a single meaning with words that denote action and end in a case suffix. For example: purobhūya (having come before), tirobhūya (having disappeared), tirokariya (having made to disappear), urasikariya (having taken to heart), manasikariya (having borne in mind), majjhekariya (having placed in the middle), tuṇhībhūya (having become silent).

17. Vānekaññatthe.

17. Optionally, many words in the sense of another.

Anekaṃ [M 0.0124] syādyantamaññassa padassatthe ekatthaṃ vā hoti, bahūni dhanāni yassa so bahudhano, lambā kaṇṇā yassa so lambakaṇṇo, vajiraṃ pāṇimhi yassa soyaṃ vajirapāṇi, mattā bahavo mātaṅgā ettha mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ, āruḷho vānaro yaṃ rukkhaṃ so āruḷhavānaro, jitāni indriyāni yena so jitindriyo, dinnaṃ bhojanaṃ yassa so dinnabhojano, apagataṃ kāḷakaṃ yasmā paṭā so-yamapagatakāḷako, upagatā dasa yesaṃ te upadasā, āsannadasā, adūradasā, adhikadasā, tayo dasa parimāṇamesaṃ tidasā, kathaṃ dasasaddo saṅkhyāne vattate? Parimāṇasaddasannidhānā, yathā pañca parimāṇamesaṃ pañcakā sakunāti, dve vā tayo vā parimāṇamesaṃ dvattayo vāsaddatthe vā dve vā tayo vā dvattayo.

Many words ending in case suffixes are optionally compounded into a single meaning in the sense of another word. For example: he whose wealth is much is bahudhano; he whose ears are long is lambakaṇṇo; he in whose hand is a thunderbolt is vajirapāṇi; a forest wherein are many intoxicated elephants is mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ; a tree which a monkey has climbed is āruḷhavānaro; he by whom the faculties have been conquered is jitindriyo; he to whom food has been given is dinnabhojano; a cloth from which the black mark has departed is apagatakāḷako. Those who have approached ten are upadasā (around ten); also āsannadasā (near ten), adūradasā (not far from ten), adhikadasā (more than ten). Those whose measure is three tens are the tidasā (the thirty gods). How does the word 'ten' function in enumeration? Through proximity to a word of measure. For example: 'birds whose measure is five' are pañcakā sakunā (a group of five birds). Those whose measure is two or three are dvattayo; or, in the sense of the word vā (or), 'two or three' becomes dvattayo.

Dakkhiṇassā ca pubbassā ca disāya yadantarāḷaṃ dakkhiṇapubbā disā, dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā cāti vā, saha puttenāgato saputto, salomako vijjamānalomakoti attho, evaṃ sapakkhako, atthī khīrā brāhmaṇīti atthisaddo vijjamānatthe nipāto, kvaci gatatthatāya padantarānamappayogo, kaṇṭhaṭṭhā kāḷā assa kaṇṭhekāḷo, oṭṭhassa mukhamiva mukhamassa oṭṭhamukho, kesasaṅghāto cūḷā assa kesacūḷo, suvaṇṇavikāro alaṅkāro assa suvaṇṇālaṅkāro, papatitaṃ paṇṇamassa papatitapaṇṇo, papaṇṇo, avijjamānā puttā assa avijjamānaputto, na santi puttā assa aputte, kvaci na hoti pañca bhuttavanto assa bhātuno putto assa atthīti bahulādhikārato.

The interval between the southern and eastern direction is the dakkhiṇapubbā disā (southeast direction); or, that which is southern and eastern. He who came with his son is saputto. Salomako means 'he who has existing hair.' Similarly, sapakkhako (he who has wings). In atthikhīrā brāhmaṇī (a brahmin woman who has milk), the word atthi is a particle in the sense of 'existing.' Sometimes, because the meaning is understood, intermediate words are not used: he who has black located at his throat is kaṇṭhekāḷo; he whose mouth is like a camel's mouth is oṭṭhamukho; he whose topknot is a mass of hair is kesacūḷo; he whose ornament is made of gold is suvaṇṇālaṅkāro; a tree whose leaves have fallen is papatitapaṇṇo or papaṇṇo. He whose sons are non-existent is avijjamānaputto; he who has no sons is aputto. Sometimes, because of the governing rule 'variously,' a compound is not formed, as in: pañca bhuttavanto assa (he has five who have eaten) or bhātuno putto assa atthi (he has a brother's son).

18. Tattha gahetvā tena paharitvā yuddhe sarūpaṃ.

18. In a battle of the same form: 'having seized by this, having struck with that'.

Sattamyantaṃ [M 0.0125] tatiyantañca sarūpamanekaṃ tattha gahetvā tena paharitvā yuddhe-ññapadatthe ekatthaṃ vā hoti, kesesu ca kesesu ca gahetvā yuddhaṃ pavattaṃ kesākesi, daṇḍehi ca daṇḍehi ca paharitvā yuddhaṃ pavattaṃ daṇḍādaṇḍi, muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi, “ci vītiyāre” (3-51) ti ci samāsanto, “cismiṃ” (3.66) ti akāro. Tattha teneti kiṃ? Kāyañca kāyañca gahetvā yuddhaṃ pavattaṃ. Gahetvā paharitvāti kiṃ? Rathe ca rathe ca ṭhatvā yuddhaṃ pavatti. Yuddheti kiṃ? Hatthe ca hatthe ca gahetvā sakhyaṃ pavattaṃ. Sarūpanti kiṃ? Daṇḍehi ca musalehi ca paharitvā yuddha pavattaṃ.

Many identical words ending in the locative and instrumental are optionally compounded into a single meaning in the sense of another word, when the meaning is a battle involving 'seizing by this' and 'striking with that.' For example: the battle that proceeded by seizing hair with hair is kesākesi; the battle that proceeded by striking with sticks against sticks is daṇḍādaṇḍi; also muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi (fist-fighting). By the rule '-ci in reciprocity,' -ci is the compound ending; by the rule 'cismiṃ,' there is the vowel a. Why 'by this' and 'with that'? To exclude a battle that proceeded by seizing body with body. Why 'having seized and having struck'? To exclude a battle that proceeded by standing on chariot against chariot. Why 'in battle'? To exclude friendship that proceeded by taking hand in hand. Why 'of the same form'? To exclude a battle that proceeded by striking with sticks and clubs.

19. Catthe.

19. In the sense of 'and'.

Anekaṃ syādyantaṃ catthe ekatthaṃ vā bhavati. Samuccayonvācayo itarītarayogo samāhāro ca ca saddatthā, tattha samuccayānvācayesu nekatthībhāvo sambhavati, tesu hi samuccayo aññamaññanirapekkhā namattappadhānānaṃ katthaci kiriyāvisese cīyamānatā, yathā ‘dhave ca khadire ca palāse ca chindā’ti. Anvācayo ca yattheko padhānabhāvena vidhīyate aparo ca guṇabhāvena, yathā ‘bhikkhañcara gāvo cānaye’ti. Itaradvaye tu sambhavati, tesu hi aññamaññasāpekkhānamavayavabhadānugato itarītarayogo, yathā ‘sāriputtamoggallānā’ti, assāvayavappadhānattā bahuvacanameva. Aññamaññasāpekkhānameva tirohitāvayavabhedo samudāyappadhāno samāhāro, yathā ‘chattupāhana’nti, assa pana samudāyappadhānattā ekavacanameva.

Many words ending in a case suffix, in the sense of 'ca' (and), optionally become a single compound. Conjunction, subsequent collection, mutual connection, and aggregation are the meanings of the word 'ca.' Among these, in conjunction and subsequent collection, becoming a single compound is not possible. For in conjunction, it is the collecting together in some specific action of things that are independent of each other and have their own nature as primary, as in: 'Cut the dhava, and the khadira, and the palāsa.' And subsequent collection is where one is enjoined as primary and another as secondary, as in: 'Go for alms, and bring the cows.' But in the other two, it is possible. For mutual connection follows the division of the members, which are dependent on each other, as in: 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna.' Since its members are primary, it is always in the plural. Aggregation is when the division of the members, which are also dependent on each other, is concealed, and the collective whole is primary, as in: 'umbrella-and-sandals.' Since its collective whole is primary, it is always in the singular.

Te [M 0.0126] ca samāhārītarītarayogā bahulaṃ vidhānā niyatavisayāyeva honti, tatrāyaṃ visayavibhāgo nirutthipiṭakāgato-pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgānaṃ, niccaverīnaṃ, saṅkhyāparimāṇa-saññānaṃ, khuddajantukānaṃ, pacanacaṇḍālānaṃ, caraṇasādhāraṇānaṃ, ekajjhāyanapāvacanānaṃ, liṅgavisesānaṃ, vividhaviruddhānaṃ disānaṃ, nadīnañca niccaṃ samāhārekattaṃ bhavati, tiṇarukkhapasusakunadhanadhaññabyañjanajanappadānaṃ vā, aññesamitarītarayogova.

And those two, aggregation and mutual connection, being formed in many ways, have fixed domains. Herein, this is the division of the domains, which comes from the Niruttipiṭaka: For the parts of living beings, musical instruments, vehicles, and armies; for perpetual enemies; for number, measure, and designation; for small creatures; for those who slaughter and outcastes; for common practices; for recitations and scriptures studied together; for specific genders; for various opposites; for directions; and for rivers, there is always singularity in an aggregative compound. For grasses, trees, beasts, birds, wealth, grains, condiments, and provinces, there is an option. For others, there is only mutual connection.

Pāṇyaṅgānaṃ-cakkhusotaṃ, mukhanāsikaṃ, hanugīvaṃ, chavimaṃsalohitaṃ, nāmarūpaṃ, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Turiyaṅgānaṃ-alasatālambaraṃ, murajagomukhaṃ, saṅkhadeṇḍimaṃ, maddavikapāṇavikaṃ, gītavāditaṃ, sammatālaṃ. Yoggaṅgānaṃ phālapācanaṃ, yuganaṅgalaṃ. Senaṅgānaṃ-asisattitomarapiṇḍaṃ, asicammaṃ, dhanukalāpaṃ, paharaṇāvaraṇaṃ. Niccaverīnaṃ-ahinakulaṃ, bīḷālamūsikaṃ, kākolūkaṃ, nāgasupaṇṇaṃ. Saṅkhyāparimāṇa saññānaṃ-ekakadukaṃ, dukatikaṃ, tikacatukkaṃ, catukkapañcakaṃ, dasekādasakaṃ. Khuddajantukānaṃ kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ, kunthakipillikaṃ, ḍaṃsamakasaṃ, makkhikakipillikaṃ. Pacanacaṇḍālānaṃ-orabbhikasūkarikaṃ, sākunti kamāgavikaṃ, sapākacaṇḍālaṃ, venarathakāraṃ, pukkusa chavaḍāhakaṃ. Caraṇasādhāraṇānaṃ-atisabhāradvājaṃ, kaṭhakalāpaṃ, sīlapaññāṇaṃ, samathavipassanaṃ, vijjācaraṇaṃ. Ekajjhāyanapāvacanānaṃ dīghamajjhimaṃ, ekuttarasaṃyuttakaṃ, khandhakavibhaṅgaṃ. Liṅgavisesānaṃ-itthipukhaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ, cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ, tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ, ‘lābhī hoti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenā- sanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna’ntipi dissati. Vividhaviruddhānaṃ kusalākusalaṃ[M 0.0127], sāvajjānavajjaṃ, hīnappaṇītaṃ, kaṇhasukkaṃ, chekapāpakaṃ. Disānaṃ pubbāparaṃ, dakkhiṇuttaraṃ, pubbadakkhiṇaṃ, pubbuttaraṃ, adharuttaraṃ, aparadakkhiṇaṃ, aparuttaraṃ. Nadīnaṃ-gaṅgāyamunaṃ, mahisarabhu.

Of the parts of living beings: eye-and-ear, mouth-and-nose, jaw-and-neck, skin-flesh-and-blood, name-and-form, aging-and-death. Of the parts of musical instruments: cymbals-and-drums, drum-and-horn, conch-and-kettledrum, lute-and-tabor, song-and-music, hand-clapping-and-cymbals. Of the parts of a vehicle: ploughshare-and-goad, yoke-and-plough. Of the parts of an army: sword-spear-javelin-and-club, sword-and-shield, bow-and-quiver, weapon-and-armor. Of perpetual enemies: snake-and-mongoose, cat-and-mouse, crow-and-owl, nāga-and-supaṇṇa. Of number, measure, and designation: one-and-two, two-and-three, three-and-four, four-and-five, ten-and-eleven. Of small creatures: insect-and-moth, flea-and-ant, gadfly-and-mosquito, fly-and-ant. Of those who slaughter and outcastes: sheep-butchers-and-pig-butchers, fowlers-and-deer-hunters, dog-cookers-and-caṇḍālas, bamboo-workers-and-chariot-makers, refuse-collectors-and-corpse-burners. Of common practices: Atisabhāradvāja, Kaṭhakalāpa, virtue-and-wisdom, serenity-and-insight, knowledge-and-conduct. Of recitations and scriptures studied together: Dīgha-and-Majjhima, Ekuttara-and-Saṃyutta, Khandhaka-and-Vibhaṅga. Of specific genders: female-and-male, female-slave-and-male-slave, robe-almsfood-lodging-and-medicines, grass-wood-branches-and-leaves; it is also seen thus: ‘is a gainer of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.’ Of various opposites: wholesome-and-unwholesome, blameworthy-and-blameless, inferior-and-superior, dark-and-bright, clever-and-wicked. Of directions: east-and-west, south-and-north, southeast, northeast, below-and-above, southwest, northwest. Of rivers: Ganges-and-Yamunā, Mahī-and-Sarabhū.

Tiṇavisesānaṃ-kāsakusaṃ kāsakusā, usīrabīraṇaṃ usīrabīraṇā, muñjapabbajaṃ muñjapabbajaṃ muñjapabbajā. Rukkhavisesānaṃ khadirapalāsaṃ khadirapalāsā, vossakaṇṇaṃ dhavāssakaṇṇā, pilakkhanigrodhaṃ pilakkhanigrodhā, assatthakapitthanaṃ assatthakapitthanā, sākasālaṃ sākasālā. Pasuvisesānaṃ-gajagavajaṃ gajagavajā, gomahisaṃ gomahisā, eṇeyyagomahisaṃ eṇeyyagomahisā, eṇeyyavarāhaṃ eṇeyyavarāhā, ajeḷakaṃ ajeḷakā, kukkurasūkaraṃ kukkurasūkarā, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ hatthigavāssavaḷavā. Sakunavisesānaṃ-haṃsabalāvaṃ haṃsabalāvā, kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ kāraṇḍavacakkavākā, bakabalākaṃ bakabalākā. Dhanānaṃ-hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇā, maṇisaṅkhamuttāveḷuriyaṃ maṇisaṅkhamuttāveḷuriyā, jātarūparajataṃ jātarūparajatā. Dhaññānaṃ-sāliyavakaṃ sāliyavakā, tilamuggamāsaṃ tilamuggamāsā, nipphāvakulatthaṃ nipphāvakulatthā. Byañjanānaṃ-sākasuvaṃ sākasuvā, gabyamāhisaṃ gabyamāhisā, eṇeyyavārāhaṃ eṇeyyavārāhā, migamāyūraṃ migamāyūrā. Janapadānaṃ-kāsikosalaṃ kāsikosalā, vajjimallaṃ vajjimallā, cetivaṃsaṃ cetivaṃsā, macchasūrasenaṃ macchasūrasenā, kurupañcālaṃ kurupañcālā. Itarītarayogo yathā-candimasūriyā, samaṇabrāhmaṇā mātāpitaro iccādi.

Of specific grasses: kāsa-and-kuśa (singular) or kāsas-and-kuśas (plural); usīra-and-bīraṇa (s.) or usīras-and-bīraṇas (pl.); muñja-and-pabbaja (s.) or muñjas-and-pabbajas (pl.). Of specific trees: khadira-and-palāsa (s.) or khadiras-and-palāsas (pl.); dhava-and-assakaṇṇa (s.) or dhavas-and-assakaṇṇas (pl.); pilakkha-and-nigrodha (s.) or pilakkhas-and-nigrodhas (pl.); assattha-and-kapitthana (s.) or assatthas-and-kapitthanas (pl.); sāka-and-sāla (s.) or sākas-and-salas (pl.). Of specific beasts: elephant-and-ox (s.) or elephants-and-oxen (pl.); cow-and-buffalo (s.) or cows-and-buffaloes (pl.); deer-cow-and-buffalo (s.) or deer-cows-and-buffaloes (pl.); deer-and-boar (s.) or deer-and-boars (pl.); goat-and-sheep (s.) or goats-and-sheep (pl.); dog-and-pig (s.) or dogs-and-pigs (pl.); elephant-ox-horse-and-mare (s.) or elephants-oxen-horses-and-mares (pl.). Of specific birds: swan-and-crane (s.) or swans-and-cranes (pl.); kāraṇḍava-duck-and-ruddy-goose (s.) or kāraṇḍava-ducks-and-ruddy-geese (pl.); heron-and-egret (s.) or herons-and-egrets (pl.). Of wealth: gold-and-bullion (s.) or gold-and-bullion (pl.); jewel-conch-pearl-and-lapis-lazuli (s.) or jewels-conches-pearls-and-lapis-lazuli (pl.); gold-and-silver (s.) or gold-and-silver (pl.). Of grains: rice-and-barley (s.) or rice-and-barley (pl.); sesame-mung-bean-and-black-gram (s.) or sesame-mung-beans-and-black-grams (pl.); bean-and-horse-gram (s.) or beans-and-horse-grams (pl.). Of condiments: vegetable-and-soup (s.) or vegetables-and-soups (pl.); cow-product-and-buffalo-product (s.) or cow-products-and-buffalo-products (pl.); deer-product-and-boar-product (s.) or deer-products-and-boar-products (pl.); game-and-peacock (s.) or game-and-peacocks (pl.). Of provinces: Kāsi-and-Kosala (s.) or Kāsis-and-Kosalans (pl.); Vajji-and-Malla (s.) or Vajjis-and-Mallas (pl.); Ceti-and-Vaṃsa (s.) or Cetis-and-Vaṃsas (pl.); Maccha-and-Sūrasena (s.) or Macchas-and-Sūrasenas (pl.); Kuru-and-Pañcāla (s.) or Kurus-and-Pañcālas (pl.). Mutual connection is as in: the moon and the sun, ascetics and brahmins, mother and father, and so on.

Etasmiṃ [M 0.0128] ekatthībhāvakaṇḍe yaṃ vuttaṃ pubbaṃ, tadeva pubbaṃ nipatati kamātikkame payojanābhāvā. Kvaci vipallāsopi hoti bahulādhikārato, dantānaṃ rājā rājadanto, katthaci kamaṃ paccānādarā pubbakālassāpi paranipāto, littavāsito, naggamusito, sittasammaṭṭho, bhaṭṭhaluñcito. Catthe yadekatthaṃ tattha keci pubbapadaṃ bahudhā niyamenti, tadiha byabhicāradassāna na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In this section on forming a single compound, whatever is stated first, that same word is placed first, as there is no reason for transgressing the order. Sometimes there is also an inversion due to the authority of a general rule; for example, 'dantānaṃ rājā' (king of teeth) becomes 'rājadanto' (a prominent tooth). In some cases, out of disregard for the order, there is post-position even of a word that should be prior, as in: 'smeared-and-perfumed,' 'naked-and-shaven,' 'sprinkled-and-swept,' 'roasted-and-plucked.' In the sense of 'ca' where there is a single compound, some regulate the first member in many ways; but that is not stated here, it should be understood, because exceptions are seen.

20. Samāhāre napuṃsakaṃ.

20. An aggregative compound is neuter.

Catthe samāhāre yadekatthaṃ, taṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ bhavati, tathācevodāhaṭaṃ, katthaci na hoti ‘sabhāparisāyā’ti ñāpakā, ādhipaccaparivāro, chandapārisuddhi, paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ.

In the sense of 'ca,' a single compound that is an aggregative compound is in the neuter gender, and it has been exemplified thus. Sometimes it is not, with 'sabhāparisāyā' (assembly and council) being an indicator. Other examples are: 'ādhipaccaparivāro' (sovereignty and retinue), 'chandapārisuddhi' (purity of intention), 'paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ' (in rebirth and continuity).

21. Saṅkhyādi.

21. Beginning with a numeral.

Ekatthe samāhāre saṅkhyādi napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ bhavati, pañcagavaṃ, catuppathaṃ, samāhārassekattā ekavacanameva hoti, samāhāretveva pañcakāpālo pūvo, tiputto.

A single compound that is an aggregative compound beginning with a numeral is in the neuter gender: 'pañcagavaṃ' (an aggregate of five cows), 'catuppathaṃ' (a crossroads). Because an aggregative compound is a single entity, it is always in the singular number. Why 'in an aggregative compound'? Consider: 'pañcakapālo pūvo' (a cake made with five cups), 'tiputto' (a father of three sons).

22. Kvacekattañca chaṭṭhiyā.

22. And sometimes for a genitive, singularity.

Chaṭṭhiyekatthe kvaci napuṃsakattaṃ hotekatthañca, salabhānaṃ chāyā salabhacchāyaṃ, evaṃ sakuntānaṃ chāyā sakuntacchāyaṃ, pāsādacchāyaṃ pāsādacchāyā, gharacchāyaṃ gharacchāyā, amanussasabhāya napuṃsakekattaṃ bhavati brahmasabhaṃ, devasabhaṃ, indasabhaṃ, yakkhasabhaṃ, sarabhasabhaṃ, manussasabhāyaṃ pana khattiyasabhā, rājasabhā iccevamādi, kvacīti kiṃ rājapuriso.

For a genitive single compound, there is sometimes neuter gender and singularity. 'The shadow of locusts' becomes 'salabhacchāyaṃ.' Similarly, 'the shadow of birds' becomes 'sakuntacchāyaṃ.' 'pāsādacchāyaṃ' or 'pāsādacchāyā' (shadow of a palace); 'gharacchāyaṃ' or 'gharacchāyā' (shadow of a house). For an assembly of non-humans, there is neuter singularity: 'brahmasabhaṃ' (assembly of Brahmās), 'devasabhaṃ' (assembly of gods), 'indasabhaṃ' (assembly of Indra), 'yakkhasabhaṃ' (assembly of yakkhas), 'sarabhasabhaṃ' (assembly of mythical beasts). But for an assembly of humans: 'khattiyasabhā' (assembly of nobles), 'rājasabhā' (royal assembly), and so on. Why 'sometimes'? To exclude cases like 'rājapuriso' (a king's man).

23. Syādīsu rasso.

23. Before case endings, shortening.

Napuṃsake [M 0.0129] vattamānassa rasso hoti syādīsu. Salabhacchāyaṃ, syādīsūti kiṃ? Salabhacchāye.

Of a word that is neuter, there is shortening before case endings. For example: 'salabhacchāyaṃ.' Why 'before case endings'? Consider 'salabhacchāye'.

24. Ghapassantassāppadhānassa.

24. Of a non-primary final `ghapa`.

Antabhūtassa appadhānassa ghapassa syādīsu rasso hoti. Bahumālo poso, nikkosambi, ativāmoru, antassāti kiṃ? Rājā kaññāpiyo, appadhānassāti kiṃ? Rājakumārī brahmabandhū.

Of a non-primary `ghapa` word that is the final member of a compound, there is shortening before case endings. For example: 'bahumālo poso' (a man with many garlands); 'nikkosambi' (one who has left Kosambī); 'ativāmoru' (one with very beautiful thighs). Why 'final member'? Consider: 'Rājā kaññāpiyo' (A king for whom maidens are dear). Why 'non-primary'? Consider: 'Rājakumārī' (a princess); 'brahmabandhū' (a kinswoman of Brahmā).

25. Gossu.

25. For 'go', 'u'.

Antabhūtassa appadhānassa gossa syādīsu u hoti. Cittagu, appadhānassātveva? Sugo, antassātveva? Gokulaṃ.

For the word 'go,' when it is the final member of a compound and is non-primary, 'u' occurs before case endings. For example: 'cittagu' (one who has a brindled cow). Why 'non-primary'? Consider: 'sugo' (a fine cow). Why 'final member'? Consider: 'gokulaṃ' (a herd of cows).

26. Itthiyamatvā.

26. In the feminine, from '-a', 'ā'.

Itthiyaṃ vattamānato akārantato nāmasmā āpaccayo hoti. Dhammadinnā.

From a noun ending in the vowel 'a' that denotes the feminine, the suffix 'ā' occurs. For example: Dhammadinnā.

37. Nadādito vī.

37. From the 'nadī' group, 'ī'.

Nadādīhi itthiyaṃ vīppaccayo hoti. Nadī, mahī, kumārī, taruṇī, vāruṇī, gotamī. (14) “Gotovā” gāvī go, ākatigaṇo-yaṃ, koro “ntantūnaṃ vīmhi to vā” (3-36) ti visesanattho.

From the 'nadī' group and so on, the suffix 'ī' occurs in the feminine. For example: nadī, mahī, kumārī, taruṇī, vāruṇī, gotamī. This is an open-ended group. From 'go' comes 'gāvī' or 'go'.

28. Yakkhāditinī ca.

28. And from the 'yakkha' group, 'inī'.

Yakkhādito [M 0.0130] itthiyaṃ inī hoti vīca. Yakkhinī yakkhī, nāginī nāgī, sīhinī sīhī.

From the 'yakkha' group, in the feminine, 'inī' occurs, and also 'ī'. For example: 'yakkhinī' or 'yakkhī' (female yakkha); 'nāginī' or 'nāgī' (female nāga); 'sīhinī' or 'sīhī' (lioness).

26. Ārāmikādīhi.

26. From the 'ārāmika' group and so on.

Ārāmikādito inī hotitthiyaṃ. Ārāmikinī, anantarāyikinī, rājinī (15) “saññāyaṃ mānuso” mānusinī, aññatra mānusī.

From the 'ārāmika' group and so on, 'inī' occurs in the feminine. For example: 'ārāmikinī' (female park-keeper), 'anantarāyikinī', 'rājinī' (queen). When it is a specific designation, from 'mānusa' (human) comes 'mānusinī'; otherwise, 'mānusī' (human female).

30. Yuvaṇṇehi nī.

30. From stems ending in 'i' and 'u', 'nī'.

Itthiyamivaṇṇuvaṇṇantehi nī hoti bahulaṃ. Sadāpayatapāṇinī, daṇḍinī, bhikkhunī, khattabandhunī, paracittavidunī, mātuādito kasmā na hoti? Itthippaccayaṃ vināpi itthattābhidhānato.

In the feminine, from stems ending in the vowels 'i' and 'u', the suffix 'nī' occurs frequently. For example: 'sadāpayatapāṇinī' (she who always has outstretched hands), 'daṇḍinī' (female staff-bearer), 'bhikkhunī' (nun), 'khattabandhunī' (kinswoman of a khattiya), 'paracittavidunī' (female knower of others' minds). Why does this not occur after 'mātu' (mother) and so on? Because they express the feminine even without a feminine suffix.

31. Ktimhāññatthe.

31. From '-kti', in a different sense.

Ktimhāññattheyeva itthiyaṃ nī hoti bahulaṃ. Sāhaṃ ahiṃ sāratinī, tassā muṭṭhassatiniyā, sā gāvī vacchagiddhinī, aññattheti kiṃ? Dhammarati.

Only from a stem ending in '-kti' used in a different sense does the suffix 'nī' frequently occur in the feminine. For example: 'Sāhaṃ ahiṃ sāratinī' (I am she who remembers the snake); 'tassā muṭṭhassatiniyā' (of her who has confused mindfulness); 'sā gāvī vacchagiddhinī' (that cow who is greedy for her calf). Why 'in a different sense'? Consider: 'Dhammarati' (delight in the Dhamma).

32. Gharaṇyādayo.

32. 'Gharaṇī' and so on.

Gharaṇippabhutayo nīppaccantāsādhavo bhavanti. Gharaṇī, pokkharaṇī, īssa-ttaṃ nipātanā, (16) “ācariyā vā ya-lopo ca” ācarinī, ācariyā.

The words `gharaṇī` and so on are valid forms with the suffix `nī` by irregular formation. For example: `gharaṇī` (housewife), `pokkharaṇī` (lotus pond). The word `īssā` (envy) is also formed irregularly. (16) 'From `ācariya`, optionally with elision of ya': `ācarinī`, `ācariyā` (female teacher).

33. Mātulāditvānī bhariyāyaṃ.

33. From `mātula` and so on, the suffix `ānī` is used in the sense of 'wife'.

Mātulādito [M 0.0131] bhariyāyamānī hoti. Mātulānī, vāruṇānī, gahapatānī, ācariyānī, (17) “abhariyāyaṃ khattiyā vā” khattiyānī khattiyā, nadādipāṭhā bhariyāyantu khattiyī.

From `mātula` and so on, the suffix `ānī` is used in the sense of 'wife'. For example: `mātulānī` (maternal uncle's wife), `vāruṇānī` (Varuṇa's wife), `gahapatānī` (householder's wife), `ācariyānī` (teacher's wife). (17) 'From `khattiya`, optionally, when not meaning 'wife'': `khattiyānī`, `khattiyā`. But in the sense of 'wife', according to the `nadī` group, it is `khattiyī`.

34. Upamāsaṃhita sahita saññata saha saphavāma lakkhaṇāditūrutū.

34. From `ūru` preceded by `upamā`, `saṃhita`, `sahita`, `saññata`, `saha`, `sapha`, `vāma`, `lakkhaṇa`, and so on, the suffix `ū` is used.

Ūrusaddā upamānādipubbā ittiyamū hoti. Karabhorū, saṃhitorū, sahitorū, saññatorū, sahorū, saphorū, vāmorū, lakkhaṇorū, ūtiyogavibhāgā ū brahmabandhū.

From the word `ūru` preceded by a word of simile and so on, the suffix `ū` is used in the feminine. For example: `karabhorū`, `saṃhitorū`, `sahitorū`, `saññatorū`, `sahorū`, `saphorū`, `vāmorū`, `lakkhaṇorū`. By splitting the rule, the suffix `ū` is also used for `brahmabandhū`.

35. Yuvā ti.

35. From `yuvan`.

Yuvasaddato ti hotitthiyaṃ. Yuvati.

From the word `yuvan`, the suffix `ti` is used in the feminine. For example: `yuvati` (a young woman).

36. Ntantūnaṃ vīmhito vā.

36. Optional rule for stems ending in `-nt` and `-ant` with the suffix `ī`.

Vīmhi ntantūnaṃ to vā hoti. Gacchatī gacchantī, sīlavatī sīlavantī.

Before the suffix `ī`, the `n` of stems ending in `-nt` and `-ant` is optionally elided. For example: `gacchatī` or `gacchantī`; `sīlavatī` or `sīlavantī`.

37. Bhavato bhoto.

37. For `bhavant`, `bhot` is substituted.

Vīmhi bhavato bhotādeso hoti vā. Bhotī bhavantī.

Before the suffix `ī`, `bhot` is optionally substituted for `bhavant`. For example: `bhotī` or `bhavantī` (venerable lady).

38. Gossāvaṅa.

38. For `go`, the substitute `āva`.

Gosaddassa vīmhāvaṅa hoti. Gāvī.

For the word `go`, the substitute `āva` occurs before the suffix `ī`. For example: `gāvī` (cow).

39. Puthussa pathavaputhavā.

39. For `puthu`, the substitutes `pathava` and `puthava`.

Vīmhi [M 0.0132] puthussa pathavaputhavā honti. Pathavī, puthavī, ṭhe pathavī.

Before the suffix `ī`, the substitutes for `puthu` are `pathava` and `puthava`. For example: `pathavī`, `puthavī`. In the text: `pathavī`.

40. Samāsantva.

40. Compound Endings.

Samāsantva iti cādhikarīyati.

And the heading 'Compound Endings' is to be supplied in the following rules.

41. Pāpādīhi bhūmiyā.

41. From `bhūmi` after `pāpa` and so on.

Pāpādīhī parā yā bhūmi tassā samāsanto a hoti. Pāpabhūmaṃ, jātibhūmaṃ.

For `bhūmi` when it follows `pāpa` and so on, the compound ending is `a`. For example: `pāpabhūmaṃ`, `jātibhūmaṃ`.

42. Saṅkhyāhi.

42. After numerals.

Saṅkhyāhi parā yā bhūmi tassā samāsanto a hoti. Dvibhūmaṃ, tibhūmaṃ.

For `bhūmi` when it follows a numeral, the compound ending is `a`. For example: `dvibhūmaṃ`, `tibhūmaṃ`.

43. Nadīgodāvarīnaṃ.

43. For `nadī` and `godāvarī`.

Saṅkhyāhi parāsaṃ nadīgodāvarīnaṃ samāsanto a hoti, pañcanadaṃ, sattagodāvaraṃ, saṅkhyāhitveva? Mahānadī, nadīgodāvarīnanti kiṃ? Dasitthi.

For `nadī` and `godāvarī` when they follow a numeral, the compound ending is `a`. For example: `pañcanadaṃ`, `sattagodāvaraṃ`. Why the condition 'after a numeral'? Consider `mahānadī`. Why the condition 'for `nadī` and `godāvarī`'? Consider `dasitthi`.

44. Asaṅkhyehi cāṅgulyānaññāsaṅkhyatthesu.

44. And from `aṅguli` after non-numerals, except in the sense of another word or an uncountable number.

Asaṅkhyehi saṅkhyāhi ca parāya aṅgulyā samāsanto a hoti no ce aññapadatthe asaṅkhyatthe ca samāso vattate. Niggatamaṅgulīhi niraṅgulaṃ, accaṅgulaṃ, dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭā dvaṅgulaṃ, anaññāsaṅkhyatthesūti kiṃ? Pañcaṅguli hattho, upaṅguli, kathaṃ [M 0.0133] ‘dve aṅgulīmānamassāti dvaṅgula’nti? Nātra samāsoññapadatthe vihito mattādīnaṃ lope kate tattha vattate. Aṅgulasaddo vā pamāṇavāci saddantaraṃ, yathā ‘senaṅgulappamāṇena aṅgulānaṃ sataṃ puṇṇaṃ catuddasa vā aṅgulānī’ti.

From `aṅguli` when it follows a non-numeral or a numeral, the compound ending is `a`, provided the compound is not in the sense of another word or in an uncountable sense. For example: `niraṅgulaṃ` (from `niggatam aṅgulīhi`); `accaṅgulaṃ`; `dvaṅgulaṃ` (from `dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭā`). Why the condition 'except in the sense of another word or an uncountable number'? Consider `pañcaṅguli hattho` or `upaṅguli`. How then is `dvaṅgula` formed, meaning 'that which has a measure of two fingers'? Here the compound is not enjoined in the sense of another word, but it applies when a word of measure has been elided. Or, `aṅgula` is another word denoting measure, as in 'by the measure of a `senaṅgula`, a hundred fingers full, or fourteen fingers'.

45. Dīghāhovassekadesehi ca rattyā.

45. And from `ratti` after `dīgha`, `aho`, `vassa`, and words denoting a part.

Dīghādīhi asaṅkhyehi saṅkhyāhi ca paramasmā rattiyā samāsanto a hoti. Dīgharattaṃ, ahorattaṃ (tto), vassārattaṃ (tto), pubbarattaṃ, apararattaṃ, aḍḍhurattaṃ, atikkanto rattiṃ atiratto, dverattī samāhaṭā dirattaṃ (tto), vā kvaci bahulādhikārā ekarattaṃ (tto), ekaratti, anaññāsaṅkhyatthesutveva? Dīgharattihemanto, uparatti, kvaci hoteva bahulaṃ vidhānāyathārattaṃ.

For `ratti`, when following `dīgha` and so on, indeclinables, and numerals, the compound ending is `a`. For example: `dīgharattaṃ`, `ahorattaṃ`, `vassārattaṃ`, `pubbarattaṃ`, `apararattaṃ`, `aḍḍharattaṃ`, `atiratto`, `dirattaṃ`. Optionally, due to the governing rule of 'variously', one finds `ekarattaṃ` or `ekaratti`. The condition 'except in the sense of another word or an uncountable number' is still in effect. Consider: `dīgharattihemanto`, `uparatti`. It does occur in some cases due to the 'variously' rule, as in `yathārattaṃ`.

46. Gotvacatthe cālope.

46. From `go`, when not in the sense of a part and when there is no elision.

Gosaddā alopavisayā samāsanto a hoti na ce catthe samāso aññapadatthe asaṅkhyatthe ca, rājagavo, paramagavo, pañcagavadhano, dasagavaṃ, alopeti kiṃ? Pañcahi gohi kīto pañcagu, acattheti ki? Ajassagāvo, anaññāsaṅkhyatthesutveva? Cittagu, upagu.

For the word `go`, in a context where there is no elision, the compound ending is `a`, provided the compound is not in the sense of a part; this also applies in the sense of another word and in a numerical sense. For example: `rājagavo`, `paramagavo`, `pañcagavadhano`, `dasagavaṃ`. Why the condition 'when there is no elision'? Consider `pañcagu` (from `pañcahi gohi kīto`). Why 'not in the sense of a part'? Consider `ajassagāvo`. The condition 'except in the sense of another word or a numeral' is still in effect. Consider: `cittagu`, `upagu`.

47. Rattindivadāragavacaturassā.

47. The words `rattindiva`, `dāragava`, and `caturassa`.

Ete saddā aantā nipaccante. Ratto ca divā ca rattindivaṃ, ratti ca divā ca rattindivaṃ, dārā ca gāvo ca dāragavaṃ, catasso assiyo assa caturasso.

These words are irregularly formed with an `a`-ending. `rattindivaṃ` is formed from `ratto ca divā ca` or `ratti ca divā ca`. `dāragavaṃ` is formed from `dārā ca gāvo ca`. `caturasso` is formed from `catasso assiyo assa`.

48. Āyāmenugavaṃ.

48. `anugavaṃ` in the sense of 'length'.

Anugavanti [M 0.0134] nipaccate āyāme gamyamāne. Anugavaṃ sakaṭaṃ, āyāmeti kiṃ? Gunnaṃ pañchā anugu.

The word `anugavaṃ` is irregularly formed when the meaning is 'length'. For example: `anugavaṃ sakaṭaṃ`. Why the condition 'in the sense of length'? Consider `anugu` (from `gunnaṃ pacchā`).

49. Akkhismāññatthe. Akkhismā samāsanto a hoti aññatthe ce samādhasā. Visālakkho, visālakkhī.

49. From `akkhi` in the sense of another word. From `akkhi` the compound ending is `a` if the compound is in the sense of another word. For example: `visālakkho`, `visālakkhī`.

50. Dārumyaṅgulyā.

50. From `aṅguli` when meaning 'wood'.

Aṅgulantā aññapadatthe dārumhi samāsanto a hoti. Dvaṅgulaṃdāru, pañcaṅgulaṃ, aṅgulisadisāvayavaṃ dhaññādīnaṃ vikkhepakaṃ dāruṃ vuccate, pamāṇe tu pubbe viya siddhaṃ sakharājasaddā akārantāva, sissopi na dissati, gāṇḍī vadhanvāti pakatantarena siddhaṃ.

From a word ending in `aṅguli`, in the sense of another word, the compound ending is `a` when it means 'wood'. For example: `dvaṅgulaṃ dāru`, `pañcaṅgulaṃ`. 'Wood' here refers to a tool for scattering grain and so on with finger-like parts. In the sense of pure measure, however, the form is established as before. The words `sakhā` and `rāja` already end in `a`. `sissa` is not seen. `gāṇḍīvadhanvā` is established by another rule.

51. Ci vītihāre.

51. The suffix `ci` in the sense of reciprocal action.

Oghābyatihāre gamyamāne aññapadatthe vattamānato ci hoti. Kesākesi daṇḍādaṇḍi, cakāro “cismi”nti (3.66) visesanattho, sugandhi, duggantīti payogo na dissate.

When reciprocal action is meant, the suffix `ci` is used from a word in a bahubbīhi compound. For example: `kesākesi`, `daṇḍādaṇḍi`. The word `ca` in the rule is for specification from rule 3.66. The usage `sugandhi` or `duggandhī` is not found.

52. Ltvitthiyūhi ko.

52. After stems ending in `-tu` and feminine stems ending in `-ī` and `-ū`, the suffix `ka`.

Ltuppaccayantehi, itthiyamīkārūkārantehi ca bahulaṃ kappaccayo hoti aññapadatthe. Bahukattuko, bahukumāriko, bahubrahmabandhuko, bahulaṃtveva? Subbhū.

After stems ending in the suffix `-tu`, and after feminine stems ending in `-ī` and `-ū`, the suffix `ka` is variously used in a bahubbīhi compound. For example: `bahukattuko`, `bahukumāriko`, `bahubrahmabandhuko`. Why the condition 'variously'? Consider `subbhū`.

53. Vāññato.

53. Optionally from others.

Aññehi [M 0.0135] aññapadatthe ko vā bahulaṃ hoti. Bahumālako, bahumālo.

From other stems, the suffix `ka` is optionally and variously used in a bahubbīhi compound. For example: `bahumālako` or `bahumālo`.

54. Uttarapade. Etamadhikataṃ veditabbaṃ.

54. 'When a subsequent word follows.' This should be understood as a governing rule.

55. Imassidaṃ.

55. For `ima`, `idaṃ` is substituted.

Uttarapade parato imassa idaṃ hoti. Idamaṭṭhitā, idappaccayatā, niggahītalopo passa ca dvibhāvo.

When a subsequent word follows, `idaṃ` is substituted for `ima`. For example: `idamaṭṭhitā`, `idappaccayatā`. In the latter, there is elision of the niggahīta and doubling of the `p`.

56. Puṃ pumassa vā. Pumassa puṃ hotuttarapade vibhāsā. Pulliṅgaṃ, pumaliṅgaṃ.

56. Optionally, `puṃ` for `puma`. For `puma`, `puṃ` is optionally substituted when a subsequent word follows. For example: `pulliṅgaṃ`, `pumaliṅgaṃ`.

57. Ṭantantūnaṃ.

57. Of stems ending in `-ṭa` and `-ant`.

Esaṃ ṭa hotuttarapade kvaci vā. Bhavampatiṭṭhāmayaṃ, bhagavaṃmūlakā no dhammā, bahulādhikārā tarādīsu ca pageva mahattarī, rattaññumahattaṃ.

For these stems, `ṃ` is optionally substituted somewhere when a subsequent word follows. For example: `bhavampatiṭṭhāmayaṃ`; `bhagavaṃmūlakā no dhammā`. Due to the 'variously' rule, it also occurs before `tara` and so on, as in `mahattara` and `rattaññumahattaṃ`.

58. A. Esaṃ a hotuttarapade. Guṇavantapatiṭṭho-smi.

58. `a`. For these stems, `a` is substituted when a subsequent word follows. For example: `guṇavantapatiṭṭho-smi`.

59. Manādyāpādīnamo maye ca. Manādīnamāpādīnaṃ ca o hotuttarapade maye ca. Manoseṭṭhā, manomayā, rajojallaṃ, rajomayaṃ, āpogataṃ, āpomayaṃ, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

59. For the `manas`-group and the `āpas`-group, `o` is substituted when a subsequent word follows, and also before the suffix `maya`. For example: `manoseṭṭhā`, `manomayā`; `rajojallaṃ`, `rajomayaṃ`; `āpogataṃ`, `āpomayaṃ`; `anuyanti disodisaṃ`.

60. Parassa saṅkhyāsu.

60. For `para`, before numerals.

Saṅkhyāsuttarapadesu [M 0.0136] parassa o hoti. Parosataṃ, parosahassaṃ, saṅkhyāsūti kiṃ? Paradattūpajīvino.

When a numeral follows as the subsequent word, `o` is substituted for the final of `para`. For example: `parosataṃ`, `parosahassaṃ`. Why the condition 'before numerals'? Consider `paradattūpajīvino`.

61. Jane puthassu.

61. For `putha`, `u` is substituted before `jana`.

Jane uttarapade puthassa u hoti. Ariyehi puthagevāyaṃ janoti puthujjano.

When `jana` is the subsequent word, `u` is substituted for the final of `putha`. For example: `puthujjano`, from the explanation 'this person is separate from the noble ones'.

62. So chassāhāyatane vā.

62. Optionally, `so` for `cha` before `aha` and `āyatana`.

Ahe āyatane cuttarapade chassa so vā hoti. Sāhaṃ chāhaṃ, saḷāyatanaṃ, chaḷāyatanaṃ.

When `aha` and `āyatana` are the subsequent words, `so` is optionally substituted for `cha`. For example: `sāhaṃ` or `chāhaṃ`; `saḷāyatanaṃ` or `chaḷāyatanaṃ`.

63. Ltupitādīnamāraṅaraṅa.

63. For stems ending in -tu, and for pitar and so on, the substitutes āra and ara.

Ltuppaccayantānaṃ pitādīnañca yathākkamamāraṅaraṅa vā hontuttarapade, satthāradassanaṃ, kattāraniddeso, mātarapitaro, vātveva? Satthudassanaṃ, mātāpitaro.

For stems ending in the suffix -tu, and for pitar and so on, āra and ara are optionally substituted respectively when a subsequent word follows. For example: satthāradassanaṃ, kattāraniddeso, mātarapitaro. Why the condition 'optionally'? Consider satthudassanaṃ and mātāpitaro.

64. Vijjāyonisambandhānamā tatra catthe.

64. For those related by knowledge or birth, ā is substituted when they themselves follow in a dvanda compound.

Ltupitādīnaṃ vijjāsambandhīnaṃ yonisambandhīnaṃ ca tesveva ltupitādīsu vijjāyonisambandhisuttarapadesu catthavisaye ā hoti. Hotāpotaro mātāpitaro, ltupitādīnaṃ tveva? Puttabhātaro, tatreti kiṃ? Pitupitāmahā, cattheti kiṃ? Mātubhātā, vijjāyonisambandhānanti kiṃ? Dātubhattāro.

For stems ending in -tu, and for pitar and so on, that are related by knowledge or birth, ā is substituted when a subsequent word from that same group, also related by knowledge or birth, follows in a dvanda compound. For example: hotāpotaro, mātāpitaro. Why the condition 'for stems ending in -tu, and for pitar and so on'? Consider puttabhātaro. Why 'when they themselves follow'? Consider pitupitāmahā. Why 'in a dvanda compound'? Consider mātubhātā. Why 'related by knowledge or birth'? Consider dātubhattāro.

65. Putte.

65. Before putta.

Putte [M 0.0137] uttarapade catthavisaye ltupitādīnaṃ vijjāyoni sambandhānamā hoti. Pitāputtā, mātāputtā.

When putta is the subsequent word in a dvanda compound, ā is substituted for the final of stems ending in -tu, and for pitar and so on, that are related by knowledge or birth. For example: pitāputtā, mātāputtā.

66. Cismiṃ.

66. Before the suffix ci.

Cippaccayante uttarapade ā hoti. Kesākesi, muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi.

When a word ending in the suffix ci follows, ā is substituted for the final of the preceding word. For example: kesākesi, muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi.

67. Itthiyambhāsitapumitthī pumevekatthe.

67. A feminine word with a corresponding masculine form becomes like the masculine in a compound referring to a single entity.

Itthiyaṃ vattamāne ekatthe samānādhikaraṇe uttarapade pare bhāsitapumā itthī pumeva hoti. Kumārabhariyo, dīghajaṅgho, yuvajāyo, itthiyanti kiṃ? Kalyāṇī padhānamesaṃ kalyāṇippadhānā, bhāsitapumeti kiṃ? Kaññābhariyo, itthīti kiṃ? Gāmaṇikulaṃ diṭṭhi assa gāmaṇidiṭṭhi, ekattheti kiṃ? Kalyāṇiyā mātā kalyāṇimātā.

When a subsequent word in apposition follows, referring to a single feminine entity, a feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form becomes like the masculine. For example: kumārabhariyo, dīghajaṅgho, yuvajāyo. Why the condition 'feminine entity'? Consider kalyāṇippadhānā. Why 'with a corresponding masculine form'? Consider kaññābhariyo. Why 'a feminine word'? Consider gāmaṇidiṭṭhi. Why 'a single entity'? Consider kalyāṇimātā.

68. Kvaci paccaye.

68. Sometimes before a suffix.

Bhāsitapumitthī paccaye kvaci pumeva moti. Byattatarā, byattatamā.

A feminine word with a corresponding masculine form sometimes becomes like the masculine before a suffix. For example: byattatarā, byattatamā.

69. Sabbādayo vuttimatte.

69. Sabba and so on, in a derivative formation.

Itthivācakā sabbādayo vuttimatte pumeva honti. Tassā mukhaṃ tammukhaṃ, tassaṃ tatra, tāya tato, tassaṃ velāyaṃ tadā.

Pronouns like sabba and so on, when referring to a feminine entity, become like the masculine in a derivative formation. For example: tammukhaṃ from tassā mukhaṃ; tatra from tassaṃ; tato from tāya; tadā from tassaṃ velāyaṃ.

70. Jāyāya jayaṃ patimhi.

70. For jāyā, jayaṃ is substituted before pati.

Patimhi pare jāyāya jayaṃ hoti, jayampatī, ‘jānipatī’ti pakatantarena siddhaṃ, tathā ‘dampatī, jampatī’ti.

When pati follows, jayaṃ is substituted for jāyā. For example: jayampatī. The form jānipatī is established by another rule, as are dampatī and jampatī.

71. Saññāyamudodakassa.

71. For udaka, uda is substituted in a proper name.

Saññāyamudakassuttarapade [M 0.0138] udādeso hoti. Udadhi, udapānaṃ.

In a proper name, when a subsequent word follows, uda is substituted for udaka. For example: udadhi, udapānaṃ.

72. Kumbhādīsu vā.

72. Optionally before kumbha and so on.

Kumbhādīsuttarapadesu udakassa udādeso vā hoti. Udakumbho udakakumbho, udapatto udakapatto, udabindhu udakabindhu, ākatigaṇo-yaṃ.

When kumbha and so on are the subsequent words, uda is optionally substituted for udaka. For example: udakumbho or udakakumbho; udapatto or udakapatto; udabindhu or udakabindhu. This is an open-ended list.

73. Sotādīsūlopo.

73. Before sota and so on, elision of u.

Sotādīsuttarapadesu udakassa ussa lopo hoti. Dakasotaṃ, dakarakkhaso.

When sota and so on are the subsequent words, the u of udaka is elided. For example: dakasotaṃ, dakarakkhaso.

74. Ṭa naña ssa.

74. For the negative particle nañ, a is substituted.

Uttarapade naña saddassa ṭa hoti. Abrāhmaṇo, ñakāro kiṃ? Kevalassa mā hotu pāmanaputto.

When a subsequent word follows, the particle nañ becomes a. For example, abrāhmaṇo. Why is the letter ñ specified? So that this does not happen to a simple na, as in pāmanaputto.

75. Ana sare.

75. Ana before a vowel.

Sarādo uttarapade naña saddassa ana hoti. Anakkhātaṃ.

When a subsequent word beginning with a vowel follows, the particle nañ becomes ana. For example, anakkhātaṃ.

76. Nakhādayo.

76. Nakha, etc.

Nakhādayo saddā anana ṭādesā nipaccante. Nāssa khamatthīti nakho, akhamaññaṃ, saññāsaddesu ca nipphattimattaṃ yathākathañci kattabbaṃnāssa kulamathīti nakulo, akulamaññaṃ, nakha nakula napuṃsakanakkhatta nāka evamādi.

Words such as nakha are formed irregularly, without the substitutions ana and a. For example: nakho is from 'nāssa khamatthi' (it has no forbearance); another form is akhama. And in the case of conventional terms, the derivation is merely a formation to be made in some way or other. For example: nakulo is from 'nāssa kulamatthi' (it has no family); another form is akula. Examples: nakha, nakula, napuṃsaka, nakkhatta, nāka, and so on.

77. Nago vāppāṇini.

77. Nago, optionally, when not denoting a living being.

Nagaiccappāṇini [M 0.0139] vā nipaccate. Nago rukkho, nago pabbato, ago rukkho, ago pabbato, appāṇinīti kiṃ? Ago vasalo sītena.

The form naga is optionally formed irregularly when not denoting a living being. For example: nago rukkho (a tree that is a naga), nago pabbato (a mountain that is a naga); or ago rukkho, ago pabbato. Why the condition 'when not denoting a living being'? Consider: ago vasalo sītena (the outcast does not go because of the cold).

78. Sahassa so-ññatthe.

78. Of `saha`, `sa` in another meaning.

Aññapadatthavutthimhi samāse uttarapade pare sahassa so vā hoti. Saputto, sahaputto, aññattheti kiṃ? Saha katvā, saha yujjhitvā.

In a compound that refers to another referent, `saha` optionally becomes `sa` when a subsequent word follows. For example: `saputto` or `sahaputto` (one who is with his son). Why the condition 'in another meaning'? Consider: `saha katvā` (having done together), `saha yujjhitvā` (having fought together).

79. Saññāyaṃ.

79. In a conventional term.

Sahassuttarapade so hoti saññāyaṃ. Sāssatthaṃ, sapalāsaṃ.

When it is a conventional term, `saha` becomes `sa` when a subsequent word follows. For example: `sāssatthaṃ`, `sapalāsaṃ`.

80. Appaccakkhe.

80. When not directly perceived.

Appaccakkhe gamyamāne sahassa so hotuttarapade, sāggi kapoto, sapisācā vātamaṇḍalikā.

When something not directly perceived is understood, `saha` becomes `sa` when a subsequent word follows. For example: `sāggi kapoto` (a pigeon with fire-like qualities); `sapisācā vātamaṇḍalikā` (a whirlwind with spirits).

81. Akāle sakatthe.

81. When not denoting time, and in its own meaning.

Sakatthappadhānassa sahasaddassa akāle uttarapade so hoti. Sampannaṃ brahmaṃ sabrahmaṃ, sacakkaṃ nidhehi, sadhuraṃ pājehi, akāleti kiṃ? Saha pubbaṇhaṃ, sahāparaṇhaṃ.

When the meaning 'with' is primary and the subsequent word does not denote time, the word `saha` becomes `sa`. For example: `sabrahmaṃ` (with Brahma); `sacakkaṃ nidhehi` (place it with the wheel); `sadhuraṃ pājehi` (drive it with the yoke). Why the condition 'when not denoting time'? Consider: `saha pubbaṇhaṃ` (with the forenoon); `sahāparaṇhaṃ` (with the afternoon).

82. Ganthantādhikye.

82. In the sense of 'end of a text' and 'excess'.

Ganthante [M 0.0140] ādhikye ca vattamānassa sahassa so hotuttarapade. Sakalaṃ jotimadhīte samuhuttaṃ, kālattho ārambho, ādhikye-sadoṇā khārī, samāsako kahāpaṇo, niccatthoyamārambho.

When `saha` has the meaning 'end of a text' or 'excess', it becomes `sa` when a subsequent word follows. In the sense of 'end of a text': `sakalaṃ jotimadhīte` (he studies the entire Jyotiṣa text). In the sense of 'excess': `sadoṇā khārī` (a `khārī` with a `doṇa` in excess); `samāsako kahāpaṇo` (a `kahāpaṇa` with a `māsaka` in excess). This rule is for invariable application.

83. Samānassa pakkhādīsu vā.

83. Of `samāna`, optionally before `pakkha`, etc.

Pakkhādīsuttarapadesu samānassa so hoti vā. Sapakkho samānapakkho, sajoti samānajoti, pakkhādīsūti kiṃ? Samānasīlo, pakkha, joti, janapada, ratti, pattinī, pattī, nābhi, bandhu brahmacārī, nāma, gotta, rūpa, ṭhāna, vaṇṇa, vayo, vacana, dhamma, jātiya, ghacca.

Before subsequent words such as `pakkha`, etc., `samāna` optionally becomes `sa`. For example: `sapakkho` or `samānapakkho` (of the same faction); `sajoti` or `samānajoti` (of the same light). Why the condition 'before `pakkha`, etc.'? To exclude cases like `samānasīlo` (of equal virtue). The list includes: `pakkha`, `joti`, `janapada`, `ratti`, `pattinī`, `pattī`, `nābhi`, `bandhu`, `brahmacārī`, `nāma`, `gotta`, `rūpa`, `ṭhāna`, `vaṇṇa`, `vayo`, `vacana`, `dhamma`, `jātiya`, `ghacca`.

84. Udare iye.

84. When `udara` is followed by the suffix `iya`.

Udare iye pare parato samānassa so vā hoti. Sodariyo, samānodariyo, iyeti kiṃ? Samānodaratā.

After `samāna`, when `udara` is followed by the suffix `iya`, `samāna` optionally becomes `sa`. For example: `sodariyo` or `samānodariyo` (born of the same womb). Why the condition 'before `iya`'? Consider: `samānodaratā` (the state of being from the same womb).

85. Rīrikkhakesu.

85. Before `-rī`, `-rikkha`, and `-isa`.

Etesu samānassa so hoti. Sarī, sarikkho, sariso.

Before these, `samāna` becomes `sa`. For example: `sarī`, `sarikkho`, `sariso` (similar, like).

86. Sabbādīnamā.

86. Of `sabba`, etc., `ā`.

Rīrikkhakesu sabbādīnamā hoti. Yādī, yādikkho, yādiso.

Before the suffixes `-rī`, `-rikkha`, and `-isa`, the final vowel of the pronouns `sabba`, etc., becomes `ā`. For example, from `ya`: `yādī`, `yādikkho`, `yādiso`.

87. Ntakimimānaṃ ṭākīṭī.

87. Of `anta` (in `bhavanta`), `kiṃ`, and `ima`, the substitutions are `ā`, `kī`, and `ī`.

Rīrikkhakesu [M 0.0141] ntasadda kiṃsadda imasaddānaṃ ṭākīṭī honti yathākkamaṃ. Bhavādī, bhavādikkho, bhavādiso, kīdī, kīdikkho, kīdiso, īdī, īdikkho, īdiso.

Before these suffixes, the words `anta` (in `bhavanta`), `kiṃ`, and `ima` become `ā`, `kī`, and `ī` respectively. For example: `bhavādī`, `bhavādikkho`, `bhavādiso`; `kīdī`, `kīdikkho`, `kīdiso`; `īdī`, `īdikkho`, `īdiso`.

88. Tumhāmhānaṃ tāmekasmiṃ.

88. Of `tumha` and `amha`, `tā` and `mā` in the singular.

Rīrikkhakesu tumhāmhānaṃ tāmā hontekasmiṃ yathākkamaṃ. Tādī, tādikkho, tādiso, mādī, mādikkho, mādiso. Ekasminti kiṃ? Tumhādī, amhādī, tumhādikkho, amhādikkho, tumhādiso, amhādiso.

Before these suffixes, `tumha` and `amha` in the singular become `tā` and `mā` respectively. For example: `tādī`, `tādikkho`, `tādiso` (like you); `mādī`, `mādikkho`, `mādiso` (like me). Why the condition 'in the singular'? In the plural, the forms are: `tumhādī`, `amhādī`; `tumhādikkho`, `amhādikkho`; `tumhādiso`, `amhādiso`.

89. Taṃ mamaññatra.

89. `Taṃ` and `maṃ` elsewhere.

Rīrikkhakantato aññasmiṃ uttarapade tumhāmhānamekasmiṃ taṃmaṃ honti yathākkamaṃ, tandīpā, mandīpā, taṃsaraṇā, maṃsaraṇā, tayyogo, mayyogoti bindulopo.

Before a subsequent word other than one ending in `-rī`, `-rikkha`, or `-isa`, `tumha` and `amha` in the singular become `taṃ` and `maṃ` respectively. For example: `tandīpā`, `mandīpā`; `taṃsaraṇā`, `maṃsaraṇā`. In `tayyogo` and `mayyogo`, the nasal sign (`bindu`) is elided.

90. Vetasseṭa.

90. Of `eta`, optionally `e`.

Rīrikkhakesvetasseṭa vā hoti, edī, etādī, edikkho, etādikkho, ediso, etādiso.

Before these suffixes, `eta` optionally becomes `e`. For example: `edī` or `etādī`; `edikkho` or `etādikkho`; `ediso` or `etādiso`.

91. Vidhādīsu dvissa du.

91. Of `dvi`, `du` before `vidha`, etc.

Dvissa du hoti vidhādīsu, duvidho, dupaṭṭaṃ evamādi.

`Dvi` becomes `du` before `vidha`, etc. For example: `duvidho` (twofold), `dupaṭṭaṃ` (double-layered), and so on.

92. Di guṇādīsu.

92. `Di` before `guṇa`, etc.

Guṇādīsu dvissa di hoti, dviguṇaṃ, diratti, digu evamādi.

Before `guṇa`, etc., `dvi` becomes `di`. For example: `diguṇaṃ` (double), `diratti` (for two nights), `digu` (a type of compound), and so on.

93. Tīsva.

93. Before `ti`, `a`.

Tīsu [M 0.0142] dvissa ahoti. Dvattikkhattuṃ, dvittipattapurā.

Before `ti`, the `i` of `dvi` becomes `a`. For example: `dvattikkhattuṃ` (two or three times); `dvittipattapurā` (cities with two or three bowls).

94. Ā saṅkhyāyāsatādo-naññatthe.

94. `Ā` before a numeral, except `sata`, etc., and when not in a different sense.

Saṅkhyāyamuttarapade dvissa ā hoti asatādo anaññadhattha. Dvādasa, dvāvīsati dvattiṃsa, saṅkhyāyanti kiṃ? Dirattaṃ, asatādoti kiṃ? Disataṃ, disahassaṃ. Anaññattheti kiṃ? Dvidasā.

Before a subsequent numeral, except `sata`, etc., and when not in a different sense, the `i` of `dvi` becomes `ā`. For example: `dvādasa` (12), `dvāvīsati` (22), `dvattiṃsa` (32). Why the condition 'before a numeral'? Consider `dirattaṃ` (two nights). Why 'except `sata`, etc.'? Consider `disataṃ` (200), `disahassaṃ` (2000). Why 'when not in a different sense'? Consider `dvidasā` (two decades).

95. Tisse.

95. For `ti`, `e`.

Saṅkhyāyamuttarapade tissa e hoti asatādo anaññatthe, terasa, tevīsa, tettiṃsa, saṅkhyāyaṃtveva? Tirattaṃ, asatādotveva? Tisataṃ, anaññatthetveva? Ticatukā.

Before a subsequent numeral, except `sata`, etc., and when not in a different sense, `ti` becomes `te`. For example: `terasa` (13), `tevīsa` (23), `tettiṃsa` (33). Why the condition 'before a numeral'? Consider `tirattaṃ` (three nights). Why 'except `sata`, etc.'? Consider `tisataṃ` (300). Why 'when not in a different sense'? Consider `ticatukā` (groups of three or four).

96. Cattālīsādo vā.

96. Optionally before `cattālīsā`, etc.

Tisse vā hoti cattālīsādo, tecattālāsaṃ ticattālīsaṃ, tepaññāsaṃ tipaññāsaṃ, tesaṭṭhi tisaṭṭhi, tesattati tisattati, teasīti tiyāsīti, tenavuti tinavuti, asatādotveva? Tisataṃ.

Before `cattālīsā` (40) and subsequent numerals, `ti` optionally becomes `te`. For example: `tecattālīsaṃ` or `ticattālīsaṃ` (43); `tepaññāsaṃ` or `tipaññāsaṃ` (53); `tesaṭṭhi` or `tisaṭṭhi` (63); `tesattati` or `tisattati` (73); `teāsīti` or `tiyāsīti` (83); `tenavuti` or `tinavuti` (93). The exception for `sata`, etc., still applies, hence `tisataṃ`.

97. Dvissā ca.

97. And for `dvi`, `ā`.

Asatādo-naññatthe cattālīsādo dvisse vā hoti ā ca. Dvecattālīsaṃ, dvācattālīsaṃ dvicattālīsaṃ, dvepaññāsaṃ, dvāpaññāsaṃ dvipaññāsaṃ iccādi.

Except before `sata`, etc., and when not in a different sense, before `cattālīsā` and subsequent numerals, `dvi` is optionally substituted by `dve` or `dvā`. For example: `dvecattālīsaṃ`, `dvācattālīsaṃ`, or `dvicattālīsaṃ` (42); `dvepaññāsaṃ`, `dvāpaññāsaṃ`, or `dvipaññāsaṃ` (52), and so on.

98. Bācattālīsādo.

98. `Bā` before numerals other than `cattālīsā`, etc.

Dvissa [M 0.0143] bā vā hoti acattālīsādo-naññatthe. Bārasa dvādasa, bāvīsati dvāvīsati, battiṃsa dvattiṃsa, acattālīsādoti kiṃ? Dvicattālīsaṃ.

`Dvi` optionally becomes `bā` before numerals other than `cattālīsā`, etc., when not in a different sense. For example: `bārasa` or `dvādasa` (12); `bāvīsati` or `dvāvīsati` (22); `battiṃsa` or `dvattiṃsa` (32). Why the condition 'before numerals other than `cattālīsā`, etc.'? To exclude `dvicattālīsaṃ` (42).

99. Vīsatidasesu pañcassa paṇṇapannā.

99. For `pañca`: `paṇṇa` and `pannā` before `vīsati` and `dasa`.

Vīsatidasesu paresu pañcassa paṇṇapannā honti vā yathākkamaṃ. Paṇṇavīsati pañcavīsati, pannarasva pañcadasa.

Before `vīsati` and `dasa`, `pañca` optionally becomes `paṇṇa` and `pannā` respectively. For example: `paṇṇavīsati` or `pañcavīsati` (25); `pannarasa` or `pañcadasa` (15).

100. Catussa cuco dase.

100. For `catur`: `cu` and `co` before `dasa`.

Catussa cuco honti vā dasasadde pare. Cuddasa, coddasa, catuddasa.

`Catur` optionally becomes `cu` or `co` before the word `dasa`. For example: `cuddasa`, `coddasa`, or `catuddasa` (14).

101. Chassa so.

101. For `cha`, `so`.

Chassa soiccayamādeso hoti dasasadde pare. Soḷasa.

The substitute `so` occurs for `cha` before the word `dasa`. For example: `soḷasa` (16).

102. Ekaṭṭhānamā.

102. For `eka` and `aṭṭha`, `ā`.

Ekaaṭṭhānaṃ ā hoti dase pare. Ekādasa, aṭṭhārasa.

`Eka` and `aṭṭha` are lengthened to `ekā` and `aṭṭhā` before `dasa`. For example: `ekādasa` (11), `aṭṭhārasa` (18).

103. Ra saṅkhyāto vā.

103. Optionally `ra` after a numeral.

Saṅkhyāto parassa dasassa ra hoti vibhāsā. Ekārasa ekādasa, bārasa dvādasa, pannarasa pañcadasa, sattarasa sattadasa, aṭṭhārasa aṭṭhādasa, pannabādesesu niccaṃ, idha na hoti catuddasa.

After a numeral, `dasa` optionally becomes `rasa`. For example: `ekārasa` or `ekādasa` (11); `bārasa` or `dvādasa` (12); `pannarasa` or `pañcadasa` (15); `sattarasa` or `sattadasa` (17); `aṭṭhārasa` or `aṭṭhādasa` (18). With the substitutes `panna-` and `bā-`, this change is obligatory. This does not apply to `catuddasa` (14).

104. Chatīhi ḷo ca.

104. After `cha` and `ti`, also `ḷo`.

Chatīhi [M 0.0144] parassa dasassa ḷo hoti ro ca, soḷasa sorasa, teḷasa terasa.

After `cha` and `ti`, `dasa` becomes `ḷasa` and also `rasa`. For example: `soḷasa` or `sorasa` (16); `teḷasa` or `terasa` (13).

105. Catuttha tatiyāna maḍḍhuḍḍhatiyā.

105. For `catuttha` and `tatiya` after `aḍḍha`: `uḍḍha` and `tiya`.

Aḍḍhā paresaṃ catutthatatiyānaṃ uḍḍhatiyā honti yathākkamaṃ. Aḍḍhena catuttho aḍḍhuḍḍho, aḍḍhena tatiyo aḍḍhatiyo, kathaṃ aḍḍhateyyoti? Sakatthe ṇye uttarapadavuḍḍhi.

After `aḍḍha`, `catuttha` and `tatiya` become `uḍḍha` and `tiya` respectively. For example: `aḍḍhena catuttho` gives `aḍḍhuḍḍho` (three and a half); `aḍḍhena tatiyo` gives `aḍḍhatiyo` (two and a half). How is the form `aḍḍhateyyo` derived? Through the suffix `ṇya` in its own sense, which causes vṛddhi of the subsequent member.

106. Dutiyassa saha diyaḍḍhadivaḍḍhā.

106. For `dutiya`, with `aḍḍha`: `diyaḍḍha` and `divaḍḍha`.

Aḍḍhā parassa dutiyassa saha aḍḍhasaddena diyaḍḍhadivaḍḍhā honti. Aḍḍhena dutiyo diyaḍḍho, divaḍḍho vā.

After `aḍḍha`, `dutiya` together with the word `aḍḍha` itself becomes `diyaḍḍha` or `divaḍḍha`. For example: `aḍḍhena dutiyo` gives `diyaḍḍho` or `divaḍḍho` (one and a half).

107. Sare kada kussuttaratthe.

107. Before a vowel, `kada` for `ku` in a pejorative sense.

Kussuttarapadatthe vattamānassa sarādo uttarapade kadādeso hoti. Kadannaṃ, kadasanaṃ, sareti kiṃ? Kuputto, uttarattheti kiṃ? Kuoḍḍho rājā.

For `ku` used in a pejorative sense, the substitute `kad` occurs before a subsequent word beginning with a vowel. For example: `kadannaṃ` (bad food), `kadasanaṃ` (bad seat). Why the condition 'before a vowel'? Consider `kuputto` (bad son). Why 'in a pejorative sense'? Consider `kuoḍḍho rājā` (where is the king of Oḍḍha?).

108. Kāppatthe.

108. `Kā` in the sense of 'little'.

Appatthe vattamānassa kussa kā hoti uttarapadatthe, appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ kālavaṇaṃ.

For `ku` used in the sense of 'little', `kā` is the substitute when a subsequent word follows. For example: `appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ` becomes `kālavaṇaṃ` (a little salt).

109. Purise vā.

109. Optionally before `purisa`.

Kussa purise kā hoti vā. Kāpuriso kupuriso, ayamappattavibhāsā, appatthe tu pubbena niccaṃ hoti īsaṃ puriso kāpuriso.

`Ku` optionally becomes `kā` before `purisa`. For example: `kāpuriso` or `kupuriso` (a bad man). This is an option where one was not previously available. However, in the sense of 'little', the substitution is invariable by the previous rule: `īsaṃ puriso` (a slight man) becomes `kāpuriso`.

110. Pubbāparajjasāyamajjhehāhassa ṇho.

110. After `pubba`, `apara`, `ajja`, `sāya`, and `majjha`, `ṇha` is substituted for `aha`.

Pubbādīhuttarapadassa [M 0.0145] ahassa ṇhādeso hoti, pubbaṇho, aparaṇho, ajjaṇho, sāyaṇho, majjhaṇho (paṇho).

After `pubba` and so forth, for the subsequent word `aha`, the substitute `ṇha` occurs. For example: `pubbaṇho` (forenoon), `aparaṇho` (afternoon), `ajjaṇho` (today), `sāyaṇho` (evening), `majjhaṇho` (midday).

Iti moggallāne byākaraṇe vuttiyaṃ

Thus in the commentary on the Moggallāna Grammar,

Samāsakaṇḍo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter: On Compounds.

4. Catuttho kaṇḍo (ṇādi)

4. The Fourth Chapter (Beginning with ṇa).

1. Ṇo vā pacce.

1. The suffix `ṇa` is optionally used in the sense of 'descendant'.

Chaṭṭhiyantā nāmasmā vā ṇappaccayo hoti apacce-bhidheyye, ṇakāro vuddhyattho, evamaññattāpi, vasiṭṭhassāpaccaṃ vāsiṭṭho, vāsiṭṭhī vā, opagavo, opagavī vā, veti vākyasamāsavikappanatthaṃ, tassādhikāro sakatthāvadhi.

After a noun ending in the sixth case, the suffix `ṇa` is optionally used when a descendant is to be denoted; the letter `ṇ` is for the purpose of vṛddhi. Thus also elsewhere. A descendant of Vasiṭṭha is `Vāsiṭṭho`, or `Vāsiṭṭhī`; a descendant of Upagu is `Opagavo`, or `Opagavī`. The word `vā` is for the purpose of providing an option between the analytical phrase and the derivative form. Its governing rule extends to the end of its own section.

2. Vacchādito ṇānaṇāyanā.

2. After `Vaccha` and so forth, the suffixes `ṇāna` and `ṇāyana` are used.

Vacchādīhi apaccappaccayantehi gottādīhi ca saddehi ṇānaṇāyanappaccayā vā honti apacce, vacchāno vacchāyano, kaccāno kaccāyano, yāgame kātiyāno, moggallāno moggallāyano, sākaṭāno sākaṭāyano, kaṇhāno kaṇhāyano iccādi.

After words such as `Vaccha`, etc., which end in a descendant-suffix, and after words such as `gotta` (clan), etc., the suffixes `ṇāna` and `ṇāyana` are optionally used in the sense of 'descendant'. For example: `vacchāno`, `vacchāyano`; `kaccāno`, `kaccāyano`; `kātiyāno`; `moggallāno`, `moggallāyano`; `sākaṭāno`, `sākaṭāyano`; `kaṇhāno`, `kaṇhāyano`, and so forth.

3. Kattikāvidhavādīhi ṇeyyaṇerā.

3. After `Kattikā`, `Vidhavā`, and so forth, the suffixes `ṇeyya` and `ṇera` are used.

Kattikādīhi vidhavādīhi ca ṇeyyaṇerā vā yathākkamaṃ honti apacce, kattikeyyo, venateyyo, bhāgineyyo iccādi[M 0.0146], vedhavero, bandhakero, nālikero, sāmaṇero iccādi.

After words such as `Kattikā`, etc., and `Vidhavā`, etc., the suffixes `ṇeyya` and `ṇera` are optionally and respectively used in the sense of 'descendant'. For example: `Kattikeyyo`, `Venateyyo`, `Bhāgineyyo`, etc.; and `Vedhavero`, `Bandhakero`, `Nālikero`, `Sāmaṇero`, etc.

4. Ṇyadiccādīhi.

4. After `Diti` and so forth, the suffix `ṇya` is used.

Ditippabhutihi ṇyo vā hoti apacce, decco, ādicco, koṇḍañño, gaggyo, bhātabbo iccādi.

After `Diti` and other such words, the suffix `ṇya` is optionally used in the sense of 'descendant'. For example: `Decco`, `Ādicco`, `Koṇḍañño`, `Gaggyo`, `Bhātabbo`, etc.

5. Ā ṇi.

5. After a stem ending in `a`, the suffix `ṇi` is used.

Akārantato ṇi vā hoti apacce, dakkhi, datthi, doṇi. Vāsavi, vāruṇi iccādi.

After a stem ending in the letter `a`, the suffix `ṇi` is optionally used in the sense of 'descendant'. For example: `Dakkhi`, `Datthi`, `Doṇi`, `Vāsavi`, `Vāruṇi`, etc.

6. Rājato ñño jātiyaṃ.

6. After the word `rājan`, the suffix `ñña` is used in the sense of 'caste'.

Rājasaddato ñño vā hoti apacce jātiyaṃ gamyamānāyaṃ, rājañño, jātiyanti kiṃ? Rājāpaccaṃ.

After the word `rājan`, the suffix `ñña` is optionally used in the sense of 'descendant' when caste is implied, forming `rājañño`. Why specify 'in the sense of caste'? To exclude a mere 'king's offspring' (`rājāpaccaṃ`).

7. Khattā yiyā.

7. After the word `khatta`, the suffixes `ya` and `iya` are used.

Khattasaddā yaiyā honti apacce jātiyaṃ, khatyo, khattiyo, jātiyaṃtveva? Khatti.

After the word `khatta`, the suffixes `ya` and `iya` are used in the sense of 'descendant' when caste is implied, forming `khatyo` and `khattiyo`. Why only 'in the sense of caste'? To exclude `khatti`, a descendant of an individual named Khatta.

8. Manuto ssasaṇa.

8. After the word `manu`, the suffixes `ssa` and `aṇa` are used.

Manusaddato jātiyaṃ ssasaṇa honti apacce, manusso, mānuso, itthiyaṃ manussā, mānusī, jātiyaṃtveva? Mānavo.

After the word `manu`, the suffixes `ssa` and `aṇa` are used in the sense of 'descendant' when species is implied, forming `manusso` and `mānuso`. In the feminine: `manussā` and `mānusī`. Why only 'in the sense of species'? To exclude `mānavo`, a descendant of the individual Manu.

9. Janapadanāmasmā khattiyā raññe ca ṇo.

9. After the name of a country, the suffix `ṇa` is used to denote a khattiya descendant and also its king.

Janapadassa yaṃ nāmaṃ, tannāmasmā khattiyā apacce raññe ca ṇo hoti, pañcālo, kosalo, māgadho, okkāko, janapadanāmasmāti [M 0.0147] kiṃ? Dāsarathi, khattiyāti kiṃ? Pañcālassa brāhmaṇassa apaccaṃ pañcāli.

After the name of a country, the suffix `ṇa` is used to denote a khattiya descendant and the king. For example: `Pañcālo`, `Kosalo`, `Māgadho`, `Okkāko`. Why 'after the name of a country'? To exclude cases like `Dāsarathi`. Why 'a khattiya'? To exclude `Pañcāli`, the descendant of a brahmin from Pañcāla.

10. Ṇya kurusivīhi.

10. After `Kuru` and `Sivi`, the suffix `ṇya` is used.

Kurusivīhi apacce raññe ca ṇyo hoti. Korabyo, sebyo.

After `Kuru` and `Sivi`, the suffix `ṇya` is used in the sense of a descendant and a king. For example: `Korabyo`, `Sebyo`.

11. Ṇa rāgā tena rattaṃ.

11. The suffix `ṇa` is used after a word for a dye, in the sense of 'dyed with that'.

Rāgavācitatiyantato rattamicchetasmiṃ atthe ṇo hoti, kasāvena rattaṃ kāsāvaṃ, kosumbhaṃ, yāliddaṃ, rāgāti kiṃ? Devadattena rattaṃ vatthaṃ, idha kasmā na hoti? ‘Nīlaṃ pīta’nti, guṇavacanattā vināpi ṇena ṇatthassābhidhānato.

After a word ending in the third case that denotes a dye, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'dyed with that.' For example: `kāsāvaṃ`, 'dyed with kasāva'; `kosumbhaṃ`; `hāliddaṃ`. Why specify 'a dye'? To exclude 'a cloth dyed by Devadatta.' Why is the suffix not used with words like `nīlaṃ` (blue) or `pītaṃ` (yellow)? Because they are words denoting a quality, and the intended meaning is conveyed even without the suffix.

12. Nakkhatteninduyuttena kāle.

12. After a word for a constellation, when it is conjoined with the moon, in the sense of time.

Tatiyantato nakkhattā tena lakkhite kāle ṇo hoti, tañce nakkhattaminduyuttaṃ hoti, phussī ratti, phussaṃ ahaṃ, nakkhatteneti kiṃ? Gurunā lakkhitā ratti. Induyutteneti kiṃ? Katthikāya lakkhito muhutto, kāleti kiṃ? Phussena lakkhitā atthasiddhi, ajjakattikāti kattikāyutte cande kattikāsaddo vattate.

After a word for a constellation ending in the third case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'time marked by that,' provided that constellation is conjoined with the moon. For example: `phussī ratti` (a Phussa night), `phussaṃ ahaṃ` (a Phussa day). Why 'by a constellation'? To exclude 'a night marked by the teacher.' Why 'conjoined with the moon'? To exclude 'a moment marked by the Katthikā constellation.' Why 'in the sense of time'? To exclude 'success marked by Phussa.' In the expression `ajjakattikā`, the word `kattikā` is used when the moon is conjoined with the Kattikā constellation.

13. Sā-ssa devatā puṇṇamāsī.

13. In the sense of 'that is its deity,' and after a word for a full-moon day.

Seti paṭhamantā assāti chaṭṭhyatthe ṇo bhavati, yaṃ paṭhamantaṃ, sā ce devatā puṇṇamāsīvā, sugato devatā assābhi [M 0.0148] sogato, māhindo, yāmo, vāruṇo, phussī puṇṇamāsī assa sambandhinīti phusso, māso, māyo, phagguno, citto, vesākho. Jeṭṭhamūlo, āsaḷho, sāvaṇo, poṭṭhapādo, assayujo, kattiko, māgasiro, puṇṇamāsīti kiṃ? Phussī pañcamī assa, puṇṇamāsī ca bhatakamāsasambandhinī na hoti… puṇṇo mā assanti nibbacanā, ato eva nipātanā ṇo sāgamo ca, māsasutiyāva na pañcadasa rattādo vidhi.

After a word in the first case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of the sixth case '...is its...,' when that word denotes a deity or a full-moon day. For example, 'one whose deity is the Sugata' is `sogato`; also `māhindo`, `yāmo`, `vāruṇo`. 'The month connected with the Phussī full moon' is `phusso māso`; similarly `māgho`, `phagguno`, `citto`, `vesākho`, `jeṭṭho`, `āsaḷho`, `sāvaṇo`, `poṭṭhapādo`, `assayujo`, `kattiko`, `māgasiro`. Why 'full-moon day'? To exclude cases like 'the fifth day of which is Phussī'.

14. Tamadhīte taṃ jānāti kaṇikā ca.

14. In the senses 'he studies that' and 'he knows that,' the suffixes `ṇa` and `ṇika` are used.

Dutiyantato tamadhīte taṃ jānātīti etesvatthesu ṇo hoti ṇo ṇiko ca, byākaraṇamadhīte jānāti vā veyyākaraṇo, chandaso, kamako, padako, venayiko, suttantiko, dvitaggahaṇaṃ puthageva vidhānatthaṃ jānanassa ca ajjhenavisayabhāvadassanatthaṃ pasiddhūpasaṅgahatthaṃ ca.

After a word in the second case, in the senses 'he studies that' and 'he knows that,' the suffixes `ṇa` and `ṇika` are used. For example, one who studies or knows grammar (`byākaraṇa`) is a `veyyākaraṇo`; similarly, `chandaso`, `kamako`, `padako`, `venayiko`, `suttantiko`. The mention of both senses is for the purpose of separate prescription, to show that knowing is also a subject of study, and to include well-known examples.

15. Tassa visaye dese.

15. In the sense 'its domain,' when it is a country.

Chaṭṭhiyantā visaye desarūpe ṇo hoti, vasātīnaṃ visayo deso vāsāto, deseti kiṃ? Cakkhussa visayo rūpaṃ, devadattassa visayo-nuvāko.

After a word in the sixth case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'domain' when it is a country. For example, the domain of the Vasātis is the `Vāsāto` country. Why 'a country'? To exclude cases like 'the domain of the eye is form' or 'the domain of Devadatta is recitation'.

16. Nivāse tannāme.

16. In the sense of 'dwelling place,' when it is a country with that name.

Chaṭṭhiyantā nivāse dese tannāme ṇo hoti, sivīnaṃ nivāso deso sebyo, vāsāto.

After a word in the sixth case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'dwelling place' when it is a country with that name. For example, the dwelling place of the Sivis is the `Sebyo` country; also `Vāsāto`.

17. Adūrabhave.

17. In the sense of 'being not far from'.

Chaṭṭhiyantā [M 0.0149] adūrabhave dese tannāme ṇo hoti, vidisāya adūrabhavaṃ vedisaṃ.

After a word in the sixth case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'being not far from' when it is a country with that name. For example, a place not far from Vidīsā is `Vedisaṃ`.

18. Tena nibbatte.

18. In the sense 'brought into existence by that'.

Tatiyantā nibbatte dese tannāme ṇo hoti, kusambena nibbattā kosambhī nagarī, kākandī, mākandī, sahassena nibbattā sāhassī parīkhā, hotumhi kattari karaṇe ca yathāyogaṃ tatiyā.

After a word in the third case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'brought into existence' when it is a place with that name. For example, the city brought into existence by Kusamba is `Kosambhī`; also `Kākandī`, `Mākandī`. The moat brought into existence for a thousand is `Sāhassī`. The third case is used here appropriately for the agent or instrument.

19. Tamīdhatthi.

19. In the sense 'that exists here'.

Tanti paṭhamantā idhāti sattamyatthe dese tannāme ṇo hoti, yantaṃ paṭhamantamatthi ce, udumbarā asmiṃ dese santīti odumbaro, bādaro, babbajo.

After a word in the first case, in the sense of the seventh case 'here,' the suffix `ṇa` is used when it is a country with that name, provided that the thing denoted by the first-case word exists there. For example, a country where udumbara trees exist is `Odumbaro`; also `Bādaro`, `Babbajo`.

20. Tatra bhave.

20. In the sense 'occurring there'.

Sattamyantā bhavatthe ṇo hoti, udake bhavo odako, oraso, jānapado, māgadho, kāpilavatthavo, kosambo.

After a word in the seventh case, the suffix `ṇa` is used in the sense of 'occurring.' For example, occurring in water (`udake`) is `odako`; also `oraso`, `jānapado`, `māgadho`, `kāpilavatthavo`, `kosambo`.

21. Ajjādīhi tano.

21. After `ajja`, etc., the suffix `tana` is used.

Bhavatthe ajjādīhi tano hoti, ajja bhavo ajjatano, svātano, hiyyattano.

In the sense of 'occurring,' the suffix `tana` is used after `ajja`, etc. For example, occurring today is `ajjatano`; also `svātano` (of tomorrow), `hiyyattano` (of yesterday).

22. Purāto ṇo ca.

22. After `purā`, the suffix `ṇa` is also used.

Purāiccasmā bhavatthe ṇo hoti tano ca, purāṇo, purātano.

After the word `purā`, in the sense of 'occurring,' the suffixes `ṇa` and `tana` are used. For example: `purāṇo`, `purātano`.

23. Amātvacco.

23. After `amā`, the suffix `acca` is used.

Amāsaddato [M 0.0150] acco hoti bhavatthe, amacco.

After the word `amā`, the suffix `acca` is used in the sense of 'occurring.' For example: `amacco`.

24. Majjhāditvimo.

24. After `majjha`, etc., the suffix `ima` is used.

Majjhādīhi sattamyantehi bhavatte imo hoti, majjhimo, antimo. Majjha, anta, heṭṭhā, upari, ora, pāra, pacchā, abbhantara, paccanta (puratthā, bāhira).

After `majjha` and other such words ending in the seventh case, the suffix `ima` is used in the sense of 'occurring.' For example: `majjhimo`, `antimo`. The group includes: `majjha`, `anta`, `heṭṭhā`, `upari`, `ora`, `pāra`, `pacchā`, `abbhantara`, `paccanta`, (`puratthā`, `bāhira`).

25. Kaṇaṇeyyaṇeyyakayiyā.

25. The suffixes `ka`, `ṇa`, `ṇeyya`, `ṇeyyaka`, `ya`, and `iya` are used.

Sattamyantā ete paccayā honti bhavatthe, kaṇa-kusinā rāyaṃ bhavo kosinārako, māgadhako, āraññako vihāro. Ṇeyya-gaṅgeyyo, pabbateyyo, vāneyyo. Ṇeyyaka-koleyyako, bārāṇaseyyako, campeyyako, mithileyyakoti eyyako. Ya-gammo, dibbo. Iyagāmiyo, udari-yo, diviyo, pañcāliyo, bodhipakkhiyo, lokiyo.

After a word in the seventh case, these suffixes are used in the sense of 'occurring': `ka`—occurring in Kusinārā is `kosinārako`; also `māgadhako`, `āraññako`. `ṇeyya`—`gaṅgeyyo`, `pabbateyyo`, `vāneyyo`. `ṇeyyaka`—`koleyyako`, `bārāṇaseyyako`, `campeyyako`, `mithileyyako` (also `eyyaka`). `ya`—`gammo`, `dibbo`. `iya`—`gāmiyo`, `udariyo`, `diviyo`, `pañcāliyo`, `bodhipakkhiyo`, `lokiyo`.

26. Ṇiko.

26. The suffix `ṇika` is used.

Sattamyantā bhavatthe ṇiko hoti, sāradiko divaso, sāradikā ratti.

After a word in the seventh case, the suffix `ṇika` is used in the sense of 'occurring.' For example: `sāradiko divaso` (an autumn day), `sāradikā ratti` (an autumn night).

27. Tamassa sippaṃ sīlaṃ paṇyaṃ paharaṇaṃ payojanaṃ.

27. In the senses: 'that is his skill,' '...his practice,' '...his merchandise,' '...his weapon,' '...his purpose'.

Paṭhamantā sippādivācakā assetichaṭṭhiyattheṇiko hoti, vīṇāvādanaṃ sippamassa veṇiko, modaṅgiko, vaṃsiko, paṃsukū- ladhāraṇaṃ [M 0.0151] sīlamassa paṃsukūliko, tecīvarikeva, gandhopaṇyamassa gandhiko, teliko, goḷiko, cāpo paharaṇamassa cāpiko, tomariko, muggariko, upadhippayojanamassa opadhikaṃ, sātikaṃ, sāhassikaṃ.

After a word in the first case that denotes a skill, practice, merchandise, weapon, or purpose, the suffix `ṇika` is used in the sense of the sixth case '...is his...'. Skill: one whose skill is playing the lute (`vīṇā`) is a `veṇiko`; also `modaṅgiko`, `vaṃsiko`. Practice: one whose practice is wearing rag-robes (`paṃsukūla`) is a `paṃsukūliko`; also `tecīvariko`. Merchandise: one whose merchandise is perfume (`gandha`) is a `gandhiko`; also `teliko`, `goḷiko`. Weapon: one whose weapon is the bow (`cāpa`) is a `cāpiko`; also `tomariko`, `muggariko`. Purpose: `opadhikaṃ`, `sātikaṃ`, `sāhassikaṃ`.

28. Taṃ hantarahati gacchatuñchati carati.

28. In the senses: 'he kills that,' 'he deserves that,' 'he goes,' 'he gleans,' 'he practices'.

Dutiyantā hantīti evamādīsvatthesu ṇīko hoti. Pakkhīhipakkhino hantīti pakkhiko, sākuniko, māyūriko. Macchehi-macchiko, meniko. Migehi-māgaviko hāriṇiko, ‘sūkariko’ti iko. Satamarahatīti sātikaṃ, sandiṭṭhiko, ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko, sāhassiko, ‘sahassiyo’ti iyo. Paradāraṃ gacchatīti pāradāriko, maggiko, paññāsayojaniko. Badare uñchatīti bādariko, sāmākiko. Dhammaṃ caratīti dhammiko, adhammiko.

After a word in the second case, the suffix `ṇika` is used in such senses as 'he kills,' etc. He kills: one who kills birds (`pakkhī`) is a `pakkhiko`; also `sākuniko`, `māyūriko`. One who kills fish (`maccha`) is a `macchiko`; also `meniko`. One who kills deer (`miga`) is a `māgaviko`; also `hāriṇiko`. `Sūkariko` is formed with `ika`. He deserves: one who deserves a hundred (`sata`) is `sātikaṃ`; also `sandiṭṭhiko`, `ehipassiko`. `Sāhassiko` (deserving a thousand); `sahassiyo` is also formed with `iya`. He goes: one who goes to another's wife (`paradāra`) is a `pāradāriko`; also `maggiko`, `paññāsayojaniko`. He gleans: one who gleans jujubes (`badara`) is a `bādariko`; also `sāmākiko`. He practices: one who practices the Dhamma is `dhammiko`; also `adhammiko`.

29. Tena kataṃ kītaṃ baddhamabhisaṅkhataṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ hataṃ hanti jitaṃ jayati dibbati khaṇati tarati carati vahati jīvati.

29. In the senses: done by him, bought by him, bound by him, prepared by him, mixed with, killed by him, he kills, conquered by him, he conquers, he plays with, he digs, he crosses, he practices, he carries, he lives by.

Tatiyantā katādisvatthesu ṇiko hoti. Kāyena kataṃ kāyikaṃ, vācasikaṃ, mānasikaṃ, vātena kato ābādho vātiko. Satena kītaṃ sātikaṃ, sāhassikaṃ, mūlatova, devadatena kītanti na hoti tadatthāppatītiyā. Varattāya baddho vārattiko, āyasiko, pāsiko. Ghatena abhisaṅkhataṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ vā ghātikaṃ, goḷikaṃ, dādhikaṃ, māricikaṃ. Jālena hato hantīti vā jāliko, bālīsiko. Akkhehi jitamakkhikaṃ, sālākikaṃ. Akkhehi jayati dibbatīti vā akkhiko. Khaṇittiyā [M 0.0152] khaṇatīti khāṇittiko, kuddāliko, devadattena jitaṃ, aṅgulyā khaṇatīti na hoti tadatthānavagamā. Uḷumpena taratīti oḷumpiko, ‘uḷumpiko’ti iko gopucchiko, nāviko. Sakaṭena caratīti sākaṭiko, ‘rathiko, parappiko’ti iko. Khandhena vahatīti khandhiko, aṃsiko, ‘sīsiko’ti iko. Vetanena jīvatīti vetaniko, ‘bhatiko, kayiko, vikkayiko, kayavikkayiko’ti iko.
