Vattamānassevavattumiṭṭhattā taṃsamīpassa taggahaṇena gahaṇā, purepurāsaddehi vā anāgatattāvagame tadā tassa vattamānattā, kālabyattayo vā eso, bhavanteva hi kālantarepi tyādayo bāhulakā ‘santesu parigūhāmi, mā ca kiñca ito adaṃ’ ‘kāyassa bhedā abhisamparāyaṃ, sahabyataṃ gacchati vāsavassa, ‘anekajātisaṃsāraṃ sandhāvissaṃ’ ativelaṃ na massissa’nti.

The endings ti, etc., are used after a verbal root to signify the present tense, which denotes an action that has begun but is not yet finished. For example: gacchati, gacchanti, gacchasi, gacchatha, gacchāmi, gacchāma; gacchate, gacchante, gacchase, gacchavhe, gacche, gacchāmhe. How then to explain 'Formerly, unrighteousness shines (dippati)' and 'Of old, I die (marāmi)'? Because of the desire to speak of it as present, what is near to the present is included by that designation. Or, because the future sense is understood from the words pure and purā, it is then considered present. Or, this is an interchange of tenses (kālavyatyaya), for the endings ti, etc., are frequently found in other tenses as well. For example: 'I conceal (parigūhāmi) among the good, and may I not give (adaṃ) anything from here'; 'On the breakup of the body, in the life to come, he goes (gacchati) to the companionship of Vāsava'; 'I will run on (sandhāvissaṃ) through the round of many births...'; 'they will not become intoxicated (massissanti) to excess.'

2. Bhavissati [M 0.0211] ssati ssanti ssasi ssatha ssāmi ssāma ssate ssante ssase ssavhe ssaṃ ssāmhe.

2. In the future tense: ssati, ssanti, ssasi, ssatha, ssāmi, ssāma; ssate, ssante, ssase, ssavhe, ssaṃ, ssāmhe.

Bhavissati anāraddhe atthe vattamānato kriyatthā ssatyādayo honti. Gamissati gamissanti, gamissasi gamissatha, gamissāmi gamissāma, gamissate gamissante, gamissase gamissavhe, gamissaṃ gamissāmhe.

To signify the future tense, which denotes an action that has not yet begun, the endings ssati, etc., are used after a verbal root. For example: gamissati, gamissanti, gamissasi, gamissatha, gamissāmi, gamissāma; gamissate, gamissante, gamissase, gamissavhe, gamissaṃ, gamissāmhe.

3. Nāme garahāvimhayesu.

3. When the particle nāma is used to express blame and wonder.

Nāmasadde nipāte sati garahāyaṃ vimhaye ca gamyamāne ssatyādayo honti. Ime hi nāma kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissanti, na hi nāma bhikkhave tassa moghapurisassa pāṇesu anuddayā bhavissati, kathaṃ hi nāma so bhikkhave moghapuriso sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ karissati? Tattha nāma tvaṃ moghapurisa mayā virāgāya dhamme desite sarāgāya cetessasi? Atthi nāma tāta sudinna ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasi, atthiyevihāpi nindāvagamo. Vimuye-acchariyaṃ vata bho abbhutaṃ vata bho santena vata bho pabbajitā vihārena viharanti, yatra hi nāma saññī samāno jāgaro pañcamattāni sakaṭasatāni nissāya nissāya abhikkantāni neva dakkhati na pana saddaṃ sossati, acchariyaṃ andho nāma pabbatamārohissati, badhiro nāma saddaṃ sossati.

When the particle nāma is present and a sense of blame or wonder is to be conveyed, the future endings ssati, etc., are used. For example, in blame: 'Indeed, will these who have such good qualities make such a claim?'; 'Truly, bhikkhus, will that foolish man have no compassion for living beings?'; 'How indeed, bhikkhus, will that foolish man make a hut entirely of clay?'; 'In that case, foolish man, though I have taught the Dhamma for the sake of dispassion, will you set your mind on passion?'; 'Indeed, dear Sudinna, will you eat the early morning sour gruel?' Even here, an implication of censure is understood. In wonder: 'It is wonderful, sirs, it is astonishing, sirs, how peacefully the ascetics dwell, where a man who is conscious and awake will not see five hundred carts pass right by him, nor will he hear the sound!'; 'Wonderful! A blind man will climb a mountain! A deaf man will hear a sound!'

4. Bhūte īuṃ ottha iṃ mhā ā ū se vhaṃ a mhe.

4. In the past tense (Aorist): ī, uṃ, o, ttha, iṃ, mhā; ā, ū, se, vhaṃ, a, mhe.

Bhūte parisamatte atthe vattamānato kriyatthā ī ādayo honti. Agamī agamuṃ, agamo agamittha, agamiṃ agamimhā[M 0.0212], agamā agamū, agamise agamivhaṃ, agama agamimhe. Bhūtasāmaññavacanicchāyamanajjatanepi ‘suvo ahosi ānando’.

To signify the past tense (Aorist), which denotes a finished action, the endings ī, etc., are used after a verbal root. For example: agamī, agamuṃ, agamo, agamittha, agamiṃ, agamimhā; agamā, agamū, agamise, agamivhaṃ, agama, agamimhe. When one wishes to state a general past action, the Aorist is used even for the non-recent past, as in: 'suvo ahosi ānando' (Yesterday Ānanda was).

5. Anajjatane ā ū o ttha a mhā ttha tthuṃ se vhaṃ iṃ mhase.

5. In the non-recent past (Imperfect): ā, ū, o, ttha, a, mhā; ttha, tthuṃ, se, vhaṃ, iṃ, mhase.

Avijjamānajjatane bhūte-tthe vattamānato kriyatthā āādayo honti.

To signify a past action not of today (Imperfect), the endings ā, etc., are used after a verbal root.

Āñāyyā ca uṭṭhānā, āñāyyā ca saṃvesanā;

Esajjatano kālo, aharubhataḍḍharattaṃ vā.

The time of 'today' (ajjatana) is known from the rising and setting; it is the day along with the preceding midnight.

Agamā agamū, agamo, agamattha, agama agamamhā, agamattha agamatthuṃ, agamase agamavhaṃ, agamiṃ agamamhase. Aññapadattho kiṃ? Ajja hiyyo vā agamāsi.

For example: agamā (he went), agamū (they went), agamo (you went), agamattha (you all went), agama (I went), agamamhā (we went); agamattha (he went), agamatthuṃ (they went), agamase (you went), agamavhaṃ (you all went), agamiṃ (I went), agamamhase (we went). Why the specification 'non-recent'? To exclude cases like: 'He went today or yesterday (agamāsi)'.

6. Parokkhe a u e ttha a mha ttha re ttho vho i mhe.

6. In the indirect past (Perfect): a, u, e, ttha, a, mha; ttha, re, ttho, vho, i, mhe.

Apaccakkhe bhūtānajjatane-tthe vuttamānato kriyātthā a ādayo honti. Jagāma jagamu, jagame jagapittha, jagama jagamimha, jagamittha jagamire, jagamittho jagamivho, jagami jagamimhe. Mūḷhavikkhittabyāsattacittena attanāpi kriyākatābhinibbattitakāle-nupaladdhā samānā phalenā-numīyamānā parokkhāva vatthuto, tenuttamavisayepi payogasamavo.

To signify a non-recent past action that was not witnessed (Perfect), the endings a, etc., are used after a verbal root. For example: jagāma (he went), jagamu (they went), jagame (you went), jagapittha (you all went), jagama (I went), jagamimha (we went); jagamittha (he went), jagamire (they went), jagamittho (you went), jagamivho (you all went), jagami (I went), jagamimhe (we went). Even an action performed by oneself, if it was not perceived at the time of its occurrence due to a mind that was confused, distracted, or obsessed, is in reality unwitnessed, being inferred from its result. Therefore, its use in the first person is also appropriate.

7. Eyyādo vātipattiyaṃ ssā ssaṃ su sse ssatha ssaṃ ssāmhā ssatha ssiṃsu sasse ssavhe ssiṃ ssāmhase.

7. In the sense of the non-occurrence of an action (Conditional): ssā, ssaṃsu, sse, ssatha, ssaṃ, ssāmhā; ssatha, ssiṃsu, ssase, ssavhe, ssiṃ, ssāmhase.

Eyyādo [M 0.0213] visaye kriyātipattiyaṃ ssādayo honti vibhāsā. Vidhurappaccayopanipātato kāraṇavekallato vā kriyāyātipatanamanipphatti kriyātipatti, ete ca ssādayo sāmatthiyātītānāgatesveva honti na vattamāne tatra… kriyātipatyasambhavā, sace paṭhamavaye pabbajjaṃ alabhissā arahā abhavissā, dakkhiṇena ce agamissā na sakaṭaṃ pariyā bhavissā, dakkhiṇena ce agamissaṃsu, agamisse agamissatha, agamissaṃ agamissāmhā, agamissatha agamissiṃsu, agamissase agamissavhe, agamissiṃ agamissāmhase, na sakaṭaṃ pariyābhavissā, vātikiṃ? Dakkhiṇe na ce gamissati na sakaṭaṃ pariyā bhavissati.

In the domain of the Optative, to express the non-occurrence of an action (Conditional), the endings ssā, etc., are used optionally. The 'non-occurrence of an action' (kriyātipatti) is the failure or non-completion of an action due to the absence of a supporting condition or a deficiency in the cause. These endings ssā, etc., by their nature, occur only in the past and future, not in the present, as the non-occurrence of an action is not possible there. For example: 'If I had obtained ordination in my youth, I would have become an arahant'; 'If he had gone by the southern route, the cart would not have overturned.' Similarly for other persons and numbers. Why 'optionally'? To allow for the use of the future tense, as in: 'If he goes by the southern route, the cart will not overturn.'

8. Hetuphalesveyya eyyuṃ eyyāsi eyyātha eyyāmi eyyāma etha eraṃ etho eyyavho eyyaṃ eyyāmhe.

8. In the sense of cause and effect: eyya, eyyuṃ, eyyāsi, eyyātha, eyyāmi, eyyāma; etha, eraṃ, etho, eyyavho, eyyaṃ, eyyāmhe.

Hetubhūtāyaṃ elabhūtāyañca kriyāyaṃ vattamānato kriyatthā eyyādayo vā honti, sace saṅkhārā niccā bhaveyyuṃ na nirujjheyyuṃ, dakkhiṇena ce gaccheyya na sakaṭaṃ pariyābhaveyya, dakkhiṇena ce gaccheyyuṃ, gaccheyyāsi gaccheyyātha, gaccheyyāmi gaccheyyāma, gacchetha gaccheraṃ, gacchetho gaccheyyavho, gaccheyyaṃ gaccheyyāmhe, na sakaṭaṃ pariyyābhaveyya, bhavanaṃ gamanaṃ ca hetu, anirujjhanaṃ apariyābhavanaṃ ca phalaṃ, iha kasmā na hoti ‘hantīhi palāyati, vassatīti dhāvati, hanissatīti palāyissatī’ti? Iti saddeneva hetuhetumantatāya jotitattā, vāti kiṃ? Dakkhiṇena ce gamissati na sakaṭaṃ pariyābhavissati.

In the case of an action that is a cause and an action that is an effect, the endings beginning with `eyya` are optionally used after a verbal root. For example: 'If formations were permanent, they would not cease'; 'If one were to go by the southern route, the cart would not overturn.' Likewise for `gaccheyyuṃ, gaccheyyāsi, gaccheyyātha, gaccheyyāmi, gaccheyyāma, gacchetha, gaccheraṃ, gacchetho, gaccheyyavho, gaccheyyaṃ, gaccheyyāmhe`, the cart would not overturn. Becoming and going are the cause; non-ceasing and not overturning are the effect. Why is this not the case here: 'Because he strikes, he flees'; 'Because it is raining, he runs'; 'Because he will strike, he will flee'? Because the causal relationship is already illuminated by the particle `iti`. Why 'optionally'? To allow for this case: 'If he goes by the southern route, the cart will not overturn.'

9. Pañhapatthanāvidhīsu.

9. In the senses of question, request, and injunction.

Pañho=sampucchanaṃ [M 0.0214] sampadhāraṇaṃ nirūpaṇaṃ kāriyānicchayanaṃ patthanā=yācanaṃ iṭṭhāsiṃ bhanañca, vidhi=vidhānaṃ niyojanaṃ kriyāsu byāpāraṇā, sā ca duvidhāva sādarānādaravasena… visayabhedena bhinnāyapi tadubhayānativattanato, etesu pañhādīsu kriyatthato eyyodayo honti, pañhe - kimāyasmā vinayaṃ pariyāpuṇeyya? Udāhu dhammaṃ, gaccheyyaṃ vāhaṃ uposathaṃ na vā gaccheyyaṃ, patthanāyaṃ-labheyyā-haṃ bhante bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ labheyyaṃ upasampadaṃ, passeyyaṃ taṃ vassasataṃ arogaṃ, vidhimhi-bhavaṃ pattaṃ paceyya, bhavaṃ puññaṃ kareyya, iha bhavaṃ bhuñjeyya, iha bhavaṃ nisīdeyya, māṇavakaṃ bhavaṃ ajjhāpeyya, anuññāpattakālesupi siddhāva… tatthāpi vidhippatītito, anuññāyaṃ-evaṃ kareyyāsi, pattakāle-kaṭaṃ kareyyāsi, patto te kālo kaṭakaraṇe, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ saṅgho uposathaṃ kareyya, etassa bhagavā kālo etassa sugata kālo yaṃ bhagavā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeyya, pesanepicchanti ‘gāmaṃ tvaṃ bhaṇe gaccheyyāsi’.

A question is an inquiry, a thorough consideration, an investigation, a determination of what should be done. A request is a plea, a wish, and a statement of what is desired. A directive is an instruction, an assignment, an engagement in actions; it is of two kinds, by way of respect and disrespect, and though differing in subject matter, it does not go beyond these two. In these cases of question, etc., the optative endings beginning with `eyya` occur after a verbal root. In a question: “Venerable sir, would you study the Vinaya, or the Dhamma?” “Should I go to the Uposatha, or should I not go?” In a request: “Venerable sir, may I receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One? May I receive the higher ordination?” “May I see you for a hundred years in good health.” In a directive: “Sir, you should cook what is for the bowl.” “Sir, you should make merit.” “Sir, you should eat here.” “Sir, you should sit here.” “Sir, you should teach the young man.” They are also established in the senses of permission and what is timely, for there too a directive is understood. In permission: “You should do so.” At the proper time: “You should make a mat.” “The time has come for you to make a mat.” “If it is the proper time for the Sangha, the Sangha should perform the Uposatha.” “This is the time, O Blessed One, this is the time, O Sugata, for the Blessed One to lay down a training rule for the disciples.” In sending, they wish: “Friend, you should go to the village.”

10. Tu antu hi tha mi ma taṃ antaṃ ssu vho e āmase.

10. Tu, antu, hi, tha, mi, ma; taṃ, antaṃ, ssu, vho, e, āmase.

Pañhādīsvete honti kriyatthato. Gacchatu gacchantu, gacchāhi gacchatha, gacchāmi gacchāma, gacchataṃ gacchantaṃ, gacchassu gacchavho, gacche, gacchāmase, pañhe-kinnu khalu bho byākaraṇamadhīyassu, patthanāyaṃ-dadāhi me, jīvatu bhavaṃ, vidhimhi-kaṭaṃ karotu bhavaṃ, puññaṃ karotu [M 0.0215] bhavaṃ, iha bhavaṃ bhuñjatu, iha bhavaṃ nisīdatu, uddisatu bhante bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkhaṃ, pesane-gaccha bhaṇe gāmaṃ, anumatiyaṃ - evaṃ karohi, pattakāle-kālo-yaṃ te mahāvīra uppajja mātukucchiyaṃ.

In the senses of question, etc., these endings occur after a verbal root. For example: `gacchatu` (let him go), `gacchantu` (let them go); `gacchāhi` (you go), `gacchatha` (you all go); `gacchāmi` (let me go), `gacchāma` (let us go); `gacchataṃ` (let them go), `gacchantaṃ` (let them go); `gacchassu` (you go), `gacchavho` (you all go); `gacche` (let me go), `gacchāmase` (let us go). In a question: “Indeed, sir, what grammar might you be studying?” In a request: “Give to me.” “May you, sir, live long!” In a directive: “Sir, you should make a mat.” “Sir, you should make merit.” “Sir, you should eat here.” “Sir, you should sit here.” “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.” In sending: “Go, friend, to the village.” In permission: “Do so.” At the proper time: “This is the time for you, O great hero, to arise in a mother’s womb.”

11. Satyarahesveyyādī.

11. In the senses of ability and worthiness, the endings beginning with `eyya`.

Sattiyaṃ ara hatthe ca kriyatthā eyyādayo honti. Bhavaṃ khalu rajjaṃ kareyya, bhavaṃ satto araho.

In the sense of ability and in the sense of worthiness, the endings beginning with `eyya` occur after a verbal root. For ability: 'Indeed, sir, you could rule the kingdom.' This implies: 'You, sir, are able and worthy.'

12. Sambhāvane vā.

12. Or in the sense of possibility.

Sambhāvane gamyamāne dhātunā vuccamāne ca eyyādayo honti vibhāsā. Api pabbataṃ sirasā bhindeyya, kriyātipattiyantu ssādī-asaniyāpi hato nāpatissā, sambhāvemi saddahāmi avakappemi bhuñjeyya bhavaṃ bhuñjissati bhavaṃ abhuñji bhavaṃ, kriyātipattiyantu ssādī-sambhāvemi nābhuñjissā bhavaṃ.

When possibility is being understood or expressed by the root, the endings beginning with `eyya` occur optionally. For example: 'He might even split a mountain with his head.' But in the sense of the non-completion of an action, the conditional endings beginning with `ssā` are used: 'Even if struck by lightning, he would not have fallen.' When the main verb expresses possibility: 'I suppose, I believe, I assume: Sir, you might eat,' or 'Sir, you will eat,' or 'Sir, you have eaten.' But in the sense of the non-completion of an action, the conditional endings beginning with `ssā` are used: 'I suppose, sir, you would not have eaten.'

13. Māyoge īāādī.

13. In conjunction with `mā`, the endings beginning with `ī` and `ā`.

Mā yoge sati īādayo āādayo ca vā honti. Mā su punapi evarūpamakāsi, mā bhavaṃ agamā vanaṃ, vātveva? Mā te kāmaguṇe bhamassu cittaṃ, mā tvaṃ karissasi, mā tvaṃ kareyyāsi, asakakālatthoyamārambho, buddho bhavissatīti padantarasambandhenānāgatakālatā patīyate, evaṃ kato kaṭo sve bhavissati, bhāvi kiccamāsīti.

When in conjunction with `mā`, the aorist endings beginning with `ī` and `ā` optionally occur. For example: 'Do not do such a thing again.' 'Sir, do not go to the forest.' Why 'optionally'? To allow for other forms: 'Let not your mind wander among the strands of sensual pleasure.' 'You shall not do it.' 'You should not do it.' This introduction is for the sense of a time other than its own. In 'The Buddha will be,' futurity is understood through connection with another word. Thus: 'The mat, having been made, will exist tomorrow.' And: 'It was a future task.'

Lunāhi [M 0.0216] lunāhitvevāyaṃ lunāti, lunassu lunassutvevāyaṃ lunā-tīti tvādīnamevetaṃ majjhimapurisekavacanānamābhikkhaññe dvibbavacanaṃ, idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti ‘eva mesa turito aññepi niyojentoviya kiriyaṃ karotī’ti, evaṃ lunātha lunāthatvevāyaṃ lunāti, lunavho lunavhotvevāyaṃ lunāti, tathā kālantaresupi lunāhi lunāhitvevāyaṃ aluni, alunā, lulāva, lunissatīti, evaṃ ssumhi ca yojanīyaṃ, tathā samuccayepi maṭhamaṭa, vihāramaṭetvevāyamaṭati, maṭhamaṭassu, vihāramaṭassutvevāyamaṭati, byāpārabhede tusāmaññavacanasseva byāpakattā anuppayogo bhavati, odanaṃ bhuñja, yāguṃ piva, dhānā khādetvevāya-majjhoharati.

'Cut! Cut!'—thus he cuts. 'Cut! Cut!'—thus he cuts. This is the reduplication of the second person singular endings in the sense of repetition. This is said: 'Thus this one, being hurried, performs the action as if urging on others.' Similarly: 'Cut! Cut!' (plural)—thus he cuts. 'Cut! Cut!' (plural middle)—thus he cuts. Likewise in other tenses too: 'Cut! Cut!'—thus he cut (aorist), he cut (imperfect), he has cut (perfect), he will cut (future). Thus it should also be applied with `ssu`. Likewise in combination: 'Wander! Wander!' or 'Wander in the monastery!'—thus he wanders. But when the actions differ, repetition is not used; instead, a general verb is used to encompass them, as in: 'Eat rice, drink gruel, eat roasted grain'—thus he consumes.

14. Pubbaparacchakkānamekānekesu tumhāmhasesesu dve dve majjhimuttamapaṭhamā.

14. Of the first six and the next six endings, with respect to the singular and plural of the pronouns `tumha` (you), `amha` (I), and the rest (third person), the pairs of endings are for the second, first, and third persons, respectively.

Ekānekesu tumhāmhasaddavacanīyesu tadaññasaddavacanīyesu ca kārakesu pubbacchakkānaṃ paracchakkānaṃ majjhimuttamapaṭhamā dve dve honti yathākkamaṃ kriyatthā, uttamasaddo-yaṃ sabhāvato tatiyaduke ruḷho, tvaṃ gacchasi, tumhe gacchatha, tvaṃ gacchase, tumhe gacchavhe, ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma, ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmhe, so gacchati, te gacchanti, so gacchate, te gacchante, sāmatthiyā laddhattā appayujjamānesupi tumhāmhasesesu bhavanti. Gacchasi, gacchatha, gacchase, gacchavhe, gacchāmi, gacchāma, gacche, gacchāmhe, gacchati, gacchanti, gacchate, gacchante.

With regard to the agent in the singular and plural, when denoted by the words `tumha` (you) and `amha` (I), and by words other than them, the pairs of endings of the first six and the next six are, respectively, for the second, first, and third persons, and occur after a verbal root. The word `uttama` (first person) is by its nature established for the third pair (i.e., `amha`). Examples: `tvaṃ gacchasi` (you go), `tumhe gacchatha` (you all go); `tvaṃ gacchase` (you go, mid.), `tumhe gacchavhe` (you all go, mid.); `ahaṃ gacchāmi` (I go), `mayaṃ gacchāma` (we go); `ahaṃ gacche` (I go, mid.), `mayaṃ gacchāmhe` (we go, mid.); `so gacchati` (he goes), `te gacchanti` (they go); `so gacchate` (he goes, mid.), `te gacchante` (they go, mid.). Because they are understood by context, they occur even when the pronouns `tumha`, `amha`, and others are not used: `gacchasi`, `gacchatha`, `gacchase`, `gacchavhe`, `gacchāmi`, `gacchāma`, `gacche`, `gacchāmhe`, `gacchati`, `gacchanti`, `gacchate`, `gacchante`.

15. Āīssādīsvaña vā.

15. Before the endings beginning with `ā`, `ī`, and `ssā`, `a` is an optional augment.

Āādo [M 0.0217] īādo ssā ādo ca kriyatthassa vā aña hoti. Ñakāro-nubandho, agamā, gamā, agamī, gamī, agamissā, gamissā.

Before the endings beginning with `ā`, `ī`, and `ssā`, the augment `a` is optionally prefixed to the verbal root. The `ñ` is an indicatory letter. Examples: `agamā` or `gamā`; `agamī` or `gamī`; `agamissā` or `gamissā`.

16. Aādīsvāho brūssa.

16. Before the endings beginning with `a`, `āha` is the substitute for `brū`.

Brūssa āho hoti aādīsu. Āha, āhu.

For the root `brū`, `āha` is the substitute before the endings beginning with `a`. Examples: `āha`, `āhu`.

17. Bhūssa vuka.

17. For `bhū`, `vuka` is the substitute.

Aādīsu bhūssa vuka hoti. Kakāro-nubandho, ukāro uccāraṇattho, babhūva.

Before the endings beginning with `a`, `vuka` is the substitute for `bhū`. The `k` is an indicatory letter; the `u` is for the sake of pronunciation. Example: `babhūva`.

18. Pubbassa a.

18. The vowel of the preceding syllable becomes `a`.

Aādīsu dvitte pubbassa bhūssa a hoti, babhūva.

Before the endings beginning with `a`, upon reduplication, the vowel of the preceding syllable of `bhū` becomes `a`. Example: `babhūva`.

19. Ussaṃsvāhā vā.

19. For `us` after `āha`, `aṃsu` is an optional substitute.

Āhādesā parassa ussa aṃsuvā hoti. Ahaṃsu, āhu.

After the substitute `āha`, `aṃsu` is an optional substitute for the ending `us`. Examples: `ahaṃsu` or `āhu`.

20. Tyantīnaṃ ṭaṭū.

20. For `ti` and `anti`, `ṭa` and `ṭū` are the substitutes.

Āhā paresaṃ tiantīnaṃ ṭaṭū honti. Ṭakārā sabbādesatthā, āha, āhu, atoyeva ca ñāpakā tiantīsu ca brūssā-ho.

After `āha`, `ṭa` and `ṭū` are the substitutes for `ti` and `anti`. The letter `ṭ` indicates the substitution of the whole ending. Examples: `āha`, `āhu`. And for this very reason, it is an indicator that `āha` is the substitute for `brū` also with the endings `ti` and `anti`.

21. Īādo vacassoma.

21. Before the aorist endings beginning with `ī`, `oma` is the substitute for `vac`.

Īādīsu vacassa oma hoti. Makāro-nubandho, avoca, īādoti kiṃ? Avacā.

Before the endings beginning with `ī`, `oma` is the substitute for `vac`. The `m` is an indicatory letter. Example: `avoca`. Why specify 'before the endings beginning with `ī`'? To prevent application in forms like `avacā`.

22. Dāssa daṃ vā mimesvadvitte.

22. For the unreduplicated root `dā`, `daṃ` is an optional substitute before `mi` and `ma`.

Advite [M 0.0218] vattamānassa dāssa daṃ vā hoti mimesu. Dammi demi, damma dema, advitteti kiṃ? Dadādhi dadāma.

For the root `dā` occurring unreduplicated, `daṃ` is an optional substitute before `mi` and `ma`. Examples: `dammi` or `demi`; `damma` or `dema`. Why 'unreduplicated'? To prevent it from applying in reduplicated forms like `dadāhi`, `dadāma`.

23. Karassa sossa kuṃ.

23. For `karo`, `kuṃ` is the substitute.

Karassa saokārassa kuṃ vā hoti mimesu. Kummi kumma, karomi karoma.

For `karo` (from the root `kar`), `kuṃ` is an optional substitute before `mi` and `ma`. Examples: `kummi` or `karomi`; `kumma` or `karoma`.

24. Kā īādīsu.

24. `kā` is the substitute for `karo` before aorist endings.

Karassa saokārassa kā hoti vā īādīsu. Akāsi akari, akaṃsu akariṃsu, akā akarā.

For `karo`, `kā` is an optional substitute before aorist endings. Examples: `akāsi` or `akari`; `akaṃsu` or `akariṃsu`; `akā` or `akarā`.

25. Hāssa, cāhaṅa ssena.

25. And for `hā`, `āhaṅa` is the substitute with `ssa`.

Karassa sossa hāssa ca āhaṅa vā hoti ssena saha. Kāhati karissati, akāhā akarissā, hāhati hāyissati, ahāhā ahāyissā.

For `karo` and `hā`, `āhaṅa` is an optional substitute along with `ssa` (the future/conditional marker). Examples: `kāhati` or `karissati`; `akāhā` or `akarissā`; `hāhati` or `hāyissati`; `ahāhā` or `ahāyissā`.

26. Labhavasacchidabhidarudānaṃ cchaṅa.

26. For the roots `labh`, `vas`, `chid`, `bhid`, and `rud`, `cchaṅa` is the substitute.

Labhādīnaṃ cchaṅa vā hoti ssenasaha. Alacchā alabhissā, lacchati labhissāti, avacchā avasissā, vacchati vasissati, acchecchā acchindissā, checchati chindissati, abhecchā abhindissā, bhecchati bhindissati, arucchā arodissā, rucchati rodissatī[M 0.0219], aññasmimpi chidassa vā cchaṅa yogavibhāgā, acchecchuṃ acchantiṃsu, aññesañca gacchaṃ gacchissaṃ.

For the roots `labh`, etc., `cchaṅa` is an optional substitute along with `ssa`. Examples: `alacchā` or `alabhissā`; `lacchati` or `labhissati`; `avacchā` or `avasissā`; `vacchati` or `vasissati`; `acchecchā` or `acchindissā`; `checchati` or `chindissati`; `abhecchā` or `abhindissā`; `bhecchati` or `bhindissati`; `arucchā` or `arodissā`; `rucchati` or `rodissati`. By splitting the rule, `cchaṅa` is an optional substitute for `chid` in other cases too, e.g., `acchecchuṃ` or `acchindiṃsu`. And for other roots too, e.g., `gacchaṃ` or `gacchissaṃ`.

27. Bhuja muca vaca visānaṃ kkhaṅa.

27. For the roots `bhuj`, `muc`, `vac`, and `vis`, `kkhaṅa` is the substitute.

Bhujādīnaṃ kkhaṅa vā hoti ssena saha. Abhokkhā abhuñjissā, bhokkhati bhuñjissati, amokkhā amuñcissā, mokkhatimuñcissati, avakkhā avacissā, vakkhati vaccissati, pāvekkhā pāvisissā, pavekkhati pavisissati, visassā-ññasmimpi vā kkhaṅa yogavibhāgā pāvekkhi, pāvisi.

For the roots `bhuj`, etc., `kkhaṅa` is an optional substitute along with `ssa`. Examples: `abhokkhā` or `abhuñjissā`; `bhokkhati` or `bhuñjissati`; `amokkhā` or `amuñcissā`; `mokkhati` or `muñcissati`; `avakkhā` or `avacissā`; `vakkhati` or `vaccissati`; `pāvekkhā` or `pāvisissā`; `pavekkhati` or `pavisissati`. By splitting the rule, `kkhaṅa` is an optional substitute for `vis` in other cases too. Example: `pāvekkhi` or `pāvisi`.

28. Āīādīsu harassā.

28. Before aorist endings, `ā` is the substitute for the root `har`.

Āādo īādo a harassa ā hoti vā. Ahā aharā, ahāsi ahari.

Before aorist endings beginning with `ā` or `ī`, `ā` is an optional substitute for the root `har`. Examples: `ahā` or `aharā`; `ahāsi` or `ahari`.

29. Gamissa.

29. For `gam`.

Āādo īādo a gamissa ā hoti vā. Agā agamā, agā agamī.

Before aorist endings beginning with `ā` or `ī`, `ā` is an optional substitute for `gam`. Examples: `agā` or `agamā`; `agā` or `agamī`.

30. Ḍaṃsassa ca chaṅa.

30. And for `ḍaṃsa`, `chaṅa` is the substitute.

Ḍaṃsassa gamissa ca chaṅa vā hoti āīādīsu. Aḍañchā aḍaṃsā, aḍañchi aḍaṃsī, agañchā agacchā, agañchi agacchī.

For `ḍaṃsa` and `gam`, `chaṅa` is an optional substitute before aorist endings. Examples: `aḍañchā` or `aḍaṃsā`; `aḍañchi` or `aḍaṃsī`; `agañchā` or `agacchā`; `agañchi` or `agacchī`.

31. Hūssa hehehihohi ssatyādo.

31. For `hū`, `he`, `hehi`, `ho`, and `hohi` are the substitutes before future endings.

Hūssa heādayo honti ssatyādo. Hessati, hehissati, hohissati.

For the root `hū`, substitutes beginning with `he` occur before future endings. Examples: `hessati`, `hehissati`, `hohissati`.

32. Ṇānāsu rasso.

32. Before `ṇā` and `nā`, there is shortening.

Kṇāknāsu [M 0.0220] kriyatthassa rasso hoti. Kiṇāti, dhunāti.

Before the class markers `ṇā` and `nā`, the vowel of the verbal root is shortened. Examples: `kiṇāti`, `dhunāti`.

33. Ā ī ñu mhā ssā ssamhānaṃ vā.

33. For `ā`, `ī`, `uṃ`, `mhā`, `ssā`, and `ssamhā`, optionally.

Esaṃ vā rasso hoti. Gama gamā, gami gamī, gamu gamū, gamimha gamimhā, gamissa gamissā, gamissamha gamissamhā.

For these endings, the vowel is optionally shortened. Examples: `gama` or `gamā`; `gami` or `gamī`; `gamu` or `gamū`; `gamimha` or `gamimhā`; `gamissa` or `gamissā`; `gamissamha` or `gamissamhā`.

34. Kusaruhehīssa chi.

34. After `kusa` and `ruha`, `ī` becomes `chi`.

Kusā ruhā ca parassa īssa chi vā hoti. Akkocchi akkosi, abhirucchi abhiruhi.

After `kusa` and `ruha`, the following `ī` optionally becomes `chi`. Examples: `akkocchi` or `akkosi`; `abhirucchi` or `abhiruhi`.

35. A ī ssāādīnaṃ byañjanassiña.

35. Of the consonant of endings beginning with `a`, `ī`, `ssā`, etc., `iña` is the substitute.

Kriyatthā paresaṃ aādīnaṃ īādīnaṃ ssaādīnañca-byañjanassa iña hoti vibhāsā. Babhuvittha, abhavitthā, anubhavissā, anubhavissati anubhossati harisati hassati, etesanti kiṃ? Bhavati, byañjanassāti kiṃ? Babhūva.

After a verbal root, the consonant of the following endings beginning with `a`, `ī`, `ssa`, etc., optionally becomes `iña`. Examples: `babhuvittha`, `abhavitthā`, `anubhavissā`, `anubhavissati`, `anubhossati`, `harisati`, `hassati`. Why 'of these endings'? Counter-example: `bhavati`. Why 'of the consonant'? Counter-example: `babhūva`.

36. Brūto tissīña.

36. After `brū`, `ti` becomes `īña`.

Brūto parassa tissa īña vā hoti. Bravīti, brūti.

After `brū`, the following `ti` optionally becomes `īña`. Examples: `bravīti` or `brūti`.

37. Kyassa.

37. For `kya`.

Kriyatthā parassa kyassa īña vā hoti. Pacīyati, paccati.

In the passive sense, the following `kya` optionally becomes `īña`. Examples: `pacīyati`, `paccati`.

38. Eyyātha sse a ā īthānaṃ o, a, aṃ, ttha, ttho, vhoka.

38. For `eyyātha`, `sse`, `a`, `ā`, and `ītha`: `o`, `a`, `aṃ`, `ttha`, `ttho`, `vhoka`.

Eyyāthādīnaṃ oādayo vā honti yathākkamaṃ. Tumhe bhaveyyātho bhaveyyātha, tvaṃ abhavissa abhavisse, ahaṃ abhavaṃ [M 0.0221] abhava, so abhavittha abhavā, so abhavittho, abhavī, tumhe bhavathavho bhavatha, āsahacaritova akāro gayhate, tho pana-nte niddesā tvādisambandhīyeva, tasseva vā nissitattā, nissayakaraṇampi hi suttakārāciṇṇaṃ.

For `eyyātha` and so on, `o` and so on optionally occur, respectively. Examples: `tumhe bhaveyyātho`, `bhaveyyātha` (you (pl.) would be); `tvaṃ abhavissa`, `abhavisse` (you (sg.) would be); `ahaṃ abhavaṃ`, `abhava` (I was); `so abhavittha`, `abhavā` (he was); `so abhavittho`, `abhavī` (he was); `tumhe bhavathavho`, `bhavatha` (you (pl.) are). The letter `a` is understood as that which is associated with `ā`. However, `tho`, from its specification, is related only to `tvā` etc., or because of its dependence on that, for making a dependency is indeed a practice of the authors of the suttas.

39. Uṃssiṃ svaṃsu.

39. For `uṃ`: `iṃsu`, `aṃsu`.

Umīccassa iṃsu aṃsu vā honti. Agamiṃsu, agamaṃsu, agamuṃ.

For `uṃ`, `iṃsu` and `aṃsu` optionally occur. Examples: `agamiṃsu`, `agamaṃsu`, `agamuṃ` (they went).

40. Eottā suṃ.

40. For `e`, `o`, and `tā`: `suṃ`.

Eādesato oādesato ca parassa umiccassa suṃ vā hoti. Nesuṃ, nayiṃsu, assosuṃ, assuṃ, ādesattākhyāpanatthaṃttaggahaṇaṃ.

After a substitute `e` or a substitute `o`, the following `uṃ` optionally becomes `suṃ`. Examples: `nesuṃ`, `nayiṃsu` (they led); `assosuṃ`, `assuṃ` (they heard). The inclusion of `tā` is for the purpose of indicating that this is a substitution.

41. Hūto resuṃ.

41. From `hū`: `resuṃ`.

Hūto parassa umiccassa resuṃ vā hoti. Ahesuṃ, ahavuṃ.

After `hū`, the following `uṃ` optionally becomes `resuṃ`. Examples: `ahesuṃ`, `ahavuṃ` (they were).

42. Ossa a i ttha ttho.

42. For `o`: `a`, `i`, `ttha`, `ttho`.

Ossa aādayo vā honti. Tvaṃ abhava, abhavi, abhavittha, abhavittho abhavo.

For `o`, `a` and the others optionally occur. Examples: `tvaṃ abhava`, `abhavi`, `abhavittha`, `abhavittho`, `abhavo` (you were).

43. Si.

43. Si.

Ossa si vā hoti. Ahosi tvaṃ ahuvo.

For `o`, `si` optionally occurs. Example: `ahosi`, `tvaṃ ahuvo` (you were).

44. Dīghā īssa.

44. After a long vowel, for `ī`.

Dīghato parassa īssa si vā hoti. Akāsi akā, adāsi adā.

After a long vowel, the following `ī` optionally becomes `si`. Examples: `akāsi`, `akā` (he did); `adāsi`, `adā` (he gave).

45. Mhātthānamuña.

45. For `mhā` and `ttha`: `muña`.

Mhātthānamhaña [M 0.0222] vā hoti. Agamhamhā agamimhā, agamuttha agamittha.

For `mhā` and `ttha`, `mha` optionally occurs. Examples: `agamhamhā`, `agamimhā`; `agamuttha`, `agamittha`.

46. Iṃssa ca siña.

46. And for `iṃ`: `si`.

Imiccassa siña vā toti mhātthānañca bahulaṃ. Akāsiṃ akariṃ, akāsimhā akarimhā akāsittha akarittha.

For `iṃ`, `si` optionally occurs, and for `mhā` and `ttha`, it is frequent. Examples: `akāsiṃ`, `akariṃ` (I did); `akāsimhā`, `akarimhā` (we did); `akāsittha`, `akarittha` (you (pl.) did).

47. Eyyuṃssuṃ.

47. For `eyyuṃ`: `uṃ`.

Eyyumiccassa ñaṃ vā hoti. Gacchuṃ gaccheyyuṃ.

For `eyyuṃ`, `uṃ` optionally occurs. Example: `gacchuṃ`, `gaccheyyuṃ` (they should go).

48. Hissa-to lopo.

48. Elision of `hi` after `a`.

Ato parassa hissa lopo vā hoti. Gaccha gacchāhi, atoti kiṃ? Karohi.

After `a`, the following `hi` is optionally elided. Examples: `gaccha`, `gacchāhi`. Why 'after `a`'? In `karohi`.

49. Kyassa sse.

49. Of `kya`, before `ssa`.

Kyassa vā lopo hoti sse. Anvabhavissā anvabhūyissā, anubhavissati anuchūyissati.

`kya` is optionally elided when `ssa` follows. Examples: `anvabhavissā`, `anvabhūyissā`; `anubhavissati`, `anubhūyissati`.

50. Atthiteyyādicchannaṃ sa su sa satha saṃ sāma.

50. For the six optative endings after `atthi` (root `as`), the substitutes are `sa`, `su`, `sa`, `satha`, `saṃ`, and `sāma`.

Asa=bhuviccasmā paresaṃ eyyādicchannaṃ sādayo honti yathākkamaṃ. Assa, assu, assa, assatha, assaṃ, assāma.

After the roots `as` and `bhū`, for the six following optative endings beginning with `eyya`, the substitutes are `sa` and the others, respectively. Examples: `assa`, `assu`, `assa`, `assatha`, `assaṃ`, `assāma`.

51. Ādidvinnamiyāiyuṃ.

51. Of the first two: `iyā` and `iyuṃ`.

Atthiteyyādicchannaṃ ādibhūtānaṃ dvinnaṃ iyā iyuṃ honti yathākkamaṃ. Siyā, siyuṃ.

For the first two of the six optative endings after `atthi` (root `as`), the substitutes are `iyā` and `iyuṃ` respectively. Examples: `siyā`, `siyuṃ`.

52. Tassa tho.

52. For `ta`: `tho`.

Atthito [M 0.0223] parassa takārassa tho hoti. Atthi, atthu.

Following the root `as` (in the form `atthi`), a subsequent `t` becomes `th`. For example: `atthu`.

53. Sihisvaṭa.

53. Before `si` and `hi`, `aṭa`.

Atthissa aṭa hoti sihisu, ṭo sabbādesattho. Asi ahi.

For the root `as` (in the form `atthi`), `aṭa` is the substitute before the endings `si` and `hi`; the `ṭ` indicates that it is a substitute for the entire root. For example: `asi`, `ahi`.

54. Mimānaṃ vā mhimhā ca.

54. For `mi` and `ma`, optionally `mhi` and `mhā`.

Atthismā paresaṃ mimānaṃ mhimhā vā honti, taṃsanniyogenaatthissa aṭa ca. Amhi asmi, amha asma.

After the root `as` (in the form `atthi`), for the following endings `mi` and `ma`, the optional substitutes are `mhi` and `mhā` respectively; and in conjunction with this, `aṭa` is the substitute for the root. For example: `amhi` or `asmi`; `amha` or `asma`.

55. Esu si.

55. Before these, the letter `s`.

Esu mimesu atthissa sakāro hoti. Asmi asma, pararūpabādhanatthaṃ.

Before these endings `mi` and `ma`, the `s` of the root `as` is present. For example: `asmi`, `asma`. This is for the purpose of preventing coalescence with the following form.

56. Īādo dīgho.

56. Before `ī`, etc., there is lengthening.

Atthissa dīgho hoti īādimhi. Āsi, āsuṃ, āsi, āsittha, āsiṃ, āsiṃ mhā.

For the root `as`, the vowel is lengthened before aorist endings beginning with `ī`. For example: `āsi`, `āsuṃ`, `āsi`, `āsittha`, `āsiṃ`, `āsimhā`.

57. Himimesvassa.

57. Before `hi`, `mi`, and `ma`, of `a`.

Akārassa dīgho hoti himimesu. Pacāhi, pacāmi, pacāma, muyhāmi.

The vowel `a` of a verbal stem is lengthened before the endings `hi`, `mi`, and `ma`. For example: `pacāhi`, `pacāmi`, `pacāma`, `muyhāmi`.

58. Sakā ṇāssa kha īādo.

58. After `sak`, for `ṇā`, `kha` before `ī`, etc.

Sakasmā kṇāssakhohoti īādīsu. Asakkhi, asakkhiṃsu.

After the root `sak`, `kh` is the substitute for the suffix `ṇā` before aorist endings. For example: `asakkhi`, `asakkhiṃsu`.

59. Sse vā.

59. Optionally before `ssa`.

Sakasmā [M 0.0224] kṇassakho vā hoti sse. Sakkhissā sakkuṇissā, sakkhissati, sakkuṇissati.

After the root `sak`, `kh` is the optional substitute for the suffix `ṇā` before the future ending `ssa`. For example: `sakkhissā` or `sakkuṇissā`; `sakkhissati` or `sakkuṇissati`.

60. Tesu suto kṇokṇānaṃ roṭa.

60. After `su`, in those cases, elision of `kṇo` and `kṇā`.

Tesu īādissesu suto paresaṃ kṇokṇānaṃ roṭa vā hoti. Assosi asuṇi, assossā asuṇissā, sossati suṇissati.

In those cases, i.e., before aorist and future endings, after the root `su`, the suffixes `ṇo` and `ṇā` are optionally elided. For example: `assosi` or `asuṇi`; `assossā` or `asuṇissā`; `sossati` or `suṇissati`.

61. Ñāssa sanāssa nāyo timhi. Sanāssa ñāssa nāyo vā hoti timhi. Nāyati, jānāti.

61. For the root `ñā` with its suffix `nā`, `nāya` is the optional substitute before the ending `ti`. For example: `nāyati`, `jānāti`.

62. Ñāmhi jaṃ.

62. In the case of `ñā`, `jaṃ`.

Ñādese sanāssa ñāssa jaṃ (vā) hoti. Jaññā (jāneyya).

In place of the root `ñā` with its suffix `nā`, `jaṃ` is the optional substitute before the optative ending. For example: `jaññā` (equivalent to `jāneyya`).

63. Eyyāssiyāñā vā.

63. For `eyya`, optionally `iyā` and `ñā`.

Ñāto eyyāssa iyāñā honti vā. Jāniyā, jaññā jāneyya.

After the root `ñā`, `iyā` and `ñā` are optional substitutes for the optative ending `eyya`. For example: `jāniyā`, `jaññā`, `jāneyya`.

64. Īssatyādīsu knālopo.

64. Before `ī`, `ssati`, etc., there is elision of `nā`.

Īādo ssatyādo ca ñāto knālopo vā hoti. Aññāsi ajāni, ñassati jānissati.

After the root `ñā`, the suffix `nā` is optionally elided before aorist and future endings. For example: `aññāsi` or `ajāni`; `ñassati` or `jānissati`.

65. Ssassa hi kamme.

65. For `ssa`, `hi` in the passive.

Ñāto parassa ssassa hi vā hoti kamme. Paññāyihiti paññāyissati.

After the root `ñā`, the future ending `ssa` is optionally replaced by `hi` in the passive voice. For example: `paññāyihiti` or `paññāyissati`.

66. Etismā.

66. From `e` (root `i`).

Etismā [M 0.0225] parassa ssassa hi hoti vā. Ehiti essati.

After `e` (from the root `i`, to go), the future ending `ssa` is optionally replaced by `hi`. For example: `ehiti` or `essati`.

67. Hanā chakhā.

67. From `han`, `cha` and `khā`.

Hanā ssassa chakhā vā honti. Hañchāmi hanissāmi, paṭihaṅkhāmi paṭihanissāmi.

After the root `han`, the future ending `ssa` is optionally replaced by `cha` or `khā`. For example: `hañchāmi` or `hanissāmi`; `paṭihaṅkhāmi` or `paṭihanissāmi`.

68. Hāto ha.

68. After `hā`, `ha`.

Hāto parassa ssassa ha hoti vā. Hāhati jahissati.

After the root `hā`, the future ending `ssa` is optionally replaced by `ha`. For example: `hāhati` or `jahissati`.

69. Dakkha kha hehi hohīhi lopo.

69. After `dakkha` (from `dis`), `kha` (from `khyā`), and in the forms `hehi` and `hohi` (from `bhū`), there is elision of the imperative `hi` ending.

Dakkhādīhi ādesehi parassa ssassa lopo vā hoti. Dakkhati dakkhissati, sakkhati sakkhissati, hehiti hehissatihohiti hohissati.

After the substitutes beginning with `dakkha`, the `ssa` of the future ending is optionally elided. For example: `dakkhati` for `dakkhissati`; `sakkhati` for `sakkhissati`; `hehiti` for `hehissati`; `hohiti` for `hohissati`.

70. Kayireyyasseyyumādīnaṃ.

70. Of `kayira`, `eyya`, `assa`, `eyyum`, and others.

Kayirā parassa eyyumādīnaṃ eyyassa lopo hoti. Kayiruṃ, kayirāsi, kayirātha, kahirāmi, kayirāma.

After `kayir`, the `eyya` of the following optative endings beginning with `eyyum` is elided. For example: `kayiruṃ`, `kayirāsi`, `kayirātha`, `kayirāmi`, `kayirāma`.

71. Ṭā.

71. Ṭā.

Kayirā parassa eyyassa ṭā hoti. So kayirā.

After `kayir`, the following ending `eyya` becomes `ā`. For example: `so kayirā`.

72. Ethassā.

72. Of `etha`, `ā`.

Kayirā parassa ethassa ā hoti. Kayirātha.

After `kayir`, the following ending `etha` becomes `ātha`. For example: `kayirātha`.

73. Labhā iṃ īnaṃ thaṃ thā vā.

73. From `labh`: of `iṃ` and `ī`, `thaṃ` and `thā` are the optional substitutes.

Labhasmā [M 0.0226] iṃīiccesaṃ thaṃthā honti vā. Alatthaṃ alabhiṃ, alattha alabhi.

From the root `labh`, the aorist endings `iṃ` and `ī` are optionally replaced by `thaṃ` and `thā` respectively. For example: `alatthaṃ` or `alabhiṃ`; `alattha` or `alabhi`.

74. Gurupubbā rassā re ntentīnaṃ.

74. After a short vowel preceded by a heavy syllable: `re` for `nte` and `ntī`.

Gurupubbasmā rassā paresaṃ ntentīnaṃ re vā hoti. Gacchare gacchanti, gacchare gacchante, gamissare gamissanti, gamissare gamissante, gurupubbāti kiṃ? Paca, rassati kiṃ? Honti.

After a stem ending in a short vowel that is preceded by a heavy syllable, the following endings `nte` and `ntī` are optionally replaced by `re`. For example: `gacchare` for `gacchanti`; `gacchare` for `gacchante`; `gamissare` for `gamissanti`; `gamissare` for `gamissante`. Why the condition 'preceded by a heavy syllable'? Consider `paca`. Why the condition 'short vowel'? Consider `honti`.

75. Eyyeyyāseyyannaṃ ṭe.

75. Of `eyya`, `eyyāsi`, and `eyyaṃ`, the substitute is `e`.

Eyyādīnaṃ ṭe vā hoti. So kare kareyya, tvaṃ kare kareyyāsi, ahaṃ kare kareyyaṃ.

The endings `eyya`, `eyyāsi`, and `eyyaṃ` are optionally replaced by `e`. For example: `so kare` or `kareyya`; `tvaṃ kare` or `kareyyāsi`; `ahaṃ kare` or `kareyyaṃ`.

76. Ovikaraṇassu paracchakke.

76. Of the conjugational sign `o`: `u` in the middle voice.

Ovikaraṇassa u hoti paracchakke visaye. Tanute.

The conjugational sign `o` becomes `u` in the domain of the middle voice. For example: `tanute`.

77. Pubbacchakke vā kvaci.

77. In the active voice, optionally in some cases.

Ovikaraṇassa u hoti vā kvaci pubbacchakke. Vanuti vanoti.

The conjugational sign `o` optionally becomes `u` in some cases in the active voice. For example: `vanuti` or `vanoti`.

78. Eyyāmassemu ca.

78. Of `eyyāma`, also `emu`.

Eyyāmassemu vā hoti u ca. Bhavemha, bhaveyyāmu bhaveyyāma.

The optative ending `eyyāma` is optionally replaced by `emu`, and its `ā` also becomes `u`. For example: `bhavemha`, `bhaveyyāmu`, `bhaveyyāma`.

Iti moggallāne byākaraṇe vuttiyaṃ

Thus in the Vutti on the Moggallāna Grammar,

Tyādikaṇḍo chaṭṭho.

The Sixth Chapter: On the Verbal Endings.

7. Sattamo kaṇḍo (ṇvādi)

7. The Seventh Chapter (Kṛt Suffixes beginning with `ṇvu`)

“Bahulaṃ” [M 0.0227] (1.58) “kriyatthā”ti (5.14) ca sabbattha vatthate.

The principles of `bahulaṃ` (wide application) (1.58) and `kriyatthā` (denoting the meaning of an action) (5.14) apply throughout.

1. Cara dara kara raha jana sana tala sāda sādha kasāsa caṭāya vāhi ṇu.

1. From the roots `car`, `dar`, `kar`, `rah`, `jan`, `san`, `tal`, `sād`, `sādh`, `kas`, `as`, `caṭ`, `ay`, and `vā`, the suffix `ṇu` is added.

Cara-gatibhakkhaṇesu, dara-daraṇe, kara-karaṇe, raha-cāge, jana-janane, sana-sambhattiyaṃ, tala-patiṭṭhāyaṃ, sāda-assādane, sādha-saṃsiddhiyaṃ, kasa-vilekhane, asa-khepane, caṭa-bhedane, aya-iti gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, vā-gatigandhanesu, etehi kriyatthehi bahulaṃ ṇu hoti. “Assā ṇānubandhe”ti (5.84) upantassa assa ā, carati hadaye manuññabhāvenāti cāru=sobhanaṃ. Darīyatīti dāra=kaṭṭhaṃ. Karotīti kāru=sippī, magha vā, visukammo ca. Rahati candādīnaṃ sobhāvisesaṃ nāsetīti rāhu=asurindo. Jāyati gamanāgamanaṃ anenātijānu=jaṅghorūnaṃ sandhi. Saneti attani bhattiṃ uppādetīti sānu=girippadeso. Talanti patiṭṭhahanti ettha dantāti tālu=vadanekadeso. Sā dīyati assādīyatīti sādu=madhuraṃ. Sādheti attaparahitanti sādhu=sajjano. Kasīyatīti kāsu=āvāṭo, asati sīghabhāvena pavattatīti āsu=sīghaṃ. Caṭati bhindati amanuññabhāvanti cāṭu=manuñño. Ayanti pavattanti sattā etenāti āyu=jīvitaṃ. “Assā ṇāpimhi yuka” iti (5.91) yuka- vāti gacchatīti vāyu-vāto.

The root `car` in the sense of 'moving' and 'eating'; `dar` in 'splitting'; `kar` in 'doing'; `rah` in 'abandoning'; `jan` in 'producing'; `san` in 'devotion'; `tal` in 'establishing'; `sād` in 'tasting'; `sādh` in 'accomplishing'; `kas` in 'scratching'; `as` in 'throwing'; `caṭ` in 'splitting'; `ay` in 'going' (a root from the Daṇḍaka list); `vā` in 'moving' and 'smelling'—from these roots in these meanings, the suffix `ṇu` is added with wide application. By the rule '`ā` for `a` when `ṇ` is an anubandha' (5.84), the preceding `a` becomes `ā`. `cāru` (beautiful) from `carati hadaye manuññabhāvena iti cāru` (it moves in the heart in a pleasing way). `dāru` (wood) from `darīyati iti dāru` (it is split). `kāru` (artisan, or Magha, or Visukamma) from `karoti iti kāru` (he makes). `rāhu` (the Asura lord) from `rahati candādīnaṃ sobhāvisesaṃ nāseti iti rāhu` (it makes the special splendor of the moon, etc., disappear). `jānu` (the joint of the shin and thigh) from `jāyati gamanāgamanaṃ anena iti jānu` (coming and going is produced by this). `sānu` (a mountain ridge) from `saneti attani bhattiṃ uppādeti iti sānu` (it generates devotion in oneself). `tālu` (a part of the mouth) from `talanti patiṭṭhahanti ettha dantā iti tālu` (teeth are established here). `sādu` (sweet) from `sādīyati assādīyatīti sādu` (it is tasted, it is savored). `sādhu` (a virtuous person) from `sādheti attaparahitanti sādhu` (he accomplishes his own and others' welfare). `kāsu` (a pit) from `kasīyati iti kāsu` (it is dug/scratched). `āsu` (swift) from `asati sīghabhāvena pavattati iti āsu` (it proceeds with speed). `cāṭu` (pleasing) from `caṭati bhindati amanuññabhāvanti cāṭu` (it splits/destroys what is unpleasing). `āyu` (life) from `ayanti pavattanti sattā etena iti āyu` (beings proceed/live by this). By the rule '`yuk` after `ā` even when `ṇ` is not present' (5.91), the augment `yuk` is added. `vāyu` (wind) from `vāti gacchati iti vāyu` (it blows, it moves).

2. Bhara [M 0.0228] mara cara tara ara gara hana tana mana bhama kita dhana baṃha kambamba cakkha bhikkha saṃkindanda yaja paṭāṇāsa vasa pasa paṃsa bandhā u.

2. From the roots `bhar`, `mar`, `car`, `tar`, `ar`, `gar`, `han`, `tan`, `man`, `bham`, `kit`, `dhan`, `baṃh`, `kamb`, `amb`, `cakkh`, `bhikkh`, `saṃk`, `ind`, `and`, `yaj`, `paṭ`, `aṇ`, `as`, `vas`, `pas`, `paṃs`, and `bandh`, the suffix `u` is added.

Bhara-bharaṇe, mara-pāṇacāge, cara-gatibhakkhaṇesu, tara taraṇe, ara-gamane, gara ghara-secane, girāti vā nipātanā akāro, hana-hiṃ sāyaṃ, tana-vittāre, mana-ñāṇe, bhama-anavaṭṭhāne, kita-nivāse, dhana-sadde, baṃha braha brūha-vuddhiyaṃ, kamba-saṃvaraṇe, amba-sadde, cakkha ikkha dassane, bhikkha-yācane, saṃkasaṅkāyaṃ, inda-paramissariye, anda-bandhane, yaja-devapūjāyaṃ, aṭa paṭa-gamanathā, aṇa-saddattho, asa-khepane, vasa-nivāse, pasabādhane, paṃsa-nāsane, bandha-bandhane, etehi kriyatthehi u hoti. Bharatīti bhara=bhattā. Marati rūpakāyena sahevāti maru=devo, nijjaladeso ca. Carīyati bhakkhīyatīti caru=habyapā ko. Taranti anenāti taru=rukkho. Arati sūnabhāvena uddhaṃ gacchatīti aru=vaṇo. Garati siñcati, girati vamati vā sissesu sinehanti garu=ācariyo. Hanati odanādīsu vaṇṇavisesaṃ nāsetīti hanu=vadanekadeso. Tanoti saṃsāra dukkhanti tanu-sarīraṃ. Maññati sattānaṃ hitāhitanti manu=pajāpati. Bhamati calatīti bhamu=nayano patiṭṭhānaṃ. Ketati uddhaṃ gacchati, upari nivasatīti vā ketu=dhajo. Dhanati saddaṃ karotīti dhanu=cāpo. Baṃha iti niddesā umhi niccaṃ niggahītalopo, baṃhati vuddhiṃ gacchatīti bahu=anappakaṃ. Kambati saṃvaraṃ karotīthi kambu=valayo, saṅkho [M 0.0229] ca. Ambati nādaṃkarotīti ambu=vāri. Cakkhati rūpanti cakkhu=nayanaṃ. Bhikkhatīti bhikkhu=samaṇo. Saṃkiratīti saṃku=sūlaṃ. Indati nakkhattānaṃ paramissariyaṃ pavattetīti indu=cando. Andanti bandhanti sattā etāyāti andu=saṅkhalikā. Yajanti anenāti yaju=vedo. Paṭati byattabhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṭu=vicakkhaṇo. Aṇati sukhumabhāvena pavattatīti aṇu=sukhumo, vīhibhedo ca. Asanti pavattanti sattā etehīti asavo=pāṇā. Sukhaṃ vasantyanenāti vasu=dhanaṃ. Pasīyati bādhīyati sāmikehīti pasu. Catuppado. Paṃsati sobhāvisesaṃ nāsetīti paṃsu=reṇu. Bandhīyati sinehabhāvenāti bandhu=ñāti.

From the root `bhar` in the sense of 'bearing'; `mar` in 'giving up life'; `car` in 'moving' and 'eating'; `tar` in 'crossing'; `ar` in 'going'; `gar` or `ghar` in 'sprinkling' (or from `girati`, 'swallows/vomits', the `a` is by irregular formation); `han` in 'harming'; `tan` in 'spreading'; `man` in 'knowing'; `bham` in 'unsteadiness'; `kit` in 'dwelling'; `dhan` in 'making a sound'; `baṃh`, `brah`, or `brūh` in 'growing'; `kamb` in 'covering'; `amb` in 'making a sound'; `cakkh` or `ikkh` in 'seeing'; `bhikkh` in 'begging'; `saṃk` in 'doubting'; `ind` in 'supreme lordship'; `and` in 'binding'; `yaj` in 'worshipping gods'; `aṭ` or `paṭ` in 'going'; `aṇ` in 'making a sound'; `as` in 'throwing'; `vas` in 'dwelling'; `pas` in 'oppressing'; `paṃs` in 'destroying'; `bandh` in 'binding'—from these roots in these meanings, the suffix `u` is added. `bhara` (husband) from `bharati iti bhara` (he supports). `maru` (a god, or a desert) from `marati rūpakāyena saha eva iti maru` (he dies along with his physical body). `caru` (an oblation pot) from `carīyati bhakkhīyati iti caru` (it is moved, it is eaten). `taru` (tree) from `taranti anena iti taru` (they cross by means of it). `aru` (a wound) from `arati sūnabhāvena uddhaṃ gacchati iti aru` (it goes upwards with a swollen nature). `garu` (teacher) from `garati siñcati, girati vamati vā sissesu sinehanti garu` (he sprinkles, or swallows and vomits, affection upon his students). `hanu` (jaw) from `hanati odanādīsu vaṇṇavisesaṃ nāseti iti hanu` (it destroys the distinct appearance in rice, etc.). `tanu` (body) from `tanoti saṃsāradukkhanti tanu` (it extends the suffering of saṃsāra). `manu` (progenitor) from `maññati sattānaṃ hitāhitanti manu` (he knows the welfare and harm of beings). `bhamu` (eyebrow) from `bhamati calatīti bhamu` (it wanders, it moves). `ketu` (banner) from `ketati uddhaṃ gacchati, upari nivasatīti vā ketu` (it goes up, or it dwells above). `dhanu` (bow) from `dhanati saddaṃ karoti iti dhanu` (it makes a sound). `bahu` (much) from `baṃhati vuddhiṃ gacchati iti bahu` (it grows); due to the form `baṃha` being cited, the `niggahīta` is always elided before `u`. `kambu` (a bracelet, or a conch) from `kambati saṃvaraṃ karoti iti kambu` (it makes a covering). `ambu` (water) from `ambati nādaṃ karoti iti ambu` (it makes a sound). `cakkhu` (eye) from `cakhati rūpanti cakkhu` (it sees form). `bhikkhu` (monk) from `bhikkhati iti bhikkhu` (he begs). `saṅku` (a stake) from `saṃkirati iti saṅku` (it pierces). `indu` (moon) from `indati nakkhattānaṃ paramissariyaṃ pavatteti iti indu` (it exercises supreme lordship over the stars). `andu` (a chain) from `andanti bandhanti sattā etāya iti andu` (beings are bound by it). `yaju` (the Veda) from `yajanti anena iti yaju` (they sacrifice with it). `paṭu` (clever) from `paṭati byattabhāvaṃ gacchati iti paṭu` (he goes to a state of clarity). `aṇu` (subtle, or a type of grain) from `aṇati sukhumabhāvena pavattati iti aṇu` (it proceeds with subtlety). `asavo` (life-breaths) from `asanti pavattanti sattā etehīti asavo` (beings proceed by these). `vasu` (wealth) from `sukhaṃ vasanti anena iti vasu` (they live happily by means of it). `pasu` (a quadruped) from `pasīyati bādhīyati sāmikehi iti pasu` (it is bound and oppressed by its owners). `paṃsu` (dust) from `paṃsati sobhāvisesaṃ nāseti iti paṃsu` (it destroys special beauty). `bandhu` (a relative) from `bandhīyati sinehabhāvenāti bandhu` (he is bound by affection).

3. Bandhā ū vadho ca.

3. From `bandh`: the suffix `ū`, and the substitute `vadh`.

Bandha-bandhane timasmā ū hoti, bandhassa vadhādeso ca. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attani satthe bandhatīti vadhū-suṇisā, itthīca.

From the root `bandh` in the sense of 'binding', the suffix `ū` is added, and `bandh` is replaced by `vadh`. `vadhū` (a daughter-in-law, a woman) is from `pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attani satthe bandhati iti vadhū` (she binds beings to herself with the five cords of sensual pleasure).

4. Jambādayo.

4. `Jambū` and others.

Jambūādayo saddāūpaccayantā nipaccante, nipātanaṃ appattassa pāpanaṃ pattassa paṭisedho ca. Janismā ū, bukāgamo, “manānaṃ niggahīta”nti (5.96) nassa niggahītaṃ, “vagge vagganto”ti (1.41) niggahītassa mo, jāyati, janīyatī vā jambū=rukkho. Bhamissa amalopo, bhamati kampatīti bhū=bhamu. Karotismā ū, tassa kandhuña ca, “pararūpamayakāre byañjane”ti (5.95) dhātvantassa byañjanassa pararūpattaṃ, rudhiruppādaṃ karotīti kakkandhū=badarī. Lamba-avasaṃsane[M 0.0230], āpubbo, saṃyogādilopadīgharassā, ālambati avasaṃsatīti alābū=tumbi. Sara-gati hiṃsācintāsu, ūmhi abhuka abuka ca, sarati gacchatīti sarabhū=ekā mahānadī. Sarati pāṇe hiṃsatīti sarabū=khuddajantukaviseso. Camaadane, camati bhakkhati nivāpanti camū=senā. Tana-vitthāre, tanoti saṃsāradukkhanti tanu=sarīraṃ, evamaññepi payogato daṭṭhabbā.

Words beginning with `jambū` are irregularly formed with the suffix `ū`. Irregular formation (`nipātana`) is the accomplishment of what is not obtained by general rules and the prohibition of what is obtained. `jambū` (a tree) is from the root `jan` with the suffix `ū` and the augment `buk`; the `n` becomes `niggahīta` by '`niggahīta` for `m` and `n`' (5.96), and the `niggahīta` becomes `m` by 'the nasal of the class' (1.41); from `jāyati` or `janīyati` (it is born). `bhū` (eyebrow) is from `bham` with elision of `am`; from `bhamati kampati iti bhū` (it wanders, it trembles). `kakkandhū` (the jujube tree) is from `karoti` with `ū` and the addition of `kandhu`; the final consonant of the root assimilates to the following consonant by 'assimilation to the following consonant...' (5.95); from `rudhiruppādaṃ karoti iti kakkandhū` (it produces an outflow of blood). `alābū` (gourd) is from the root `lamb` ('to hang down') with the prefix `ā`, with elision of the initial part of the conjunct consonant, lengthening, and shortening; from `ālambati avasaṃsati iti alābū` (it hangs down). `sarabhū` (a great river) is from `sar` ('to go,' 'to harm,' 'to think') with `ū` and the augment `abhuk` or `abuk`; from `sarati gacchati iti sarabhū` (it flows, it goes). `sarabū` (a type of small creature) is from `sarati pāṇe hiṃsati iti sarabū` (it harms living beings). `camū` (an army) is from `cam` ('to eat'); from `camati bhakkhati nivāpanti camū` (it eats, it consumes offerings). `tanu` (body) is from `tan` ('to extend'); from `tanoti saṃsāradukkham iti tanu` (it extends the suffering of saṃsāra). In this way, others too should be understood from usage.

5. Tapusa vi dha kura putha mudā ku.

5. From `tap`, `us`, `vidh`, `kur`, `puth`, and `mud`, the suffix `ku` is added.

Tapa-santāpe, usa-dāhe, vidha-vedhane, kura-sadde, putha patha-vitthāre, muda-tose, etehi ku, hoti. Kakāronubandho “na te kānubandhanāgamesū”ti (5.85) eonamabhāvattho. Tapa iti niddesatova assa ittaṃ, tāpīyatīti tipu=lohaviseso. Usati dāhaṃ karotīti usu=saro. Vedhati raṃsīhi timiranti vidhu=cando. Kurati kiccākiccaṃ vadatīti kuru=rājā, kuravo=janapado. Puthati mahanthabhāvena patthiratīti puthu=vitthiṇṇo, modanaṃ, mudīyatīti vā mudu=athaddho.

From the root `tap` in the sense of 'heating'; `us` in 'burning'; `vidh` in 'piercing'; `kur` in 'making a sound'; `puth` or `path` in 'spreading'; `mud` in 'rejoicing'—from these the suffix `ku` is added. The `k` is an `anubandha` for the purpose of preventing the substitution of `e` and `o`, according to the rule 'not for those with `k` as anubandha or in augments' (5.85). `tipu` (a type of metal, lead or tin) is from `tāpīyati iti tipu` (it is heated); the `a` of `tap` becomes `i` because it is cited as `tapa`. `usu` (arrow) is from `usati dāhaṃ karoti iti usu` (it causes a burning sensation). `vidhu` (moon) is from `vedhati raṃsīhi timiram iti vidhu` (it pierces the darkness with its rays). `kuru` (a king, or `kuravo`, a country) is from `kurati kiccākiccaṃ vadati iti kuru` (he makes a sound, i.e., speaks about what should and should not be done). `puthu` (wide) is from `puthati mahantabhāvena patthirati iti puthu` (it spreads with greatness). `mudu` (soft) is from `modanaṃ` (delight), or `mudīyati iti mudu` (one rejoices).

6. Sindhādayo.

6. `Sindhu` and others.

Sindhu ādayo kupaccayantā nipaccante. Sanda-passavane, assa ittaṃ, dhocāntā deso nipātanā, sandati passavatīti sindhu=nadi, vahisupantassa dīghādibatte, bādhissa vāntahatte ca, vahantyanenāti bāhu, bādhati upaddave vāretī ti vā bāhu=bhujo. Raṃgha-gamane, niggahītalopo, raṅghati pavattahi rājadhammeti raghu=rājā. Vida-lābhe, nakārāgamo, vassa bo, vindatyanena nandananti bindu=kaṇikā. Mana-ñāṇe, nassa dho, maññati ñāyati [M 0.0231] madhuranti madhu=madhukarīhi katamadhu, rapa lapa japa jappa-vacane, assaittaṃ, rapati jappati mantantī ripu=paccāmitto. Sasa-gati hiṃ sāpāṇanesu, assa uttaṃ, sasati jīvatīti susu=yuvā. Ara gamane, assautta mūttañca, arati mahantabhāvaṃ gacchatīti uru=mahā, aratinenāti ūru-satthi. Khaṇa-avadāraṇe, ā pubbo analopo, ākhanatīti ākhu=undūro. Tarataraṇe, tassa tho, taratīti tharu=khaggāvayavo. Laṃgha-gati sosanesu ghassa vā hattaṃ, niggahītalopo ca, laṅghati pavattati laghubhāvenāti laghu lahū ekatthā, (bhaṃja-omaddane, pa-pubbo, jassa gattaṃ, pabhañjati visesenāti pabhaṅgu=bhaṅguro.) Ṭhā-gatinivattiyaṃ, supubbo, ṭhāti pavattati sundarabhāvenāti suṭṭhu=sobhanaṃ, dupubbo ṭhāti pavattati asundarabhāvenāti duṭṭhu=asobhanaṃ. Evamaññepi viññeyyā.

The words `sindhu` and so on are irregularly formed with the `ku` suffix. From the root `sand` (to flow), `sindhu` (river) is formed from `sandati passavati` (it flows), with the irregular change of `a` to `i` and the final consonant to `dh`. From the root `vah` (to carry), with lengthening of the initial vowel, and from the root `bādh` (to ward off), with the final consonant becoming `h`, `bāhu` (arm) is formed from `vahanti anena` (they carry with this) or `bādhati upaddave vāreti` (it wards off dangers). From the root `raṃgh` (to go), with elision of the `niggahīta`, `raghu` (a king) is formed from `raṅghati pavattahi rājadhamme` (he proceeds according to royal duties). From the root `vid` (to obtain), with the augment `n` and the change of `v` to `b`, `bindu` (a drop) is formed from `vindati anena nandanam` (one obtains delight with this). From the root `man` (to know), with the change of `n` to `dh`, `madhu` (honey) is formed from `maññati ñāyati madhuram` (it is known or considered to be sweet). From the root `rap`, `lap`, `jap`, or `japp` (to speak), with the change of `a` to `i`, `ripu` (an enemy) is formed from `rapati jappati mantam` (he speaks or mutters a spell). From the root `sas` (to go, harm, or breathe), with the change of `a` to `u`, `susu` (a youth) is formed from `sasati jīvati` (he breathes, he lives). From the root `ar` (to go), with the change of `a` to `u` or `ū`, `uru` (great) is formed from `arati mahantabhāvaṃ gacchati` (it goes to greatness), and `ūru` (thigh) is formed from `arati anena` (one goes with this). From the root `khaṇ` (to dig) with the prefix `ā` and non-elision of `a`, `ākhu` (a rat) is formed from `ākhanati` (it digs up). From the root `tar` (to cross), with the change of `t` to `th`, `tharu` (a sword-hilt) is formed from `tarati` (it crosses). From the root `laṃgh` (to go or dry up), with elision of the `niggahīta` and optional change of `gh` to `h`, `laghu` or `lahu` (light), which are synonymous, are formed from `laṅghati pavattati laghubhāvena` (it proceeds with lightness). (From the root `bhañj` (to crush) with the prefix `pa`, with the change of `j` to `g`, `pabhaṅgu` (fragile) is formed from `pabhañjati visesena` (it breaks especially).) From the root `ṭhā` (to stand) with the prefix `su`, `suṭṭhu` (well) is formed from `ṭhāti pavattati sundarabhāvena` (it stands or proceeds in a good way); with the prefix `du`, `duṭṭhu` (badly) is formed from `ṭhāti pavattati asundarabhāvena` (it stands or proceeds in a bad way). Other such words should be understood in the same way.

7. I.

7. I.

Kriyatthā bahulaṃ i hoti, abha-khepane, asīyati khipīyatīti asi=khaggo. Kasa-vilekhane, kasīyate kasi=kasanaṃ. Masa-āmasane, masīyatīti masi=meḷā. Ku-sadde o avādesā, kavati kathebhīti kavi=kabbakāro. Rusadde, ravati gajjatīti ravi=ādicco. Sappa-gamane, sappati pavattatīti sappi=ghataṃ. Gantha-ganthane, “ta tha na rānaṃ ṭa ṭha ṇalā”ti (1.25) nathānaṃ ṇaṭhā, ganthetīti gaṇṭhi=pabbo, gaṇṭhica. Rāja-dittiyaṃ, rājati pavattatīti rāji=pāḷi. Kala-saṅkhyāne, kalīyati parimīyatīti kali=pāpaṃ. Bala-pāṇane, balanti jīvanti [M 0.0232] anenāti bali=karo. Dhana-sadde, dhanati nadatīti dhani=saddo. Acca añca-pūjāyaṃ, accīyati pūjīyatīti acci=jālā. Vala valla-saṃvaraṇe, valanaṃ saṃkocanaṃ vali=udarādīsu pali, vallīyanti saṃvarīyanti sattā etāyāti valli=latā. Vimhi valī vallītipi hoti, soyevattho, evamaññepi.

The suffix `i` is often added to roots denoting action. From the root `abh` (to throw), `asi` (sword) is from `asīyati khipīyati` (it is thrown). From `kas` (to scratch), `kasi` (ploughing) is from `kasīyate` (it is ploughed). From `mas` (to touch), `masi` (soot) is from `masīyati` (it is touched). From `ku` (to sound), with `u` becoming `o` and then `av`, `kavi` (a poet) is from `kavati katheti` (he sounds, he speaks). From `ru` (to sound), `ravi` (the sun) is from `ravati gajjati` (it sounds, it roars). From `sapp` (to go), `sappi` (ghee) is from `sappati pavattati` (it moves, it flows). From `ganth` (to bind), with `nth` becoming `ṇṭh` by the rule 'for `t`, `th`, `n`, `r`...' (1.25), `gaṇṭhi` or `gaṇṭhica` (a knot) is from `gantheti` (it binds). From `rāj` (to shine), `rāji` (a line) is from `rājati pavattati` (it shines, it extends). From `kal` (to count), `kali` (demerit) is from `kalīyati parimīyati` (it is counted, it is measured). From `bal` (to live), `bali` (a tax) is from `balanti jīvanti anena` (they live by this). From `dhan` (to sound), `dhani` (a sound) is from `dhanati nadati` (it sounds). From `acc` or `añc` (to honour), `acci` (a flame) is from `accīyati pūjīyati` (it is honoured). From `val` or `vall` (to cover), `vali` (a wrinkle), meaning a folding or contracting, is a fold on the belly and so on; and `valli` (a creeper) is from `vallīyanti saṃvarīyanti sattā etāya` (beings are covered by this). Sometimes `valī` and `vallī` also occur with the same meaning. So too for others.

8. Dajhādayo.

8. Dadhi and so on.

Dadhiādayo saddā ipaccayantā nipaccante. Dhā-dhāraṇe, dvibhāvo nipātanā, ghatamādadhātīti dadhi=gora saviseso. Aṃha-gamane, niggahītalopo, aṃhati gacchatīti ahi=sappo. Kampa calane, saṃyogādilopo, kampati calatīti kapi=vānaro. Mana-ñāṇe, assa uttaṃ, manati jānātīti muni=samaṇo. Nassa ṇattaṃ, manati mahagghabhāvaṃ gacchatītī maṇi=ratanaṃ. Ikkha cakkha-dassane, issa attaṃ ikkhati anenāti akkhi=nayanaṃ. Kamapavikkhepe, assa ittaṃ, kamati yātīti kimi=khuddajantukaviseso. Tara taraṇe, tittirādeso, turito tarati yātīti tittiri=pakkhiviseso. Kīḷa-vihāre, īssa ettaṃ, kīḷanaṃ keḷi=kīḷā. Usismā issa khaluña, usati dahatī ukkhali=bhājanaṃ, evamaññepi.

The words `dadhi` and so on are irregularly formed with the `i` suffix. From the root `dhā` (to hold), with irregular reduplication, `dadhi` (curd) is from `ghatam ādadhāti` (it holds ghee). From the root `aṃh` (to go), with elision of the `niggahīta`, `ahi` (snake) is from `aṃhati gacchati` (it goes). From the root `kamp` (to move), with elision of the initial part of the conjunct consonant, `kapi` (monkey) is from `kampati calati` (it moves). From the root `man` (to know), with `a` becoming `u`, `muni` (a sage) is from `manati jānāti` (he knows). With `n` becoming `ṇ`, `maṇi` (a gem) is from `manati mahagghabhāvaṃ gacchati` (it attains great value). From the root `ikkh` or `cakkh` (to see), with `i` becoming `a`, `akkhi` (eye) is from `ikkhati anena` (one sees with this). From the root `kam` (to step), with `a` becoming `i`, `kimi` (a small creature) is from `kamati yāti` (it goes). From the root `tar` (to cross), with substitution of `tittir` for the root, `tittiri` (a partridge) is from `turito tarati yāti` (it crosses quickly). From the root `kīḷ` (to play), with `ī` becoming `e`, `keḷi` (sport) is from `kīḷanaṃ` (playing). From the root `us` (to burn), `ukkhali` (a pot) is formed from `usati dahati` (it burns). So too for others.

9. Yuvaṇṇupantā ki.

9. From roots ending in `i` and `u`, the suffix `ki` is added.

Ivaṇṇupantehi ca uvaṇṇupantehi ca kriyatthehi bahulaṃ ki hoti. Kakāro-nubandho, isa sisa-icchāyaṃ, sivaṃ icchatīti isi=tapassī. Gira-nigiraṇe, girati pasavati chavimaṃsasārabhūtaṃ bhesajjādinti giri=selo. Suca-socane. Socanaṃ [M 0.0233] suci=soceyyaṃ, ruca-abhilāse rucanti etāyāti ruci=ābhilāso, evamaññepi.

The suffix `ki` is often added to roots denoting action that end in `i` or `u`. The `k` is an indicatory letter. From the root `is` or `sis` (to desire), `isi` (a seer) is from `sivaṃ icchati` (he desires what is auspicious). From the root `gir` (to swallow), `giri` (a mountain) is from `girati pasavati chavimaṃsasārabhūtaṃ bhesajjādim` (it swallows, or it produces medicines which are the essence of skin, flesh, etc.). From the root `suc` (to be pure), `suci` (purity) is from `socanaṃ` (purity). From the root `ruc` (to desire), `ruci` (desire) is from `rucanti etāya` (they desire by this). So too for others.

10. Vapa vara vasa rasa nabha hara hana paṇā iṇa.

10. To the roots `vap`, `var`, `vas`, `ras`, `nabh`, `har`, `han`, and `paṇ`, the suffix `iṇa` is added.

Vapa-bījanikkhepe, vara-varaṇasambhattīsu, vasa-nivāse, rasa-assādane, nabha-hiṃsāyaṃ, hara haraṇe, hana hiṃsāyaṃ, paṇa-byavahārathutisu, etehi iṇa hoti. Vapanti etāyāti vāpi=jalāsayo. Vārenti etenāti vāri=jalaṃ. Vasanti etāyāti vāsi=tacchaka bhaṇḍaṃ. Rasīyati assādanavasena samo sarīyatīti rāsi=samūho. Nabhati hiṃsatīti nābhi=sarīrāvayavo. Hāretīti hāri=manuññaṃ. “Hanassa ghāto ṇānubandhe” (5.99) ti hanassa ghāto, hananti etenāti ghāti=paharaṇaṃ, paṇati voharatīti pāṇi, paṇati voharati etenāti vā pāṇi=karo.

To the roots `vap` (to sow), `var` (to choose or share), `vas` (to dwell), `ras` (to taste), `nabh` (to harm), `har` (to carry), `han` (to kill), and `paṇ` (to transact and praise), the suffix `iṇa` is added. From `vap`, `vāpi` (a reservoir) is from `vapanti etāya` (they sow in this). From `var`, `vāri` (water) is from `vārenti etena` (they ward off with this). From `vas`, `vāsi` (an adze) is from `vasanti etāya` (they dwell by means of this). From `ras`, `rāsi` (a heap) is from `rasīyati assādanavasena samo sarīyati` (it is moved together for the purpose of being tasted). From `nabh`, `nābhi` (navel) is from `nabhati hiṃsati` (it harms). From `har`, `hāri` (charming) is from `hāreti` (it captivates). From `han`, according to the rule 'for `han`, there is `ghāt` when an affix with an indicatory `ṇ` follows' (5.99), `ghāti` (a weapon) is from `hananti etena` (they kill with this). From `paṇ`, `pāṇi` (the hand) is from `paṇati voharati` (he transacts) or `paṇati voharati etena` (he transacts with this).

11. Bhūgamā īṇa.

11. To the roots `bhū` and `gam`, the suffix `īṇa` is added.

Bhū-sattāyaṃ, ama gama-gamane etehi īṇa hoti bhavissati kāle. Bhavissatīti bhāvī=bhavissamāno. Gamissatīti gāmī=gamissāmāno.

From the root bhū in the sense of being, and gam in the sense of going, the suffix īṇa is added in the future tense. Bhāvī is from bhavissati (he will be), meaning bhavissamāno (one who will be). Gāmī is from gamissati (he will go), meaning gamissāmāno (one who will go).

12. Tandalakkhā ī.

12. From the roots tand and lakkh, the suffix ī is added.

Tanda-ālasiye, lakkha-dassanaṅkesu, etehi ī hoti. Tandanaṃ tandī=ālasyaṃ, lakkhīyanti sattā etāyāti lakkhī=sirī.

From the root tand in the sense of laziness, and lakkh in the sense of seeing or marking, the suffix ī is added. Tandī is from tandanaṃ (being lazy), meaning sloth (ālasyaṃ). Lakkhī is from lakkhīyanti sattā etāya (beings are marked by this), meaning fortune (sirī).

13. Gamā ro.

13. From the root gam, the suffix ro is added.

Gamismā [M 0.0234] ro hoti. “Rānubandhentasarādissā”ti (4.132) amalopo, gacchatīti go=pasu.

The suffix ro is added to the root gam. According to the rule Rānubandhentasarādissā (4.132), 'elision of the final vowel and the preceding consonant when an affix with an indicatory r follows,' the am of gam is elided. Go (cattle) is from gacchati (it goes).

(Iti sarapaccayavidhānaṃ).

(Thus ends the section on vowel suffixes).

14. I bhī kā karāra vaka saka vāhi ko.

14. From the roots i, bhī, kā, kara, ara, vaka, saka, and vāh, the suffix ko is added.

I-ajjhena gatīsu, bhī-bhaye, kā gā-sadde, kara-karaṇe, ara-gamane, kuka vaka-ādāne, saka-sattiyaṃ, vā-gatibandhanesu, etehi kapaccayo hoti. Eti pavattatīti eto=asahāyo. Bhāyanti etasmāti bheko=maṇḍūko. Kāyati saddaṃ karotīti kāko=vāyaso. Karoti vaṇṇakanti kakko=vaṇṇaviseso, pisitadabbañca. Arati yātīti akko=sūro, viṭapiviseso ca. Vakati odanaṃ ādadātīti vakkaṃ=dehakoṭṭhāsaviseso, sakkatīti sakko-devindo, samattho ca. Vāti bandhati etenāti vāko=vakkalaṃ.

From the roots i (to study, to go), bhī (to fear), kā or gā (to make a sound), kara (to do), ara (to go), kuka or vaka (to take), saka (to be able), and vā (to go or bind), the suffix ka is added. Eto (alone, asahāyo) is from eti (he goes) or pavattati (he proceeds). Bheko (a frog, maṇḍūko) is from bhāyanti etasmā (they are afraid of this). Kāko (a crow, vāyaso) is from kāyati or saddaṃ karoti (it makes a sound). Kakko (a particular color or a paste of ground meat) is from karoti vaṇṇaṃ (it makes a color). Akko (the sun, or a type of tree) is from arati or yāti (it goes). Vakkaṃ (a kidney, a particular part of the body) is from vakati odanaṃ ādadāti (it takes rice). Sakko (the lord of devas, or 'capable') is from sakkoti (he is able). Vāko (bark, vakkalaṃ) is from vāti or bandhati etena (one binds with this).

15. Ñukādayo.

15. The word ūkā and others.

Ñukādayo kapaccayantā nipaccante. Ūha-vitakke, halopo nipātanā ūhīyati vicinīyatīti ūkā-okodanī. Unda kiledane, saṃyogādi lopo, aka ca. Undati dravaṃ karotīti udakaṃ=jalaṃ. Bhī-bhaye, ettābhāvo, bhāyanti etasmāti bhīko=bhīru. Saka-sattiyaṃ, upantassi, sakkoti dhāretunti sikkā=upakaraṇaviseso. Hā-cāge, hīyati sādhūhi jahīyatīti hāko=kodho. Samba-maṇḍane, kassa uña[M 0.0235], sambati udakaṃ maṇḍetīti sambuko=jalajantuvisebho. Putha patha-vitthāre, ottābhāvo, kassa uña, puthati pattharati attano bālabhāvanti puthuko=bālo. Suca-soke, socanti etenāti sukkaṃ=sambhavo, setañca. Ci-caye, upapubbo, ettābhāvo, upacinantīti upacikā=vammika kārā. Kampa-calane, kampissa paṃ, kampati calatīti paṅko=kaddamo. Usa-dāhe, usatīti ukkā=jālā. Kassa muña, usati dahatībhi ummukaṃ=alātaṃ. Vama-uggiraṇe, kassa miña, vamīyatīti vammiko=upacikākato cayo, masa-āmasane, sassa tthaṅa, masīyati pemenāti matthakaṃ=sīsaṃ, evamaññepi.

Words such as ūkā are irregularly formed with the suffix ka. From the root ūh (to reason), with elision of h, ūkā (a louse) is from ūhīyati (it is considered). From the root und (to be wet), with elision of the initial conjunct and the suffix aka, udakaṃ (water) is from undati (it moistens). From the root bhī (to fear), bhīko (fearful) is from bhāyanti etasmā (they are afraid of this). From the root sak (to be able), with shortening of the penultimate vowel, sikkā (a carrying-pole) is from sakkoti dhāretum (it is able to hold). From the root hā (to abandon), hāko (anger) is from hīyati sādhūhi (it is abandoned by the good). From the root samb (to adorn), with the suffix uka, sambuko (an oyster) is from sambati udakaṃ (it adorns the water). From the root puth (to spread), with the suffix uka, puthuko (a child) is from puthati attano bālabhāvaṃ (he spreads his childishness). From the root suc (to grieve), sukkaṃ (semen, or white) is from socanti etena (they grieve because of this). From the root ci (to heap up) with the prefix upa, upacikā (a termite) is from upacinanti (they heap up). From the root kamp (to move), with substitution of paṃ for kamp, paṅko (mud) is from kampati (it moves). From the root us (to burn), ukkā (a torch) is from usati (it burns); with the suffix muka, ummukaṃ (a firebrand) is from usati (it burns). From the root vam (to vomit), with the suffix mika, vammiko (an anthill) is from vamīyati (it is vomited forth). From the root mas (to touch), with substitution of tthaka for s, matthakaṃ (the head) is from masīyati pemena (it is touched with affection). So too for others.

16. Bhītvā nako.

16. From the root bhī, the suffix ānako is added.

Bhī-bhaye tīmasmā ānako hoti. Bhāyanti etasmāki bhayānako=bhayajanako.

From the root bhī in the sense of fear, the suffix ānako is added. Bhayānako (frightful) is from bhāyanti etasmā (they are afraid of this).

17. Siṅghā āṇikāṭakā.

17. From the root siṅgh, the suffixes āṇika and āṭaka are added.

Siṅgha-ghāyanetīmasmā āṇika āṭakā honti. “Itthiyamatvā”ti 93.260 ā, siṅghayati passavatīti siṅghāṇikā=nāsāssavo. Siṅghati ekībhāvaṃ yātīti siṅghāṭakaṃ=vīthicatukkaṃ.

From the root siṅgh in the sense of smelling, the suffixes āṇika and āṭaka are added. By the rule Itthiyamā, the final ā in siṅghāṇikā indicates the feminine gender. Siṅghāṇikā (nasal mucus) is from siṅghayati (it smells) or passavati (it flows). Siṅghāṭakaṃ (a crossroads) is from siṅghati (it comes together).

18. Karāditvako.

18. From the roots kara and so on, the suffix ako is added.

Kara-karaṇe, sara-gatihiṃsācintāsu, nara-naye, tarataraṇe, vara-varaṇa sambhattīsu, jana-janane, kara-ditti gatikantīsu, kaṭa-mandane, kura-sadde, thu-abhitthave, evamādīhi ako [M 0.0236] hoti. Karīyatīti karako=kamaṇḍalu. Karotīti karakā=vassopalā. Sarati udakametthāti sarako=pānabhājanaṃ. Naranti pāpuṇanti sattā etthāti narako=nirayo. Tarantyanenāti tarako=taraṇaṃ. Vāretītivarako=varaṇo, dhaññaviseso ca. Janetīti janako=pitā. Kanati dibbatīti kanakaṃ=suvaṇṇaṃ. Kaṭati maddati ripavoti kaṭakaṃ=nagaraṃ. Kuratīti korako=kalikā. Thavīyatīti thavako-guccho.

From the roots kara (to do); sara (to go, harm, or think); nara (to guide); tara (to cross); vara (to choose or apportion); jana (to produce); kana (to shine, go, or desire); kaṭa (to adorn); kura (to make a sound); and thu (to praise), and others like them, the suffix ako is added. Karako (a water pot) is from karīyati (it is made). Karakā (hailstones) is from karoti (it makes). Sarako (a drinking vessel) is from sarati udakam ettha (water flows in it). Narako (hell) is from naranti sattā ettha (beings are led to it). Tarako (a crossing) is from taranti anena (one crosses by means of it). Varako (the varaṇa tree, or a type of grain) is from vāreti (it obstructs). Janako (a father) is from janeti (he begets). Kanakaṃ (gold) is from kanati or dibbati (it shines or glitters). Kaṭakaṃ (a city) is from kaṭati or maddati ripavo (it crushes enemies). Korako (a bud) is from kurati (it makes a sound). Thavako (a cluster) is from thavīyati (it is praised).

19. Bala patehyāko.

19. From bala and pata, the suffix āko is added.

Bala-pāṇane, pata patha-gamane, etehi āko hoti. Balati jīvatīti balākā=pakkhiviseso. Patati yātīti patākā=dhajo.

From the root bala in the sense of living, and pata or patha in the sense of going, the suffix āko is added. Balākā (a type of bird) is from balati or jīvati (it lives). Patākā (a banner) is from patati or yāti (it goes).

20. Sāmākādayo.

20. Sāmāka and others.

Sāmākaādayo ākantā nipaccante. Sā-tanu karaṇāvasānesu, sāssa muka, sāti dehaṃ ta nuṃ karotīti sāmāko=tiṇadhaññaṃ. Pā-pāne, inaṅa, pivati rattanti pināko=mahissaradhanu. Gu-sadde, “yuvaṇṇāna miyaṅuvaṅa sare”ti (5.136) uvaṅa, gavati nadati etenāti guvako=pūgaphalaṃ. Aṭa paṭa-gamanatthā, paṭati yātīti paṭākā=vejayantī. Sala pila pala hula-gamanatthā, salati yātīti salākā=vejjopakaraṇadabbaṃ. Vida-ñāṇe, vidati jānātīti vidāko=vidvā. Paṇabyavahārathutīsu assa ittaṃ, ūka ca, paṇīyati voharīyatīti piññāko=tilakakko, evamaññepi.

Words such as sāmāka are irregularly formed with the suffix āka. From the root sā in the senses of making thin and ending, with muka substituted for sā; 'it makes the body thin,' thus sāmāko = a type of grass-grain. From pā in the sense of drinking, with the suffix inaṅa; 'it drinks blood,' thus pināko = Maheśvara's bow. From gu in the sense of making a sound, with the uvaṅa substitution according to rule 5.136; 'one makes a sound with it,' thus guvako = areca nut. From aṭa and paṭa in the sense of going; 'it goes,' thus paṭākā = a banner. From sala, pila, pala, and hula in the sense of going; 'it goes,' thus salākā = a medical instrument. From vida in the sense of knowing; 'he knows,' thus vidāko = a wise person. From paṇa in the senses of transacting and praising, with a changed to i and the suffix ūka; 'it is transacted,' thus piññāko = sesame cake. And so for others.

21. Vicchālagamamusā kiko.

21. From vicchā, ala, gama, and musā, the suffix kiko is formed.

Vicchā-gamane[M 0.0237], ala=bandhane, ama gama-gamane, musa-theyye, etehi kiko hoti. Vicchati yātīti vicchiko=kīṭo. Alati bandhati etenāti alikaṃ=asaccaṃ. Gacchatīti gamiko=gantā. Musāti niddesā dīgho, musati thenetīti mūsiko=undūro.

From the roots vicchā (to go); ala (to bind); ama and gama (to go); and musa (to steal), the suffix kiko is added. Vicchiko (a scorpion) is from vicchati or yāti (it goes). Alikaṃ (falsehood) is from alati or bandhati etena (one binds with it). Gamiko (a goer) is from gacchati (he goes). The long vowel in mūsiko is by instruction; mūsiko (a rat) is from musati or theneti (it steals).

22. Kiṃkaṇikādayo.

22. Kiṃkaṇikā and others.

Kiṃkaṇikādayo saddā kikantā nipaccante. Kaṇaiti daṇḍako dhātu saddattho, kassa dvittaṃ, assa ittaṃ, niggahītāgamo ca, kaṇati saddaṃ karotī kiṃkaṇikā=ghaṇḍikā. Muda-tose, dassa dvittaṃ, mudanti etamayāti muddikā=aṅguliyāveṭṭhanaṃ, phalaviseso a. Mahīyati pūjīyatīti mahikā=himaṃ. Kala-saṅkhyāne, kalīyati parimītayatīti kalikā=korako. Sappa-gamane, assa ittaṃ. Sappati gacchatīti sippikā=jalajantuviseso, evamaññepi.

Words such as kiṃkaṇikā are irregularly formed with the suffix kika. The root kaṇa has the meaning of sound; with doubling of k, change of a to i, and insertion of a niggahīta, from 'it makes a sound' comes kiṃkaṇikā = a small bell. From muda in the sense of rejoicing, with doubling of d; 'they rejoice in this,' thus muddikā = a finger-ring or a type of fruit. 'It is honored, it is revered,' thus mahikā = frost. From kala in the sense of counting; 'it is counted or measured,' thus kalikā = a bud. From sappa in the sense of going, with a changed to i; 'it creeps, it goes,' thus sippikā = a type of aquatic creature. And so for others.

23. Isā kīko.

23. From is, the suffix kīko is formed.

Isa siṃsa-icchāyaṃ, iccasmā kīko hoti. Icchīyatīti isīkā=tūlanissayo.

From the root is or siṃs in the sense of desiring, the suffix kīko is added. Isīkā (a reed) is from icchīyati (it is desired).

24. Kamapadā ṇuko.

24. From kama and pada, the suffix ṇuko is formed.

Kama-icchāyaṃ, pada-gamane, etehi ṇuko hoti. “Ṇiṇāpīna”nti (5.160) yogavibhāgā ṇilopo. Kāmetīti kāmuko=kāmayitā[M 0.0238]. Pajjati yāti etāyāti pādukā=pādopakaraṇaṃ.

From the root kama in the sense of desiring, and pada in the sense of going, the suffix ṇuko is formed. By splitting the rule Ṇiṇāpīna (5.160), the ṇ is elided. He desires, thus kāmuko = a lover. One goes by means of it, thus pādukā = footwear.

25. Maṇḍasalā ṇūko.

25. From maṇḍa and sala, the suffix ṇūko is formed.

Maṇḍa-bhūsane, sala-gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, etehi ṇūko hoti. Maṇḍeti jalaṃ bhūsetīti maṇḍūko=bheko, salati gocaratta mupayātīti sālūkaṃ=uppalakaṇḍo.

From the root maṇḍa in the sense of adorning, and the root sala in the sense of going, the suffix ṇūko is added. Maṇḍūko (a frog) is from maṇḍeti jalaṃ (it adorns the water). Sālūkaṃ (a lotus stalk) is from salati gocarattham (it goes for food).

26. Ulūkādayo.

26. `Ulūka` and others.

Ulūkādayo saddā ṇūkantā nipaccante. Ula-gavesane, ottābhāvo nipātanā, ulati gavesatīti ulūko=kosiyo. Mana=ñāṇe, nassa dhattaṃ, maññatīti madhūko=rukkho. Jala-dittiyaṃ, jalatīti jalūkā=lohitapo, evamaññepi.

Words such as `ulūka` are irregularly formed with the suffix `ṇūka`. From the root `ula` in the sense of searching; 'it searches,' thus `ulūko` = an owl. From the root `mana` in the sense of knowing, with `n` changed to `dh`; 'he thinks,' thus `madhūko` = the Madhuca tree. From the root `jala` in the sense of shining; 'it shines,' thus `jalūkā` = a leech. And so for others.

27. Kasā sako.

27. From `kasa`, the suffix `sako`.

Kasa-vilekhanetīmasmā sako hoti. Kasatīti kassako=kasikammakāro.

From the root `kasa` in the sense of ploughing, the suffix `sako` is employed. He ploughs, thus `kassako` = a farmer.

28. Karā tiko.

28. From `kara`, the suffix `tiko`.

Karotismā tiko hoti. Karonti kīḷaṃ etthāti kattiko=bāhulo.

From the root `kara`, the suffix `tiko` is employed. They play a game herein, thus `kattiko` = the month Kārttika.

29. Isā ṭhakana.

29. From `isa`, the suffix `ṭhakana`.

Isa siṃsa-icchāyaṃ, iccasmā ṭhakana hoti. Icchīyatīti iṭṭhakā=mattikāvikāro.
