From the root hi in the sense of going and dhū in the sense of shaking, the suffix ma is derived. 'It goes, it proceeds,' thus himaṃ means frost. 'It shakes, it trembles,' thus dhūmo means smoke, that which is born from fire.

135. Bhīto rīsano ca.

135. From the root bhī, the suffixes ma and īsana are also derived.

Bhī-bhayetīmasmā rīsano hoti makaca. Antasarādilopo, bhāyanti etasmāti bhīsano=bhayānako. Bhīmo=sova.

From the root bhī in the sense of fear, the suffixes īsana and ma are derived. 'They fear because of it,' thus bhīsano means frightful. Bhīmo has the same meaning.

136. Khī su vī yā gāhi sā lū khu hu mara dhara ghara jamāma samā mo.

136. From the roots khī, su, vī, yā, gāh, sā, lū, khu, hu, mar, dhar, ghar, jam, am, and sam, the suffix ma is derived.

Khī-khaye. Su-savane, vī-tantasantāne, yā-pāpuṇane, gā-sadde, hi-gatiyaṃ, sā-tanukaraṇāvasānesu, lū-chedane, khu-sadde, hu-havane, mara-pāṇacāge, dhara-dhāraṇe, kara-karaṇe, ghara-secane, jama-adane, ama gama-gamane, sama-upame, etehi dhātūhi mo hoti. Khepanaṃ nirupaddavakaraṇatāya khemo=nirupaddavo. Sunotīti somo=cando. Vāyanti etenāti vemo=tantavāyopakaraṇaṃ. Yātīti yāmo=dinassa chaṭṭho bhāgo, aṭṭhamo vā. Gāyanti etthāti gāmo=saṃvasatho. Hinoti pavattatīti hemaṃ=suvaṇṇaṃ. Sāti sundarattaṃ tanuṃ karotīti sāmo=kāḷo. Lūyateti lomaṃ=tanuruhaṃ. Khūyate uttamabhāvenāti khomaṃ=atasi. Havanaṃ, hūyate vā homaṃ=huti. Marantyanenāti mambaṃ=yasmiṃ tāḷite na jīvati taṃ. Attānaṃ dhārente apāye vaṭṭadukkhe ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo=pariyatyādi[M 0.0268]. Karaṇaṃ, karīyatīti vā kammaṃ=sukhadukkhaphalādi. Sedo paggharati anenāti ghammo=nidāgho. Jameti abhakkhi tabbaṃ adatīti jammo=nihīno, anisammakārī ca. Ameti pemena puttakesu pavattatīti ammā=mātā. Samenti anenāti sammā=piyasamudācāro.

The root khī is in the sense of destruction; su in hearing; vī in weaving thread; yā in reaching; gā in sound; hi in going; sā in making thin and ending; lū in cutting; khu in sound; hu in offering; mara in abandoning life; dhara in holding; kara in doing; ghara in sprinkling; jama in eating; ama and gama in going; sama in comparing. From these roots, the suffix mo is applied. Because it makes one safe from danger, khemo means 'safe.' Because one hears it, somo means 'the moon.' Because they weave with it, vemo means 'a weaver's instrument.' Because it goes, yāmo means 'a watch,' the sixth or eighth part of the day. Because they sing in it, gāmo means 'a village.' Because it proceeds, hemaṃ means 'gold.' Because it makes beauty thin, sāmo means 'black.' Because it is cut, lomaṃ means 'body hair.' Because it is sounded in an excellent way, khomaṃ means 'linen.' An offering, or because it is offered, homaṃ means 'an oblation.' Because one dies by it, mambaṃ means 'a vital spot,' that which, when struck, one does not live. Because it holds those who uphold it, preventing them from falling into states of woe and the suffering of the cycle of rebirth, dhammo means 'the teaching,' etc. Doing, or because it is done, kammaṃ means 'action,' the fruit of which is happiness and suffering, etc. Because sweat flows from it, ghammo means 'heat.' Because he eats what is not to be eaten, jammo means 'a low person' and 'one who acts without consideration.' Because she goes to her children with love, ammā means 'mother.' Because they are calmed by it, sammā means 'agreeable conduct.'

137. Asmādayo.

137. Words beginning with asmā.

Asmaādayo mantā nipaccante, pararūpādīnamabhāvo nipātanā. Asa-khepane, assateti asmā=pāsāṇo. Bhasa-bhasmīkaraṇe, bhasati pakkharatīti bhasmā=chārikā. Usa-dāhe, usati dahatīti usmā=tejodhātu. Visa-pavisane, pavisanti etthāti vesmaṃ=gharaṃ. Bhī-bhaye, massa suña, bhāyanti etasmāti bhesmā=bhayānako. Asatissa dhaṅa, assati janehi cajīyatīti adhamo=nihīno. Karotissa assa uttaṃ, karotīti kummo=kacchapo. Evamaññepi.

Words such as asmā are irregularly formed with the suffix ma. The absence of assimilation and other changes is due to this irregular formation. From the root asa in the sense of throwing: because it is thrown, asmā means 'a stone.' From the root bhasa in the sense of reducing to ashes: because it reduces to ashes or scatters, bhasmā means 'ash.' From the root usa in the sense of burning: because it burns, usmā means 'heat,' the fire element. From the root visa in the sense of entering: because they enter it, vesmaṃ means 'a house.' From the root bhī in the sense of fear, with su substituted for ma: because they are afraid of it, bhesmā means 'terrible.' From the root asa, dha is substituted: because it is thrown away by people, adhamo means 'low.' From the root kara, u is substituted for a: because it does, kummo means 'a tortoise.' And so for others.

138. Nīto mi.

138. From the root nī, the suffix mi is applied.

Nayatismā mi hoti. Nayatīti nemi=cakkantaṃ.

From the root nī, the suffix mi is applied. Because it leads, nemi means 'the rim of a wheel.'

139. Ūmi bhūminimi rasmi.

139. The words ūmi, bhūmi, nimi, and rasmi.

Etesaddā miantā nipaccante. Ūha-vitakke, halopo, ūhanti vitakkenti etenāti ūmi=taraṅgo. Bhū-sattāyaṃ ottābhāvo, bhavanti etthāti bhūmi=mahī. Ni-pāpane, ettābhāvo, sugatiṃ neti pāpetīti nimi=rājā. Rasa-assādane, pararūpābhāvo, rasanti sattā etāyāti rasmi=rajju.

These words ending in mi are irregularly formed. From the root ūha in the sense of reasoning, with elision of ha: because one reasons or reflects with it, ūmi means 'a wave.' From the root bhū in the sense of being, without the change of u to o: because beings exist on it, bhūmi means 'the earth.' From the root ni in the sense of leading, without the change of i to e: because he leads to a good destination, nimi means 'a king.' From the root rasa in the sense of tasting, without assimilation: because beings taste with it, rasmi means 'a rein.'

(Iti pavaggapaccayavidhānaṃ).

(Thus ends the section on suffixes from the labial group.)

140. Māchāhi yo.

140. From the roots mā and chā, the suffix yo is applied.

Mā-māne-chā-chādane[M 0.0269], etehi yo hoti. Meti parimeti aññena uttamena guṇena attano aguṇanti māyā=santadosa paṭicchādana lakkhaṇā. Cheti chindati saṃsayanti chāyā=paṭibimbaṃ.

From the root mā in the sense of measuring and chā in the sense of covering, the suffix yo is applied. Because one measures or compares one's own faults with another's superior qualities, māyā is 'deceit,' which has the characteristic of concealing one's existing faults. Because it cuts off doubt, chāyā means 'a shadow' or 'reflection.'

141. Janissa jā ca.

141. And jā is substituted for the root jan.

Janismā yo hoti, janissa jā ca, janetīti jāyā=bhariyā.

From the root jan, the suffix yo is applied, and jā is substituted for the root. Because she gives birth, jāyā means 'a wife.'

142. Hadayā dayo.

142. Words beginning with hadaya.

Hadayaādayo yantā nipaccante. Harissa daṅa, haratīti hadayaṃ=cittaṃ, manodhātu manoviññāṇadhātu nissayo ca, tanissaaka, attani pemaṃ tanotīti tanayo=putto. Saratissa suri, sarati gacchatīti sūriyo=ādicco. Haratissa mmiṅa, sukhamāharatīti hammiyaṃ=muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Kasa-gamane, kasassa alaka, assa i ca, kasati vuddhiṃ yātīti kisalayaṃ=pallavaṃ, evamaññepi.

Words such as hadaya ending in ya are irregularly formed. From the root har, da is substituted: because it seizes, hadayaṃ means 'the heart,' which is the mind and the support for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element. From the root tan, aka is substituted: because he extends love for oneself, tanayo means 'a son.' From the root sar, suri is substituted: because it moves or goes, sūriyo means 'the sun.' From the root har, mmi is substituted: because it brings happiness, hammiyaṃ means 'a long-galleried mansion.' From the root kas in the sense of going, with the suffix alaka and the change of a to i: because it goes to growth, kisalayaṃ means 'a sprout.' And so for others.

143. Khī si si nī sī su vī kusūhi raka.

143. From the roots khī, si, si, nī, sī, su, vī, ku, and sū, the suffix raka is applied.

Khī-khaye, si-sevāyaṃ, si-bandhane, nī-pāpane, sī-saye, su-savane, vī vā-gamane, ku-sadde, sū-pasave, etehi raka hoti. Khayati duhanenāti khīraṃ=payo. Kusumādīhi sevīyatīti siro=muddhā. Seti sarīraṃ bandhatīti sirā=dehabandhanī. Neti, parehivānīyatīti nīraṃ=jalaṃ. Sayatīti sīro=halaṃ. Aniṭṭhaphala- dāyakattaṃ [M 0.0270] savatīti surā=madirā. Suṇoti uttamagītādinti suro=devo. Veti uttamabhāvaṃ yātīti vīro=vikkanto. Kavati nadatīti kuraṃ=bhattaṃ. Bhayaṭṭitānaṃ paṭhamakappiyānaṃ sūrattaṃ pasavatīti sūro=sūriyo, vikkanto ca.

From the root khī in the sense of destruction; si in serving; si in binding; nī in leading; sī in lying down; su in hearing; vī or vā in going; ku in sound; and sū in producing—from these the suffix raka is applied. Because it is destroyed by milking, khīraṃ means 'milk.' Because it is served with flowers and so on, siro means 'the head.' Because it lies in and binds the body, sirā means 'a vein.' Because it leads, or is brought by others, nīraṃ means 'water.' Because it lies down, sīro means 'a plough.' Because it flows with the quality of giving undesirable results, surā means 'liquor.' Because he hears excellent songs and so on, suro means 'a god.' Because he attains an excellent state, vīro means 'a hero.' Because it makes a sound, kuraṃ means 'boiled rice.' Because it produces courage for the frightened and for the first-of-the-aeon beings, sūro means 'the sun' and also 'a hero.'

144. Hi ci du minaṃ dīgho ca.

144. And the final vowel of the roots hi, ci, du, and mi is lengthened.

Hi-gatiyaṃ, ci-caye, du-gatiyaṃ, mi-pakkhepane, etehi raka hoti, dīgho cāntassa. Hinoti pavattatīti hīraṃ=tālahīrādi. Cayatīti cīraṃ=vakkalaṃ. Dūyati dukkhena gamīyatīti dūraṃ=anāsannaṃ. Mīyate pakkhīpīyateti mīro=samuddo.

From the root hi in the sense of going; ci in collecting; du in going; and mi in throwing in—from these the suffix raka is applied, and their final vowel is lengthened. Because it proceeds, hīraṃ means 'pith,' such as palm pith. Because it is collected, cīraṃ means 'bark cloth.' Because it is gone to with difficulty, dūraṃ means 'far.' Because things are thrown into it, mīro means 'the ocean.'

145. Dhā tānamī ca.

145. And ī is substituted for the final vowel of the roots dhā and tā.

Dhā-dhāraṇe, tā-pālane, etehi raka hoti, ī cāntādeso. Dhāretītidhīro=dhitimā. Jalaṃ tāyatīti tīraṃ=taṭaṃ.

From the root dhā in the sense of holding and tā in the sense of protecting, the suffix raka is applied, and ī is substituted for their final vowel. Because he holds, dhīro means 'wise' or 'steadfast.' Because it protects from water, tīraṃ means 'a bank' or 'shore.'

146. Bhadrāyo.

146. Words beginning with bhadra.

Bhadraādayo rakaantā nipaccante. Bhadda-kalyāṇe, dalopo pararūpābhāvo, bhajīyatīti bhadraṃ=kalyāṇaṃ. Bhī-bhaye, nadādipāṭhā vī, bhāyanti etāyāti bherī=dundubhi. Cita-sañcetane, vipubbo, vicintitabbanti vicitraṃ=nānākāraṃ, yā-pāpuṇane, rassa tuña, gamanaṃ yātrā=yānaṃ. Gupa-gopane, ussa o, passa tañca gopīyatīti gotraṃ=kulādi, bhasa-bhasmīkaraṇe, rassa tuña, bhasati bhakkhaṃ karoti toyāti bhastā-kammāragaggarī. Usa=dāhe, salopo, sokena tāḷite usati dahatīti uro=sarīrekadeso, evamaññepi.

Words such as bhadra ending in the suffix raka are irregularly formed. From the root bhanda in the sense of auspiciousness, with elision of da and no assimilation: because it is resorted to, bhadraṃ means 'auspicious.' From the root bhī in the sense of fear, with ī as in the nadādi group: because they are frightened by it, bherī means 'a drum.' From the root cita in the sense of thinking, with the prefix vi: because it is thought about, vicitraṃ means 'variegated.' From the root yā in the sense of reaching, with shortening of the vowel: going is yātrā, meaning 'a journey' or 'procession.' From the root gupa in the sense of protecting, with o for u and ta for pa: because it is protected, gotraṃ means 'lineage,' etc. From the root bhasa in the sense of reducing to ashes, with shortening of the vowel: because it consumes and makes food with water, bhastā means 'a bellows.' From the root usa in the sense of burning, with elision of sa: because it burns when struck by sorrow, uro means 'the chest,' a part of the body. And so for others.

147. Mandaṅka sasāsa matha catā uro.

147. From the roots manda, aṅka, sasa, asa, matha, and cata, the suffix uro is applied.

Manda-jaḷatte[M 0.0271], aṅka-lakkhaṇe, sasa-gatihiṃsāpāṇanesu, asa-khepane, matha mantha-viloḷane, cata-yācane, etehi uro hoti. Amandi asundarattā jaḷatthamagamīti mandurā=vājisālā. Aṅkīyati lakkhīyatīti aṅkuro=bījapasavo. Sasati hiṃsatīti sasuro=jayampatīnaṃ pitā. Asīyitthāti asuro=dānavo, arīhi mathīyati āloḷīyatīti mathurā=nagaraṃ. Catīyatīti caturo=dakkho.

From the root manda in the sense of dullness; aṅka in marking; sasa in going, harming, and breathing; asa in throwing; matha or mantha in churning; and cata in requesting—from these the suffix uro is applied. Because it was not pleasing, and due to its ugliness it became dull, mandurā means 'a stable.' Because it is marked, aṅkuro means 'a sprout.' Because he harms, sasuro means 'a father-in-law.' Because he was thrown, asuro means 'an asura' or 'titan.' Because it is churned or agitated by enemies, mathurā means 'the city of Mathurā.' Because he is requested, caturo means 'clever' or 'skillful.'

148. Vidhurādayo.

148. Words beginning with vidhura.

Vidhuraādayo urantā nipaccante. Vidha-vedhane, ettābhāvo, vedhati hiṃsatīti vidhuro=viruddho. Unda-kiledane, undati kiledatīti unduro=ākhu. Maṃka-maṇḍane, niggahītalopo, maṅkati anena attānaṃ alaṅkarotīti makuro=ādāso, ratho, kakko, maccho ca. Kuka vaka-ādāne, kassa dvittaṃ. Kukati salādayo ādadātīti kukkuro=sā. Maṅga-maṅgalye, amaṅgi pasatthamagamīti maṅguro=macchaviseso, evamaññepi.

Words such as vidhura ending in ura are irregularly formed. From the root vidha in the sense of piercing, without the change of i to e: because it pierces or harms, vidhuro means 'bereaved' or 'opposed.' From the root unda in the sense of wetting: because it wets, unduro means 'a rat.' From the root maṅka in the sense of adorning, with elision of the niggahīta: because one adorns oneself with it, makuro means 'a mirror,' and also 'a chariot,' 'a paste,' and 'a fish.' From the roots kuka and vaka in the sense of taking, with doubling of ka: because it takes away things like arrows, kukkuro means 'a dog.' From the root maṅga in the sense of being auspicious: because it went to what is praiseworthy, maṅguro means 'a kind of fish.' And so for others.

149. Tima ruha rudha badha mada manda vajāja ruca kasā kiro.

149. From the roots tima, ruha, rudha, badha, mada, manda, vaja, aja, ruca, and kasa, the suffix kira is applied.

Tima-temane, ruha-janane, rudha-āvaraṇe, badha-bādhane, madaummāde, manda-modanathutijaḷattesu, vaja aja-gamane, ruca-dittiyaṃ, kasa-gamane, etehi kiro hoti. Temetīti timiraṃ=andhakāraṃ, āpo ca. Ruhati pavattatīti ruhiraṃ=lohitaṃ. Jīvitaṃ rundhatīti rudhiraṃ=tadeva. Bādhīyatīti badhiro=sotavikalo. Janā majjanti etāyāti madirā=surā. Modanti etthāti mandiraṃ= gharaṃ[M 0.0272]. Vajatīti vajiraṃ=kulisuṃ. Ajanti gacchantī etthāti ajiraṃ=aṅgaṇaṃ gharavisayokāso ca. Rocatīti ruciraṃ=manuññaṃ. Kasīyati dukkhena gamīyatīti kasiraṃ=kicchaṃ.

From the root tima in the sense of getting wet; ruha in growing; rudha in obstructing; badha in oppressing; mada in intoxication; manda in delighting, praising, and dullness; vaja and aja in going; ruca in shining; and kasa in going—from these the suffix kira is applied. Because it makes wet, timiraṃ means 'darkness' and also 'water.' Because it grows or proceeds, ruhiraṃ means 'blood.' Because it obstructs life, rudhiraṃ also means 'blood.' Because he is oppressed, badhiro means 'deaf.' Because people get intoxicated by it, madirā means 'liquor.' Because they delight in it, mandiraṃ means 'a mansion.' Because it goes, vajiraṃ means 'a thunderbolt.' Because they go in it, ajiraṃ means 'a courtyard' and 'the area of a house.' Because it is pleasing, ruciraṃ means 'beautiful.' Because it is gone to with difficulty, kasiraṃ means 'hardship.'

150. Thirādayo.

150. Words beginning with thira.

Thiraādayo kirantā nipaccante. Ṭhā-gatinivattiyaṃ, ṭhassa thattaṃ, ṭhāti pavattatīti thiraṃ=ciraṭṭhāyī. Isa siṃsa-icchāyaṃ, niggahītalopo, icchīyatīti sisiro=utuviseso. Ada khāda-bhakkhane, āssa rassatthaṃ, khādīyati pāṇakehīti khadiro=dantadhāvano, evamaññepi.

Words such as thira ending in the suffix kira are irregularly formed. From the root ṭhā in the sense of standing still, with tha substituted for ṭha: because it stands or endures, thiraṃ means 'firm' or 'long-lasting.' From the roots isa or siṃsa in the sense of desiring, with elision of the niggahīta: because it is desired, sisiro means 'the cool season.' From the roots ada or khāda in the sense of eating, with shortening of ā: because it is eaten by living beings, khadiro means 'the acacia tree,' used as a tooth-stick. And so for others.

151. Dada garehi durabharā.

151. From the roots dada and gara, the suffixes dura and bhara are applied respectively.

Dada-dāne, gara ghara-secane, etehi yathākkamaṃ durabharā honti. Antānaṃ dadātīti dadduro=bheko. Garati siñcatīti gabbharaṃ=guhā.

From the root dada in the sense of giving and gara or ghara in the sense of sprinkling, the suffixes dura and bhara are applied respectively. Because it gives its sound, dadduro means 'a frog.' Because it swallows or sprinkles, gabbharaṃ means 'a cave.'

152. Cara dara jara gara marehi te.

152. From the roots cara, dara, jara, gara, and mara, the suffix ta is applied with reduplication.

Carādīhi dhātūhi te carādayo honti yathākkamaṃ. Caragatibhakkhanesu caranti etthāti caccaraṃ=vīthicatukkaṃ, aṅgaṇañca, dara-vidāraṇe, darīyatīti daddaraṃ=vādittaṃ, bherī ca. Jara-vayohāniyaṃ, ajarīti jajjaro=jiṇṇo. Gara ghara-secane, garati siñcatīti gaggaro=bhinnassaro, haṃsassaro ca. Mara-pāṇacāge, maratīti mammaro=sukkhapaṇṇaṃ, patthapaṇṇānaṃ saddo ca.

From the roots beginning with cara, the words caccara and so on are formed respectively. From the root cara in the senses of going and eating: because they move about in it, caccaraṃ means 'a crossroads' and 'a courtyard.' From the root dara in the sense of splitting: because it is split, daddaraṃ means 'a musical instrument' and also 'a drum.' From the root jara in the sense of decay: because it has decayed, jajjaro means 'worn out' or 'old.' From the root gara or ghara in the sense of sprinkling: because it sprinkles, gaggaro means 'a hoarse voice' and also 'the cry of a goose.' From the root mara in the sense of abandoning life: because it dies, mammaro means 'a dry leaf' and also 'the rustling of fallen leaves.'

153. Pīto kvaro.

153. From the root pī, the suffix kvara is applied.

Pī-tappanetīmasmā [M 0.0273] kvaro hoti. Appiṇīti pīvaraṃ=thūlaṃ.

From this root pī in the sense of satisfying, the suffix kvara occurs. Because it satisfies, pīvaraṃ means 'stout,' that is, gross.

154. Cīvarādayo.

154. Words beginning with cīvara.

Cīvaraādayo kvarantā nipaccante. Cinātissa dīghattaṃ. Cīyatīti cīvaraṃ=kāsāvaṃ. Sama-upasame, nadādittā vī, pariḷāhaṃ sametīti saṃvarī=ratti. Dhāssa ī, jālakuminādīni dhāretīti dhīvaro=koṭṭo, tāyatissa ī, yena kenaci attānaṃ tāyatīti tīvaro=hīnajāti. Nayatissī, nayanti ettha sattāti nīvaraṃ=gharaṃ, evamaññepi.

Words such as cīvara ending in the suffix kvara are irregularly formed. There is lengthening of the vowel of the root ci. Because it is collected, it is a cīvaraṃ, that is, a saffron robe. From the root sam in the sense of calming, with ī as in the nadādi group: because it calms the burning heat, it is saṃvarī, that is, night. For the root dhā, the vowel becomes ī; because he holds nets, fish-traps, and so on, he is a dhīvaro, that is, a fisherman. For the root tāy, the vowel becomes ī; because he protects himself by any means whatsoever, he is a tīvaro, that is, a person of low birth. For the root nī, the vowel becomes ī; because beings are led here, it is a nīvaraṃ, that is, a house. And so for others too.

155. Kuto kriro.

155. From ku, the suffix krira.

Ku-saddetīmasmā kriro hoti. Kavati nadatīti kuraro=pakkhī, itthiyaṃ vīmhi kurarī.

From this root ku in the sense of sounding, the suffix krira occurs. Because it cries out or makes a sound, it is a kuraro, that is, a bird. In the feminine, with the suffix ī, it is kurarī.

156. Vasāsā charo.

156. From vas and as, the suffix chara.

Vasa-nivāse, asa-khepane, etehi charo hoti. Vasanti etthāti vaccharo=vasso. Saṃpubbo, saṃvasanti etthāti saṃvaccharo=sova. Asati vissajjetīti accharā=devakaññā, aṅguliphoṭanañca.

From the root vas in the sense of dwelling, and from the root as in the sense of throwing, from these the suffix chara occurs. Because they dwell here, it is a vaccharo, that is, a year. Preceded by saṃ, because they dwell together here, it is a saṃvaccharo, that is, a year. Because it casts forth, it is an accharā, that is, a celestial nymph, and also the snapping of fingers.

157. Masā chero ca.

157. From mas, the suffixes chera and chara.

Masa-amasanetīmasmā chero hoti charo ca. Taṇhāya parāmasanaṃ maccheraṃ=sakasampattiniguhanaṃ, maccharaṃ=tadeva.

From this root mas in the sense of touching, the suffixes chera and chara occur. Grasping due to craving is maccheraṃ, that is, the concealing of one's own property. Maccharaṃ is the same.

158. Dhū vāto saro.

158. From dhū and vā, the suffix sara.

Dhunāti [M 0.0274] vātīhi saro hoti. Dhunātīti dhūsaro=lūkho īsaṃpaṇḍu ca. Vāti gacchatīti vāsaro=divaso.

From the roots `dhū` (to shake) and `vā` (to blow), the suffix `sara` occurs. Because it shakes, it is `dhūsaro`, that is, rough and somewhat pale. Because it blows or goes, it is `vāsaro`, that is, a day.

159. Bhamādīhyaro.

159. From `bham` and so on, the suffix `ara`.

Bhama tasa manda kandādīhi aro hoti. Bhamatīti bhamaro=madhukaro. Tasati tantaṃ gaṇhātīti tasaro=suttaveṭṭhano. Mandanti modanti etthāti mandaro=pabbato. Kandati avhāyatīti kandaro=darī. Divassa ettaṃ, devanti kīḷanti etenāti devaro=patiro bhātā.

From the roots `bham`, `tas`, `mand`, `kand`, and so on, the suffix `ara` occurs. Because it roams, it is a `bhamaro`, that is, a bee. Because it takes up the thread, it is a `tasaro`, that is, a shuttle. Because they rejoice there, it is `Mandaro`, that is, a mountain. Because it cries out, it is a `kandaro`, that is, a cave. From the root `div`, its vowel is strengthened to `e`; because they play with him, he is a `devaro`, that is, a husband's brother.

160. Vadissa badaca.

160. And for `vad`, `bada` is substituted.

Vadatismā aro yoti, vadatissa badādeso ca. Vadanti etenāti badaro=kakkandhūphalaṃ. Vīmhi badarī=kakkandhū.

From the root `vad`, the suffix `ara` occurs, and `bada` is substituted for `vad`. Because they speak with this, it is a `badaro`, that is, the jujube fruit. With the feminine suffix `ī`, it is `badarī`, that is, the jujube tree.

161. Vada janānaṃ ṭhaṅaca.

161. From `vad` and `jan`, and the substitution `ṭhaṅa`.

Vada janehi aro hoti, ṭhaṅa cāntādeso. Vadatīti vaṭharo=mūḷo vaṭharaṃ=thūlaṃ. Jāyatīti jaṭharaṃ=udaraṃ.

From the roots `vad` and `jan`, the suffix `ara` occurs, and `ṭhaṅa` is substituted for the final consonant. Because he speaks, he is a `vaṭharo`, that is, a dullard; `vaṭharaṃ` means thick or coarse. Because it is produced, it is a `jaṭharaṃ`, that is, the belly.

162. Pacissiṭhaṅaca.

162. For `pac`, and the substitution `iṭhaṅa`.

Pacatismā aro hoti iṭhaṅacāntādaso. Pacanti etenāti piṭharo=thālī.

From the root `pac`, the suffix `ara` occurs, and `iṭhaṅa` is substituted for the final consonant. Because they cook with this, it is a `piṭharo`, that is, a pot.

163. Vakā araṇa.

163. From `vak`, the suffix `araṇa`.

Vaka kuka-ādānetimasmā araṇahoti. Vaketi ādadāti etāyāti vākarā=migabandhanī.

From these roots `vak` and `kuk` in the sense of taking, the suffix `araṇa` occurs. Because one seizes with it, it is a `vākarā`, that is, a deer trap.

164. Siṅgyaṅgāga majjakalālā āro.

164. From `siṅgi`, `aṅg`, `ag`, `majj`, `kal`, and `al`, the suffix `āra`.

Siṅgiiti [M 0.0275] nāmadhātu, aṅga-gamanattho, aga-kuṭilagamane, majjasaṃsuddhiyaṃ, kala-saṅkhyāne, ala-bandhane, etehi āro hoti. Vijjhanatthena siṅgaṃ viya siṅgaṃ=nāgarikabhāvasaṅkhātassa kilesasiṅgassetaṃ nāmaṃ, taṃkaroti siṅgaṃ vā payuttaṃ, taṃ karoti rāgīsu pabhavatīti vā, “dhātvatthe nānāmasmī”ti (5.12) i, pubba saralopo, siṅgi, tato āro, “sarolopo sare”ti (1.26) ilopo, pubbe “vippaṭisedhe”ti (1.22) aniṭṭhappaṭisedho, ettha hi ārato aññattha sāvakāsapubbasaralopova, ipaccayato aññattha ca, siṅgāro=kilesasiṅgakaraṇaṃ, vilāsoti vuttaṃ hoti. Aṅgati vināsaṃ gacchatīti aṅgāro=daḍḍhakaṭṭhaṃ. Aganti gacchanti etthāti agāraṃ=gharaṃ. Līhanena attano sarīraṃ majjati nimmalattaṃ karotīti majjāro=biḷāro. Kalāti niddesā lassa ḷattaṃ, etena guṇaṃ kalīyati parimīyatīti kaḷāro=piṅgalo. Dīghattaṃ alati bandhatīti aḷāro=vaṅko visālo ca.

`Siṅgi` is a denominative root; `aṅga` has the meaning of going; `aga`, of going crookedly; `majj`, of cleansing; `kala`, of counting; `ala`, of binding. From these the suffix `āra` occurs. The derivation of `siṅgāra` is as follows: like a horn (`siṅga`) in the sense of piercing, `siṅga` is a name for the 'horn of the defilements' (`kilesasiṅga`), which is known as urbanity. One who creates this, or is endowed with this horn, or in whom it arises among the passionate, is `siṅgāra`. The grammatical process involves the suffix `i` by the rule 'in the sense of the root from various nouns' (Kaccāyana 5.12), elision of the preceding vowel, giving `siṅgi`; from that, the suffix `āra` is added, and the `i` is elided by 'elision of a vowel before a vowel' (1.26). The rule 'in case of conflict' (1.22) prevents an undesirable outcome, for here the elision of the preceding vowel has scope elsewhere than before `āra`, and the `i` suffix has scope elsewhere. `Siṅgāro` thus means the creation of the 'horn of the defilements,' which is to say, charm. Because it goes to destruction, it is an `aṅgāro`, that is, charcoal. Because they go in it, it is an `agāraṃ`, that is, a house. Because it cleanses its own body by licking, making it stainless, it is a `majjāro`, that is, a cat. From the citation `kala`, `l` becomes `ḷ`; because a quality is counted or measured by it, it is `kaḷāro`, that is, tawny. With lengthening, because it binds, it is an `aḷāro`, that is, crooked and also prominent.

165. Kamissassu ca.

165. For `kam`, its `a` also becomes `u`.

Kama-icchāyamiccasmā āro hoti, assa u ca. Kāmīyatīti kumāro=bālo.

From this root `kam` in the sense of desiring, the suffix `āra` occurs, and its `a` becomes `u`. Because he is desired, he is a `kumāro`, that is, a boy.

166. Bhiṅgārādayo.

166. `Bhiṅgāra` and so on.

Bhiṅgārappabhutayo ārantā nipaccante. Bhara=bharaṇe, bharaṇaṃ dhāraṇaṃ posanañca, dhāraṇatthassa bharatissa bhiṅgādeso, bharati [M 0.0276] dadhāti udakanti bhiṅgāro=hemabhājanaṃ. Kleda klida-alla bhāve, la lopo, kledayatīti kedāraṃ=khettaṃ, (ke jale sati dāro vidāraṇamassāti vā kedāraṃ=tadeva, bahulādhikārā sattamiyā na lopo.) Vida-lābhetīmasmā kupubbā āro dassa ḷattaṃ issa ettābhāvo samāse kussa o ca nipaccante, kuṃ pathaviṃ vindati tatruppannatāyāti koviḷāro=diguṇapatto.

Words such as `bhiṅgāra`, ending in `āra`, are irregularly formed. The root is `bhar` in the sense of bearing; `bharaṇa` means holding and nourishing. For the root `bhar` in the sense of holding, `bhiṅga` is substituted. Because it bears or holds water, it is a `bhiṅgāro`, that is, a golden vessel. From the roots `kled` or `klid` in the sense of being wet, with elision of `l`; because it becomes wet, it is `kedāraṃ`, that is, a field. (Alternatively, `kedāraṃ` is that which has splitting (`dāro`, `vidāraṇaṃ`) when there is water (`ke`, `jale`) in it; due to the principle of extended application, the locative ending is not elided.) From this root `vid` in the sense of obtaining, preceded by `ku`, the suffix `āra` occurs; `d` becomes `ḷ`, `i` does not become `e`, and in the compound `ku` becomes `o`—these are irregular formations. Because it finds the earth (`kuṃ`) by being produced there, it is a `koviḷāro`, that is, the Bauhinia tree.

167. Karā māro.

167. From `kar`, the suffix `māra`.

Karotismā māro hoti. Lohakiccaṃ karotīti kammāro=lohakāro.

From the root `kar`, the suffix `māra` occurs. Because he does iron-work, he is a `kammāro`, that is, a blacksmith.

168. Pusa sarehi kharo.

168. From `pus` and `sar`, the suffix `khara`.

Pusa sarehi kharo hoti. Posīyati jalenāti pokkharaṃ=padumaṃ. Sarati vikāraṃ gacchatīti sakkharā=ucchuvikāro.

From the roots `pus` and `sar`, the suffix `khara` occurs. Because it is nourished by water, it is a `pokkharaṃ`, that is, a lotus. Because it undergoes transformation, it is `sakkharā`, that is, a product of sugarcane.

169. Sara vasa kalā kīro vassuṭa ca.

169. From `sar`, `vas`, and `kal`, the suffix `kīra`; and for `vas`, `uṭa` is substituted.

Etehi kīro hoti vassa uṭa ca. Sarīyatīti sarīraṃ=deho. Vasanti vāsaṃ karonti etenāti usīraṃ=bīraṇamūlaṃ. Anena thūlādi kalīyati parimīyatiti kaliro=aṅkuro.

From these roots the suffix `kīra` occurs, and for `vas`, `uṭa` is substituted. Because it wastes away, it is a `sarīraṃ`, that is, the body. Because they dwell or make their dwelling with it, it is `usīraṃ`, that is, the root of Vetiver grass. Because coarse things and so on are counted or measured by it, it is a `kaliro`, that is, a sprout.

170. Gambhīrādayo.

170. `Gambhīra` and so on.

Gambhīraādayo kīrantā nipaccante. Gamissa bhuka, malopo vā, pathaviṃ, bhinditvā gacchati pavattatīti gambhīro, gabhīro= agādho[M 0.0277], kulissa lassa ḷo, pāde kulati pattharatīti kuḷīro=kakkaṭo, evamaññepi.

Words such as `gambhīra`, ending in `kīra`, are irregularly formed. For the root `gam`, `bhu` is substituted, and `m` is optionally elided; because it proceeds having split the earth, it is `gambhīro` or `gabhīro`, that is, deep. For the root `kul`, `l` becomes `ḷ`; because it gathers or spreads its feet, it is a `kuḷīro`, that is, a crab. And so for others too.

171. Khajja valla masā ūro.

171. From `khajj`, `vall`, and `mas`, the suffix `ūra`.

Khajja-majjane, vala valla-saṃvaraṇe, sama-āmasane, etehi ūro hoti, khajjīyatīti khajjūro, vīmhi khajjūrī=rukkhaviseso. Vallīyati saṃvarīyatīti vallūro=sukkhamaṃso. Masīyatīti masūro=vīhiviseso.

From the root `khajj` in the sense of scouring, `val` or `vall` in the sense of covering, and `mas` in the sense of touching, from these the suffix `ūra` occurs. Because it is eaten, it is a `khajjūro`; with the feminine suffix `ī`, it is `khajjūrī`, a particular kind of tree. Because it is covered, it is `vallūro`, that is, dried meat. Because it is touched, it is `masūro`, a particular kind of grain.

172. Kappūrādayo.

172. `Kappūra` and so on.

Kappūraādayo ūrantā nipaccante. Tuṭṭhimuppādetuṃ kappati sakkotīti kappūraṃ=ghanasāro. Karotissa assu, kibbisaṃ karotīti kurūro=pāpakārī. Pasa-bādhane, pasati pīḷetīti pasūro=duṭṭho, byañjanaṃ, evaṃnāmako ca, evamaññepi.

Words such as `kappūra`, ending in `ūra`, are irregularly formed. Because it is fit or able to produce satisfaction, it is `kappūraṃ`, that is, camphor. For the root `kar`, its `a` becomes `u`; because he does evil, he is `kurūro`, that is, an evil-doer. From the root `pas` in the sense of oppressing; because he oppresses or harasses, he is `pasūro`, that is, a wicked person, and also a name for a type of condiment. And so for others too.

173. Kaṭha cakā oro.

173. From `kaṭh` and `cak`, the suffix `ora`.

Kaṭha-kicchajīvane, caka-parivitakkane, etehi oro hoti. Kaṭhati kicchena jīvatīti kaṭhoro=thaddho. Cakati parivitakketīti cakoro=pakkhiviseso.

From the root kaṭh in the sense of 'living with difficulty' and from the root cak in the sense of 'reflecting,' the suffix oro is formed. 'One who lives with difficulty' (kaṭhati kicchena jīvati) is kaṭhoro, meaning 'harsh.' 'One who reflects' (cakati parivitakketi) is cakoro, a particular kind of bird.

174. Morādayo.

174. Mora and others.

Moraādayo orantā nipaccante. Mī-hiṃsāyaṃ, īlopo, mayati hiṃsatīti moro=mayūro. Kasa-gamane, assi[M 0.0278], kasati gacchatīti kisoro=paṭhamavayo asso. Mahīyati pūjīyatīti mahoro=vammiko, evamaññepi.

Mora and other words ending in ora are irregularly formed. From the root mī in the sense of 'harming,' with elision of ī: 'it harms' (mayati hiṃsati), hence moro, meaning 'peacock.' From the root kas in the sense of 'going,' with a becoming i: 'it goes' (kasati gacchati), hence kisoro, meaning 'a young horse of the first age.' 'It is honored' (mahīyati pūjīyati), hence mahoro, meaning 'anthill.' And so for others as well.

175. Kuto eraka.

175. From ku, the suffix eraka.

Ku-saddetīmasmā eraka hoti. “Yuvaṇṇānamiyaṅuvaṅa sare”ti (5.136) uvaṅa, kavati nadatīti kuvero=vessavaṇo.

From the root ku in the sense of 'to sound,' the suffix eraka is formed. By the rule 'Yuvaṇṇānamiyaṅuvaṅa sare' (Kacc. 5.136), u becomes uva. 'It sounds' or 'roars' (kavati nadati), hence kuvero, meaning Vessavaṇa.

176. Bhū sūhi rika.

176. From bhū and sū, the suffix rika.

Bhūsattāyaṃ, sū-pasavane, etehi rika hoti. Bhavatīti bhūri=pahūtaṃ, ṅīmhi bhūrī=medhā. Savati hitaṃ pasavatīti sūri=vicakkhaṇo.

From the root bhū in the sense of 'being' and from sū in the sense of 'generating,' from these the suffix rika is formed. 'It is' (bhavati), hence bhūri, meaning 'abundant.' With the feminine suffix ṅī, it becomes bhūrī, meaning 'wisdom.' 'It generates what is beneficial' (savati hitaṃ pasavati), hence sūri, meaning 'a wise person'.

177. Mī kasī nīhi ru.

177. From mī, kasī, and nī, the suffix ru.

Mī-hiṃsāyamiccasmā, kapubbā sayatismā, nayatismā ca ru hoti. Raṃsīhi andhakāraṃ mīyati hiṃsatīti meru=sireru, ke jale sayati pavattatīti kaseru=tiṇaviseso. Attanissite sundarattaṃ neti pāpetīti neru=pabbato.

From the root mī in the sense of 'harming,' from the root sī 'to lie' preceded by ka, and from the root nī 'to lead,' the suffix ru is formed. 'It harms the darkness with its rays' (raṃsīhi andhakāraṃ mīyati hiṃsati), hence meru, meaning Mount Sineru. 'It lies or exists in the water' (ke jale sayati pavattati), hence kaseru, a particular kind of grass. 'It leads those who depend on it to beauty' (attanissite sundarattaṃ neti pāpeti), hence neru, a mountain.

178. Sinā eru.

178. From sinā, the suffix eru.

Sinā-soceyyetīmasmā eru hoti. Sināti suciṃ karotīti sineru=pabbatarājā.

From the root sinā in the sense of 'purity,' the suffix eru is formed. 'It makes pure' (sināti suciṃ karoti), hence sineru, the king of mountains.

179. Bhī ruhi ruka.

179. From bhī and ru, the suffix ruka.

Bhī-saye, ru-sadde, etehi ruka hoti. Bhāyanti etasmāti bhīru=bhayānako. Ravatīti ruru=migo.

From the root bhī in the sense of 'fear' and from ru in the sense of 'sound,' from these the suffix ruka is formed. 'They fear it' (bhāyanti etasmā), hence bhīru, meaning 'fearsome.' 'It makes a sound' (ravati), hence ruru, a deer.

180. Tamā būlo.

180. From tam, the suffix būla.

Tama-bhūsanetīmasmā [M 0.0279] būlo hoti. Mukhaṃ tameti bhūsetīti tambūlaṃ=mukhabhūsanaṃ.

From the root tam in the sense of 'adornment,' the suffix būla is formed. 'It adorns the mouth' (mukhaṃ tameti bhūseti), hence tambūlaṃ, meaning 'mouth-adornment' (betel).

181. Sito lakavālā.

181. From si, the suffixes la, ka, and vāla.

Si-sevāyamiccasmā lakavālaiccete paccayā honti. Sattehi sevīyatīti silā=pāsāṇo, selo=pabbato. Jalaṃ sevatīti sevālo=jalatiṇaṃ.

From the root si in the sense of 'serving,' these suffixes—la, ka, and vāla—are formed. 'It is resorted to by beings' (sattehi sevīyati), hence silā, meaning 'stone,' and selo, meaning 'mountain.' 'It resorts to water' (jalaṃ sevati), hence sevālo, meaning 'water-weed'.

182. Maṅga kama samba saba saka vasa pisa keva kala palla kaṭha paṭa kuṇḍa maṇḍā alo.

182. From maṅg, kam, samb, sab, sak, vas, pis, kev, kal, pall, kaṭh, paṭ, kuṇḍ, and maṇḍ, the suffix ala.

Maṅga-maṅgalye, kama-icchāyaṃ, samba-maṇḍane, sabaiti asseva katamalopassa niddeso, saka-sattiya, vasa-nivāse, pisagamane, keva-sevane, kala-saṅkhyāne, palla-gamane, kaṭha kicchajīvane, paṭa-gamanattho, kuṇḍa-dāhe, maṇḍa-bhūsane, etehi alo hoti. Maṅganti sattā etena vuddhiṃ gacchantīti maṅgalaṃ=pasatthaṃ. Kāmīyatīti kamalaṃ-paṅkajaṃ. Sampati maṇḍetīti sambalaṃ=pātheyyaṃ. Sabalaṃ=visabhāga vaṇṇavantaṃ. Sakkoti vattunti sakalaṃ=sabbaṃ. Vasatīti vasalo=suddo. Piyabhāvaṃ pisati gacchatīti pesalo=piyasīlo. Kevati pavattatīti kevalaṃ=sakalaṃ. Kalīyati parimīyati udakametenāti kalalaṃ=apatthinnaṃ, pallati āgacchati udakametasmāti pallalaṃ=appodako saro. Kaṭhanti ettha dukkhena yantīti kaṭhalaṃ=kapālakhaṇḍaṃ, paṭati vuddhiṃ gacchatīti paṭalaṃ=samū- ho[M 0.0280]. Ghaṃsena kuṇḍati dahatīti kuṇḍalaṃ=kaṇṇābharaṇaṃ. Maṇḍīyati paricchedakaraṇavasena bhūsīyatīti maṇḍalaṃ=samantato paricchinnaṃ.

From the roots maṅg in the sense of 'auspiciousness,' kam in 'desire,' samb in 'adornment'—saba is a reference to this same root with elision of ma—sak in 'ability,' vas in 'dwelling,' pis in 'going,' kev in 'serving,' kal in 'counting,' pall in 'going,' kaṭh in 'living with difficulty,' paṭ in the sense of 'going,' kuṇḍ in 'burning,' and maṇḍ in 'adorning'—from these the suffix ala is formed. 'Beings prosper and go to growth through this' (maṅganti sattā etena vuddhiṃ gacchanti), hence maṅgalaṃ, meaning 'auspicious.' 'It is desired' (kāmīyati), hence kamalaṃ, the lotus. 'It adorns one's property' (sampati maṇḍeti), hence sambalaṃ, provisions for a journey. Sabalaṃ means 'having variegated color.' 'It is able to be' (sakkoti vattuṃ), hence sakalaṃ, meaning 'all.' 'One who dwells' (vasati), hence vasalo, a sudra. 'It goes to a state of being dear' (piyabhāvaṃ pisati gacchati), hence pesalo, one of amiable conduct. 'It exists' (kevati pavattati), hence kevalaṃ, meaning 'entire.' 'Water is measured by this' (kalīyati parimīyati udakametena), hence kalalaṃ, meaning 'unthickened' (embryo). 'Water comes from this' (pallati āgacchati udakametasmā), hence pallalaṃ, a small pool of water. 'They go here with difficulty' (kaṭhanti ettha dukkhena yanti), hence kaṭhalaṃ, a potsherd. 'It goes to growth' (paṭati vuddhiṃ gacchati), hence paṭalaṃ, a multitude. 'It burns by friction' (ghaṃsena kuṇḍati dahati), hence kuṇḍalaṃ, an earring. 'It is adorned by way of making a boundary' (maṇḍīyati paricchedakaraṇavasena bhūsīyati), hence maṇḍalaṃ, a circle defined all around.

183. Musā kalo.

183. From mus, the suffix kala.

Musatismā kalo hoti. Musati etenāti musalo=ayoggo.

From the root mus, the suffix kala is formed. 'One crushes with this' (musati etena), hence musalo, meaning 'a pestle'.

184. Thalādayo.

184. Thala and others.

Thalaādayo kalantā nipaccante. Ṭhassa tho, pubbasaralopo, tiṭṭhanti etthāti thalaṃ=unnatappadeso. Pā-pāne, upubbo, dvibhāvasaralopā, udakaṃ pivatīti uppalaṃ=kuvalayaṃ. Patissa pāṭaṃ, patati gacchati paripākanti pāṭalaṃ=phalaṃ, tambavaṇṇaṃ kusumañca. Baṃhissa niggahītalopo, baṃhati vuddhiṃ gacchatīti bahalaṃ=ghanaṃ. Cupissa ussa attaṃ, cupati ekattha na tiṭṭhatīti capalo=anavaṭṭhito, evamaññepi.

Thala and other words ending in kala are irregularly formed. For thalaṃ: ṭh becomes th, with elision of the preceding vowel; 'they stand here' (tiṭṭhanti ettha), hence thalaṃ, an elevated place. For uppalaṃ: from the root pā 'to drink,' preceded by u(pa), with doubling of the consonant and vowel elision; 'it drinks water' (udakaṃ pivati), hence uppalaṃ, a water lily. For pāṭalaṃ: pat becomes pāṭa; 'it falls or goes to maturity' (patati gacchati paripākaṃ), hence pāṭalaṃ, a fruit, and also a reddish flower. For bahalaṃ: from baṃh, with elision of the niggahīta; 'it grows' (baṃhati vuddhiṃ gacchati), hence bahalaṃ, meaning 'dense.' For capalo: from cup, with u becoming a; 'it moves, it does not stay in one place' (cupati ekattha na tiṭṭhati), hence capalo, meaning 'unsteady.' And so for others as well.

185. Kulā kālo ca.

185. From kul, the suffixes kāla and kala.

Kula-patthāretīmasmā kālo hoti kalo ca. Kulati attano sippaṃ pattharatīti kulālo=kumbhakāro. Kulati pakkhe pasāretīti kulalo=pakkhijāti.

From the root kul in the sense of 'spreading,' the suffixes kāla and kala are formed. 'He spreads his craft' (kulati attano sippaṃ pattharati), hence kulālo, a potter. 'It spreads its wings' (kulati pakkhe pasāreti), hence kulalo, a species of bird.

186. Muḷālādayo.

186. Muḷāla and others.

Muḷālaādayo kālantā nipaccante. Mīla-nimīlane, uttaḷatāni, uddhaṭamatte nimīlatīti muḷālaṃ=bhisaṃ. Bala-pāṇane, itta- ḷattāni[M 0.0281], mūsikādikhādanena balati jīvatīti biḷālo=majjāro. Kappissa saṃyogādilopo, kappanti jīvikaṃ etenāti kapālaṃ=ghaṭādikhaṇḍaṃ. Pī tappane. “Yuvaṇṇānamiyaṅuvaṅa sare”ti (5.136) iyaṅa, attano phalena satte santappetīti piyālo-rukkho. Kuṇa-sadde, vātasamuṭṭhitā vīcimālā ettha kuṇanti nadantīti kuṇālo=eko mahāsaro. Visa-pavisane, pavisanti etthāti visālo=vitthiṇṇo. Pala-gamane, vātena palati gacchatīti palālaṃ=sassānamupanītadhaññānaṃ nāḷapattāni. Saratissa sigo, sasādayo sarati hiṃsatīti sigālo=kotthu, evamaññepi.

Muḷāla and other words ending in kāla are irregularly formed. From the root mīl in the sense of 'closing the eyes,' with the substitutions of u and ḷ: 'it closes as soon as it is pulled up' (uddhaṭamatte nimīlati), hence muḷālaṃ, a lotus root. From the root bal in the sense of 'living,' with the substitutions of i and ḷ: 'it lives by eating mice and other creatures' (mūsikādikhādanena balati jīvati), hence biḷālo, a cat. For kapālaṃ: from the root kapp, with elision of the initial conjunct consonant; 'one arranges one's livelihood with this' (kappanti jīvikaṃ etena), hence kapālaṃ, a potsherd. From the root pī in the sense of 'pleasing': by the rule 'Yuvaṇṇānamiyaṅuvaṅa sare' (Kacc. 5.136), iya is substituted; 'it pleases beings with its fruit' (attano phalena satte santappeti), hence piyālo, a tree. From the root kuṇ in the sense of 'sounding': 'here the rows of waves stirred up by the wind make a sound' (vātasamuṭṭhitā vīcimālā ettha kuṇanti nadanti), hence kuṇālo, a great lake. From the root vis in the sense of 'entering': 'they enter here' (pavisanti ettha), hence visālo, meaning 'spacious.' From the root pal in the sense of 'going': 'it goes with the wind' (vātena palati gacchati), hence palālaṃ, the stalks and leaves of grain from which the corn has been taken. For sigālo: from the root sar, with the prefix si; 'it harms hares and other animals' (sasādayo sarati hiṃsati), hence sigālo, a jackal. And so for others as well.

187. Caṇḍa patā ṇālo.

187. From caṇḍ and pat, the suffix ṇāla.

Caṇḍa-caṇḍikye, pata patha-gamane, etehi ṇālo hoti. Caṇḍeti pīḷetīti caṇḍālo=mātaṅgo, patati adhogacchatīti pātālaṃ=rasātalaṃ.

From the root caṇḍ in the sense of 'fierceness' and from pat or path in the sense of 'going,' from these the suffix ṇāla is formed. 'He is fierce and torments' (caṇḍeti pīḷeti), hence caṇḍālo, an outcaste. 'One falls or goes downwards' (patati adhogacchati), hence pātālaṃ, the netherworld.

188. Mādito lo.

188. From mā and others, the suffix la.

Mā-māne, i-ajjhenagatīsu, pī-tappane, dū-paritāpe, evamādīhi lo hoti. Mīyati parimīyatīti mālā=panti. Eti gacchatīti elā=sukhumelā. Piṇeti tappeti etthāti pelā=āsittakūpadhānaṃ. Dūyati paritāpetīti dolā=kīḷanayānakaṃ. Kalasaṅkhyāne, kalanaṃ kallaṃ=yuttaṃ.

From the roots mā in the sense of 'measuring,' i in the sense of 'going towards,' pī in 'pleasing,' dū in 'tormenting,' and so on, the suffix la is used. 'It is measured' (mīyati parimīyati), hence mālā, a row or garland. 'It goes' (eti gacchati), hence elā, cardamom. 'One pleases or satisfies with this' (piṇeti tappeti ettha), hence pelā, a chest or box. 'It torments' (dūyati paritāpeti), hence dolā, a swing. From kal in the sense of 'counting': kalanaṃ, 'counting,' becomes kallaṃ, meaning 'proper' or 'fitting'.

189. Ana sala kala kuka saṭha mahā ilo.

189. From an, sal, kal, kuk, saṭh, and mah, the suffix ila is used.

Ana-pāṇane, sala-gamane, kala-saṅkhyāne, kuka vaka-ādane, saṭha-kitave, araha maha-pūjāyaṃ, etehi ilo hoti. Anati [M 0.0282] pavattatītianilo=māluto. Salati gacchatīti salilaṃ=jalaṃ. Kalati pavattatīti kalilaṃ=gahanaṃ. Kukati attano nādena sattānaṃ manaṃ gaṇhātīti kokilo=parapuṇḍo. Saṭhati vañcetīti saṭhilo=saṭho. Mahīyati pūjīyatīti mayilā=itthī.

From the roots an in the sense of 'breathing,' sal in 'going,' kal in 'counting,' kuk or vak in 'taking,' saṭh in 'deceiving,' and arah or mah in 'honoring,' from these the suffix ila is used. 'It breathes' (anati pavattati), hence anilo, the wind. 'It goes' (salati gacchati), hence salilaṃ, water. 'It proceeds' (kalati pavattati), hence kalilaṃ, dense or impenetrable. 'It takes the minds of beings with its own sound' (kukati attano nādena sattānaṃ manaṃ gaṇhāti), hence kokilo, the cuckoo. 'He deceives' (saṭhati vañceti), hence saṭhilo, a deceitful person. 'She is honored' (mahīyati pūjīyati), hence mayilā, a woman.

190. Kuṭā kilo.

190. From kuṭ, the suffix kila is used.

Kuṭa-koṭilyetīmasmā kilo hoti. Akuṭi kuṭilattamagamīti kuṭilo=vaṅko.

From the root kuṭ in the sense of 'crookedness,' the suffix kila is used. 'Being not straight, it became crooked' (akuṭi kuṭilattamagamī), hence kuṭilo, meaning 'bent' or 'crooked'.

191. Sithilādayo.

191. Sithila and others.

Sithilaādayo kilantā nipaccante. Saha khamāyaṃ, sahissa sithattaṃ, sahitumalanti sithilaṃ=adaḷhaṃ. Kampissa saṃyogādilopo, paradukkhe sati kampatīti kapilo=isi. Kaba-vaṇṇe, bassa po, akabi nīlādivaṇṇattamagamīti kapilo=vaṇṇaviseso. Mathissa mitho, mathīyatīti mithilā=pūrī, evamaññepi.

Sithila and other words ending in kila are irregularly formed. For sithilaṃ: from the root sah in the sense of 'enduring,' sah becomes sith; 'able to endure' (sahituṃ alaṃ), hence sithilaṃ, meaning 'slack' or 'not firm.' For kapilo: from the root kamp, with elision of the initial conjunct consonant; 'he trembles when there is suffering for others' (paradukkhe sati kampati), hence kapilo, a sage. Also, from the root kab in the sense of 'color,' with b becoming p: 'being not blue or another color, it became a particular color' (akabi nīlādivaṇṇattamagamī), hence kapilo, a particular color (tawny). For mithilā: from the root math, which becomes mith; 'it is churned' (mathīyati), hence mithilā, a city. And so for others as well.

192. Caṭa kaṇḍa vaṭṭa puthā kulo.

192. From caṭ, kaṇḍ, vaṭṭ, and puth, the suffix kula is used.

Caṭa-bhedane, kaṇḍa-chedane, vaṭṭa-vattane, putha patha-vitthāre, etehi kulo hoti. Caṭati mitte bhindatīti caṭulo=cāṭukārī. Kaṇḍīyati chindīyatīti kaṇḍulo=rukkho. Vaṭṭatīti vaṭṭulo=parimaṇḍalo. Apattharīti puthulo=vitthāro.

From the roots caṭ in the sense of 'splitting,' kaṇḍ in 'cutting,' vaṭṭ in 'turning,' and puth or path in 'spreading,' from these the suffix kula is used. 'He splits friends' (caṭati mitte bhindati), hence caṭulo, a flatterer. 'It is cut' (kaṇḍīyati chindīyati), hence kaṇḍulo, a tree. 'It turns' (vaṭṭati), hence vaṭṭulo, meaning 'round.' 'It spreads out' (apatthari), hence puthulo, meaning 'broad' or 'extensive'.

193. Tumulādayo.

193. Tumula and others.

Tumulaādayo kulantā nipaccante. Tama khedane, assu, atami vitthiṇṇattamagamīti tumulo=patthaṭo. Tamissa ḍuka, tamīyati [M 0.0283] vikāramāpādīyatīti taṇḍulo=vīhisāro. Nipubbassa cinātissa ilopo, atthikehi nicīyateti niculo=hijjalo, evamaññepi.

The words beginning with tumula are irregularly formed with the suffix -ula. From the root tam, 'to be distressed': because distress became widespread, it is tumula, meaning 'widespread.' From the same root tam with the suffix ḍula: because it is made to undergo change, it is taṇḍula, meaning 'husked rice.' From the root ci preceded by ni, with elision of i: because it is gathered by those in need, it is nicula, meaning the Hijjala tree. And so for others.

194. Kalla kapa takka paṭā olo.

194. From the roots kalla, kapa, takka, and paṭa, the suffix -olo is used.

Kalla-sadde, kapa-acchādane, takka-vitakke, paṭa-gamane, etehi olo hoti. Vātavegena samuddato uṭṭhahitvā kallati nadatīti kallolo=mahāvīci. Kapati dante acchādatīti kapolo=vadanekadeso. Takkīyatīti takkolaṃ=kolakaṃ. Paṭati byādhimetena gacchatīti paṭolo=tittako.

From the root kalla in the sense of 'sound,' kapa in the sense of 'covering,' takka in the sense of 'thinking,' and paṭa in the sense of 'going'—from these the suffix -olo is used. Because, having risen from the ocean with the force of the wind, it makes a sound or roars, it is kallola, meaning 'a great wave.' Because it covers the teeth, it is kapola, meaning 'a part of the face, the cheek.' Because it is thought about, it is takkola, meaning a type of aromatic plant. Because one goes to it for a disease, it is paṭola, meaning 'a bitter gourd.'

195. Aṅgā ulolī.

195. From the root aṅg, the suffixes -ula and -uli are used.

Aṅga-gamanattho, etasmā ulaulī honti. Aṅganti etena jānantīti aṅgulaṃ=pamāṇaṃ. Aṅgati uggacchatīti aṅgali=karasākhā.

The root aṅg has the meaning 'to go'; from this, the suffixes -ula and -uli are used. Because they know a limb by this, it is aṅgula, meaning 'a measure.' Because it goes or rises up, it is aṅguli, meaning 'a branch of the hand, a finger.'

196. Añjāli.

196. From the root añj, the suffix -āli is used.

Añja-byatti makkhana gati kantīsu, etasmā ali hoti. Añjeti bhattimanena pakāsetīti añjali=karapuṭo.

The root añj has the meanings 'manifestation,' 'anointing,' 'going,' and 'shining'; from this, the suffix -ali is used. Because one manifests or displays devotion with this, it is añjali, meaning 'the cupped hands.'

197. Chadā li.

197. From the root chad, the suffix -li is used.

Chada-saṃvaraṇe, etasmā li hoti. Chādetīti challī=sakalikā.

The root chad has the meaning 'covering'; from this, the suffix -li is used. Because it covers, it is challi, meaning 'bark' or 'a scale.'

198. Allyādayo.

198. Words beginning with alli.

Alliādayo liantā nipaccante. Ara-gamane, arati pavattatīti alli=rukkho. Nayatissa ettābhāvo, attikehi nīyatīti [M 0.0284]4 nīli, ṅīmhi nīlī=gacchajāti. “Saramhā dve”ti (1.34) lassa dvibhāve rassatte ca nillītipi hoti. Pālissa pā, pāleti rakkhatīti pāli, ṅīmhi pālī=panti. Pālissa palo, pāleti rakkhatīti palli=kuṭi. Cuda-codane, ottābhāvo, codīyatīti culli=uddhanaṃ, evamaññepi.

The words beginning with alli are irregularly formed with the suffix -li. From the root ar, 'to go': because it goes on, it is alli, meaning 'a tree.' From the root nī, 'to lead,' with absence of e: because it is led by those in need, it is nīli; with the feminine suffix -ī, it becomes nīlī, meaning 'a species of plant.' According to the rule 'doubling after a vowel,' with the doubling of l and shortening of the vowel, it also becomes nillī. From the root pāl, 'to protect': because it protects, it is pāli; with the feminine suffix -ī, it becomes pālī, meaning 'a line' or 'a row.' From the same root pāl: because it protects, it is palli, meaning 'a hut.' From the root cud, 'to urge,' with absence of o: because it is urged on, it is culli, meaning 'a fireplace' or 'a hearth.' And so for others.

199. Pilādīhyavo.

199. From the roots beginning with pil, the suffix -avo is used.

Pila-vattane, palla-gamane, paṇa-byavahārathutīsu, evamādīhi avo hoti. Pilyateti pelavo=lahu. Pallatīti pallavo=kisalayaṃ. Paṇīyatīti paṇavo=mudaṅgo. Evamaññepi.

From the root pil in the sense of 'turning,' palla in the sense of 'going,' paṇa in the senses of 'transacting' and 'praising,' and others such as these, the suffix -avo is used. Because it is turned, it is pelava, meaning 'light' or 'delicate.' Because it goes, it is pallava, meaning 'a sprout' or 'a shoot.' Because it is transacted with or praised, it is paṇava, meaning 'a small drum.' And so for others.

200. Sāḷavādayo.

200. Words beginning with sāḷava.

Sāḷavaādayo avantā nipaccante. Sala-gamanattho, upantassa dīgho ḷattañca nipātanā. Salati pavattatīti sāḷa vo=abhisaṅkhataṃ badarādiphalakhādanīyaṃ. Kita-nivāse, ettābhāvo, ketatīti kitavo=jūtakāro, coro ca. Mū-bandhane, ūssa rassattaṃ, tuña cāvassa, munāti bandhatīti mutavo=caṇḍālo. Vala valla-saṃvaraṇe, ḷattaṃ, valati, valyateti vā vaḷavā=turaṅgakantā. Mura-saṃveḷane, murīyatīti muravo=mudaṅgo, evamaññepi.

The words beginning with sāḷava are irregularly formed with the suffix -ava. The root sal has the meaning 'to go'; the lengthening of the penultimate vowel and the change to ḷ are by irregular formation. Because it proceeds, it is sāḷava, meaning 'a prepared edible made from jujube and other fruits.' From the root kit, 'to dwell' or 'to cheat,' with absence of e: because he cheats, he is kitava, meaning 'a gambler' and also 'a rogue.' From the root mū, 'to bind,' with shortening of ū and the augment tu: because he binds, he is mutava, meaning 'an outcaste.' From the root val or valla, 'to cover,' with change to ḷ: because she covers or is covered, she is vaḷavā, meaning 'a mare.' From the root mur, 'to encircle': because it is encircled, it is murava, meaning 'a small drum.' And so for others.

201. Sarā āvo.

201. From the root sar, the suffix -āvo is used.

Saratismā āvo hoti. Sarati pavattatīti sarāvo=bhājanaviseso.

From the root sar, the suffix -āvo is used. Because it moves along, it is sarāva, meaning 'a particular kind of vessel, an earthen bowl.'

202. Ala mala bilā ṇuvo.

202. From the roots al, mal, and bil, the suffix -ṇuva is used.

Ala-bandhane[M 0.0285], mala malla-dhāraṇe, bila-bhedane, etehi ṇuvo hoti. Latāhi alīyatīti āluvo=gacchajāti. Malati dhāretīti māluvo=pattalatā. Bilati bhindatīti beluvo=rukkho.

From the root al in the sense of 'adorning,' mal or malla in the sense of 'holding,' and bil in the sense of 'splitting'—from these the suffix -ṇuva is used. Because it is adorned with creepers, it is āluva, meaning 'a species of plant.' Because it holds, it is māluva, meaning 'a leaf-creeper.' Because it splits, it is beluva, meaning 'the Beluva tree.'

203. Gātvī vo.

203. From the root gā, the suffix -īva is used.

Kā gā-saddetīmasmā īvo hoti. Gāyanti etāyāti gīvā=galo.

From the root `gā` in the sense of 'sound,' the suffix `-īva` is used. Because they sing with this, it is `gīvā`, meaning 'the neck' or 'throat.'

204. Suto kvatvā.

204. From the root `su`, the suffixes `-kva` and `-kvā` are used.

Su-savanetīmasmā kva kvā honti. Suṇātīti suvo=kīro. Suvā=suṇo.

From the root `su` in the sense of 'hearing,' the suffixes `-kva` and `-kvā` are used. Because it hears, it is `suva`, meaning 'a parrot.' `Suvā` means 'a dog.'

205. Vidvā.

205. From the root `vid`, the suffix `-kvā` is used.

Vidatismā kvā pararūpābhāvo a nipaccante. Vidati jānātīti vidvā=vidū.

From the root `vid`, the suffix `-kvā` is irregularly formed with an absence of assimilation of the following sound. Because he knows, he is `vidvā`, meaning 'a wise person.'

206. Thuto revo.

206. From the root `thu`, the suffix `-reva` is used.

Thu-abhitthave, etasmā revo hoti. Thavati siñcatīti thevo=phusitaṃ.

The root `thu` has the meaning 'to praise'; from this, the suffix `-reva` is used. Because it praises or sprinkles, it is `thevo`, meaning 'a drop' or 'a sprinkle.'

207. Samā rivo.

207. From the root `sam`, the suffix `-riva` is used.

Sama-upasame, etasmā rivo hoti. Sameti upasametīti sivo=umāpati, sivā=sigālo, sivaṃ=santi.

The root `sam` has the meaning 'to be calm'; from this, the suffix `-riva` is used. Because he calms or is calmed, he is `siva` (masculine), meaning 'the lord of Umā'; `sivā` (feminine), meaning 'a jackal'; and `sivaṃ` (neuter), meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'

208. Chadā ravi.

208. From the root `chad`, the suffix `-ravi` is used.

Chada-saṃvaraṇe[M 0.0286], etasmā ravi hoti. Chādetīti chavi=juti.

The root `chad` has the meaning 'to cover'; from this, the suffix `-ravi` is used. Because it covers, it is `chavi`, meaning 'skin,' 'complexion,' or 'radiance.'

209. Pūra timā kiso rasso ca.

209. From the roots `pūr` and `tim`, the suffix `-isa` is used, and the root vowel is shortened.

Pūra-pūraṇe, tima-temane, etehi kiso hoti ūssa rasso ca. Pūretīti puriso=pumā. (Pure uccaṭṭhāne seti pavattatīti vā puriso=sova.) Temetīti timisaṃ=tamo.

From the root `pūr` in the sense of 'filling' and `tim` in the sense of 'moistening'—from these the suffix `-isa` is used, and the root vowel `ū` is shortened. Because he fills, he is `purisa`, meaning 'a man.' (Or, because he lies or exists in a city or a high place, he is `purisa`.) Because it moistens, it is `timisaṃ`, meaning 'darkness.'

210. Karā īso.

210. From the root `kar`, the suffix `-īsa` is used.

Karotismā īso hoti. Karīyatīti karīsaṃ=gūthaṃ.

From the root `kar`, the suffix `-īsa` is used. Because it is produced, it is `karīsaṃ`, meaning 'excrement.'

211. Sirīsādayo.

211. Words beginning with `sirīsa`.

Sirīsaādayo īsantā nipaccante. Saratissa assi, sappadaṭṭhakālādīsu sarīyatīti sirīso=rukkho. Pūrissa rassattaṃ, pūretīti purīsaṃ=gūthaṃ. Talissa dīgho, talati sattānaṃ patiṭṭhānaṃ bhavatīti tālīsaṃ=osadhiviseso, evamaññepi.

The words beginning with `sirīsa` are irregularly formed with the suffix `-īsa`. From the root `sar`, with substitution of `i` for `a`: because it is resorted to at times of snakebite and so on, it is `sirīso`, meaning 'the Sirīsa tree.' From the root `pūr`, with shortening of the vowel: because it fills, it is `purīsaṃ`, meaning 'excrement.' From the root `tal`, with lengthening of the vowel: because it becomes a foundation for beings, it is `tālīsaṃ`, meaning 'a particular medicinal plant.' And so for others.

212. Karā ribbiso.

212. From the root `kar`, the suffix `-ibbisa` is used.

Karotismā ribbiso hoti. Karīyatīti kibbisaṃ=pāpaṃ.

From the root `kar`, the suffix `-ibbisa` is used. Because it is done, it is `kibbisaṃ`, meaning 'evil' or 'a sin.'

213. Sasāsa vasa visa hana vana manāna kamā so.

213. From the roots `sas`, `ās`, `vas`, `vis`, `han`, `van`, `man`, `an`, and `kam`, the suffix `-sa` is used.

Sasa-gati hiṃsā vissasa pāṇanesu, asa-khepane, vasa-nivāse, visa-pavisane, hana-hiṃ sāyaṃ, vana sana-sambhattiyaṃ, mana-ñāṇe, ana-pāṇane, kama-icchāyaṃ, etehi so hoti, sasanti jīvanti sattā etenāti sassaṃ=kalamādi, asati khipatīti asso=hayo[M 0.0287]. Vasanti etthāti vassaṃ=saṃvaccharo. Visatīti vesso=tatiyavaṇṇo. Haññateti haṃso=sitacchado. Vanoti pattharatīti vaṃso=santāno, veḷu ca. Maññateti maṃsaṃ=pisitaṃ, anati jīvati etenāti aṃso=ekāṭṭhāso, bhujasiro ca. Kāmīyatīti kaṃso=parimāṇaṃ.

The root `sas` is in the sense of going and injuring; `as`, of throwing; `vas`, of dwelling; `vis`, of entering; `han`, of injuring; `van` and `san`, of sharing and devotion; `man`, of knowing; `an`, of breathing; and `kam`, of desiring. From these roots, the suffix `-sa` is used. Beings live (`sasanti`) by this, thus `sassaṃ` is grain, such as rice. It throws (`asati`), thus `asso` is a horse. They dwell (`vasanti`) in this, thus `vassaṃ` is a year. He enters (`visati`), thus `vesso` is a member of the third caste. It is struck (`haññate`), thus `haṃso` is a swan, the white-winged one. It spreads (`vanoti`), thus `vaṃso` is lineage, and also bamboo. It is thought (`maññate`), thus `maṃsaṃ` is flesh. One breathes (`anati`) by this, thus `aṃso` is a portion, and also the shoulder. It is desired (`kāmīyati`), thus `kaṃso` is a measure.

214. Āmi thu ku sīto saka.

214. From the roots `āmi`, `thu`, `ku`, and `sī`, the suffix `-saka` is used.

Āpubbo mi-pakkhepe, thu-abhitthave ku-sadde, sī-saye, etehi saka hoti. Āmīyati anto pakkhipīyatīti āmisaṃ=bhakkhaṃ. Thavīyatīti thuso=vīhitaco. Kavati vātena nadatīti kuso=tiṇaviseso. Sayanti ettha ūkāti sīsaṃ=muddhā, kālatipu ca.

The root `mi` in the sense of throwing, when preceded by `ā`; the root `thu` in the sense of praising; the root `ku` in the sense of making a sound; and the root `sī` in the sense of lying down. From these, the suffix `-saka` is used. It is thrown inside (`āmīyati`), thus `āmisaṃ` is food. It is praised (`thavīyati`), thus `thuso` is rice chaff. It sounds (`kavati`), resounding with the wind, thus `kuso` is a type of grass. Lice (`ūkā`) lie (`sayanti`) here, thus `sīsaṃ` is the head, and also lead.

215. Phassādayo.

215. Words such as `phassa`.

Phassaādayo sakaantā nipaccante. Phusa-samphasse, ussatthaṃ, phusatīti phasso=kāyaviññāṇavisayo. Phusso=nakkhattaṃ. Pusa posane, posīyatīti pussaṃ=phalaviseso. Bhū-sattāyaṃ, bhūssa rasso, abhavīti bhusaṃ=tucchadhaññaṃ, aṃkissa uka, aṅketi anena aññeti aṅkuso=gajapatodo. Phāya-vuddhiyaṃ, papubbo, yalopo, phāyati vuddhiṃ gacchatīti papphāsaṃ=dehakoṭṭhāsaviseso. Kalismā sassa māña, kulismā ca, kalīyati parimīyatīti kammāso=sabalo, kammāsaṃ=pāpaṃ. Kulati pattharatīti kummāso=bhakkhaviseso. Manissa jūka, maññati sadhanattaṃ etāyāti mañjūsā=kaṭṭhapeḷā. Pīssa yūka, piṇetīti pīyūsaṃ=amataṃ. Kula-saṃvaraṇe, ika, kulīyati saṃvarīyatīti kulisaṃ=vajiraṃ[M 0.0288]. Bala-saṃvaraṇe, ika, lassa ḷattañca, balati etena macche gaṇhātīti baḷiso=macchavedhanaṃ. Mahissa eka, mahīyatīti mahesī=katābhisekā padhānitthī, evamaññepi.

Words such as `phassa` are irregularly formed with their own final letters. From the root `phus` in the sense of contact, with the suffix `sa`: it touches (`phusati`), thus `phasso` is the object of body-consciousness. `Phusso` is a constellation. From the root `pus` in the sense of nourishing: it is nourished (`posīyati`), thus `pussaṃ` is a type of fruit. From the root `bhū` in the sense of being, with shortening of the vowel: it was (`abhavi`), thus `bhusaṃ` is chaff. From the root `aṅk`, with the suffix `usa`: one marks (`aṅketi`) with this, thus `aṅkuso` is an elephant goad. From the root `phāy` in the sense of increasing, preceded by `pa`, with elision of `y`: it increases (`phāyati`), thus `papphāsaṃ` is the lungs. From the root `kal` or `kul`, `sa` becomes `māsa`: it is counted (`kalīyati`), thus `kammāso` is variegated, and `kammāsaṃ` is evil. It spreads (`kulati`), thus `kummāso` is a type of food. From the root `man`, with the suffix `jūsā`: one esteems (`maññati`) it as wealth, thus `mañjūsā` is a wooden chest. From the root `pī`, with the suffix `yūsa`: it pleases (`piṇeti`), thus `pīyūsaṃ` is ambrosia. From the root `kul` in the sense of enclosing, with the suffix `isa`: it is enclosed (`kulīyati`), thus `kulisaṃ` is a thunderbolt. From the root `bal` in the sense of overpowering, with the suffix `isa`, and `l` becoming `ḷ`: one overpowers (`balati`) and catches fish with this, thus `baḷiso` is a fishhook. From the root `mah`, with the suffix `esī`: she is honored (`mahīyati`), thus `mahesī` is a consecrated chief queen. And so for others too.

216. Suto ṇisaka.

216. From the root `su`, the suffix `-ṇisaka` is used.

Suṇātismā ṇisaka hoti. Suṇātīti suṇisā=puttabhariyā.

From the root `su` (to hear), the suffix `-ṇisaka` is used. She hears (`suṇāti`), thus `suṇisā` is a daughter-in-law, the son's wife.

217. Vetāta yu panāla kala camā aso.

217. From the roots `veta`, `ata`, `yu`, `pana`, `ala`, `kala`, and `cama`, the suffix `-aso` is used.

Veta-suttiyo dhātu, ata-sātaccagamane, yu-missane, panathutiyaṃ, ala-bandhane, kala-saṅkhyāne, cama-adane, etehi aso hoti. Vetati pavattatīti vetaso=vānīro. Atati vāterito niccaṃ vedhattaṃ yātīti ataso=vanappativiseso vīmhi abhasī=gacchaviseso. Yavīyati missīyatīti yavaso=pasughāso. Paññate thavīyateti panaso=kaṇḍaṇīphalo. Alīyati bandhiyatīti alaso=mandakārī. Kalīyatīti kalaso=kumbho. Camati adati anenāti camaso=homabhājanaṃ.

The sutra root `veta`; the root `ata` in the sense of constant going; `yu` in the sense of mixing; `pana` in the sense of praising; `ala` in the sense of binding; `kala` in the sense of counting; `cam` in the sense of eating. From these, the suffix `-aso` is used. It proceeds (`vetati`), thus `vetaso` is a reed. It constantly goes (`atati`), driven by the wind, thus `ataso` is a type of tree; in the feminine, `atasī` is a type of shrub. It is mixed (`yavīyati`), thus `yavaso` is fodder for cattle. It is praised (`paññate`), thus `panaso` is the jackfruit tree. He is bound (`alīyati`), thus `alaso` is a lazy person. It is counted (`kalīyati`), thus `kalaso` is a pot. One eats (`camati`) with this, thus `camaso` is a sacrificial ladle.

218. Vaya diva kara karehyasaṇasakapāsakasā.

218. From the roots `vaya`, `diva`, `kara`, and `kara`, the suffixes `asaṇa`, `sa`, `kapāsa`, and `kasa` are formed respectively.

Vayatyādīhi asaṇaādayo honti yathākkamaṃ. Vayati gacchatīti vāyaso=kāko. Dibbanti etthāti divaso=dinaṃ. Karīyatīti kappāso=suttasambhavo. Kibbisaṃ karotīti kakkaso=pharuso.

From the roots `vaya` and so on, the suffixes `asaṇa` and so on are added respectively. It goes (`vayati`), thus `vāyaso` = a crow. They play (`dibbanti`) in this, thus `divaso` = a day. It is made (`karīyati`), thus `kappāso` = cotton, that which originates from thread. He does (`karoti`) wrong (`kibbisaṃ`), thus `kakkaso` = harsh.

219. Sasa masa daṃsāsā su.

219. From the roots `sasa`, `masa`, `daṃsa`, and `asa`, the suffix `su` is added.

Sasādīhi [M 0.0289] su hoti. Sasati jīvatīti sassu=jayampatīnaṃ mātā. Masīyatīti massu=purisamukhe pavaddhalomāni. “Lopo”ti (1.39) niggahītalopo, daṃsīyati bandhamanenāti dassu=coro. Asīyati khipīyatīti assu=bappo.

From the roots `sasa` and so on, the suffix `su` is added. She lives (`sasati`), thus `sassu` = a mother-in-law, the mother of the couple. It is smeared (`masīyati`), thus `massu` = a beard, the hair that grows on a man's face. By the rule 'Lopo' (1.39), there is elision of the nasal consonant. One is bitten (`daṃsīyati`) or bound by him (`bandhamanenāti`), thus `dassu` = a thief. It is thrown (`asīyati`), thus `assu` = a tear.

220. Vidā dasuka.

220. From the root `vid`, the suffix `dasuka` is added.

Vidismā dasuka hoti. Vidati jānātīti viddasu=vidvā.

From the root `vid`, the suffix `dasuka` is added. He knows (`vidati`), thus `viddasu` = a wise person.

221. Sasā rīho.

221. From the root `sas`, the suffix `rīho` is added.

Sasatismā rīho hoti. Sasati hiṃsatīti sīho=kesarī.

From the root `sas`, the suffix `rīho` is added. It injures (`sasati`), thus `sīho` = a lion, the maned one.

222. Jīvāmā ho vamā ca.

222. From the roots `jīva` and `ama`, the suffix `ho` is added, with `vamā` and `ca` as substitutes.

Jīva-pāṇadhāraṇe, ama-gamane, etehī ho hoti, vamā cāntādesā yathākkamaṃ, ādesavidhānaṃ pana pararūpabādhanatthaṃ. “Byañjane dīgharassā”ti (1.39) rassattaṃ, jīvanti etāyāti jivhā=rasanā. Amati pavattatīti amhaṃ=asmā. Papubbe amati pavattatīti pamhaṃ=pakhumaṃ.

From the root `jīva` in the sense of sustaining life and `ama` in the sense of going, the suffix `ho` is added, with `vamā` and `ca` as substitutes for the final parts respectively. This rule of substitution is for the purpose of preventing coalescence with the following form. By the rule 'Byañjane dīgharassā' (1.39), there is shortening. They live (`jīvanti`) by means of this, thus `jivhā` = the tongue. It goes (`amati`), thus `amhaṃ` = a stone. Preceded by `pa`, it proceeds (`amati`), thus `pamhaṃ` = an eyelash.

223. Taṇhādayo.

223. Taṇhā and so on.

Taṇhaādayo hantā nipaccante. Tasa-pipāsāyaṃ, sassa ṇattaṃ, evamupari ca, tasati pātumicchati etāyāti taṇhā=lo bho. Kasa-vilekhane, kasatīti kaṇho=kāḷo. Juta-dittiyaṃ, tassa ṇattaṃ, ottābhāvo ca, jotetīti juṇhā=canda- pabhā[M 0.0290]. Mīlissa ḷo, nimīlantyanena akkhīnīti mīḷhaṃ-gūthaṃ. Gāhissa ḷo, gayhatīti gāḷhaṃ, dahissa ḷo, dahatīti daḷhaṃ, bahissa ḷo, dīgho ca, bahati vuddhiṃ vacchatīti bāḷhaṃ, ete tayo daḷhatthā. Gamissa assi, gacchatīti gimho-nidāgho. Paṭakalānaṃ aka ca, paṭati yātīti paṭaho=bheriviseso. Kalīyati parimīyati anena sūrabhāvoti kalaho=vivādo. Kaṭavarānaṃ āka, kaṭanti ettha osadhādiṃ maddantīti kaṭāho=bhājanaviseso. Varīyatīti varāho=sūkaro. Lunātissa o, lunāti etenāti lohaṃ=ayādi. Evamaññepi.

Words such as `taṇhā` are irregularly formed ending in `ha`. From the root `tas` in the sense of thirst, with `s` becoming `ṇ`, and likewise in the following examples: one thirsts (`tasati`) or desires to drink (`pātumicchati`) because of this, thus `taṇhā` = craving, greed. From the root `kas` in the sense of ploughing: it ploughs (`kasati`), thus `kaṇho` = black. From the root `jut` in the sense of shining, with `t` becoming `ṇ`, and the absence of the `otta` vowel change: it shines (`joteti`), thus `juṇhā` = moonlight. From `mīl`, `ḷa` is the substitute: the eyes close (`nimīlanti`) by means of this, thus `mīḷhaṃ` = excrement. From `gāh`, `ḷa` is the substitute: it is seized (`gayhati`), thus `gāḷhaṃ` = firm. From `dah`, `ḷa` is the substitute: it burns (`dahati`), thus `daḷhaṃ` = firm. From `bah`, `ḷa` is the substitute, and there is lengthening: it increases (`bahati`) or goes to growth (`vuddhiṃ gacchati`), thus `bāḷhaṃ` = intense. These three have the meaning of firmness. From `gam`, there is substitution: it goes (`gacchati`), thus `gimho` = summer heat. From the roots `paṭa` and `kala`, `aka` is the suffix: it goes (`paṭati`), thus `paṭaho` = a type of drum. Heroism (`sūrabhāvo`) is diminished (`kalīyati`) or measured (`parimīyati`) by this, thus `kalaho` = a quarrel. From the roots `kaṭa` and `vara`, `āka` is the suffix: they grind (`maddanti`) herbs, etc., in this, thus `kaṭāho` = a type of vessel. It is chosen (`varīyati`), thus `varāho` = a boar. From `lunāti`, `o` is the substitute: one cuts (`lunāti`) with this, thus `lohaṃ` = metal, such as iron. And so for others too.

224. Paṇussahā hihī ṇoḷaṅa ca.

224. From the roots `paṇa` and `ussaha`, the suffixes `hi` and `hī` are added respectively, with `ṇo` and `ḷaṅa` as substitutes.

Paṇā upubbasahā ca hihī honti yathākkamaṃ, ṇaoḷaṅa cāntādesā, ādesavidhānasāmatthiyā pararūpābhāvo, paṇīyati voharīyatīti paṇhi=pādassa pacchābhāgo. Ussahatīti ussāḷhī-vīriyaṃ.

From the root `paṇa` and from the root `saha` preceded by `u`, the suffixes `hi` and `hī` are added respectively, with `ṇo` and `ḷaṅa` as substitutes for the final parts. Due to the force of this substitution rule, there is no coalescence. It is used in trade (`paṇīyati`) or transacted (`voharīyati`), thus `paṇhi` = the heel, the back part of the foot. One strives (`ussahati`), thus `ussāḷhī` = energy.

225. Khī mi pī cu mā vākāhi ḷo ussa vā dīgho ca.

225. From the roots `khī`, `mi`, `pī`, `cu`, `mā`, `vā`, and `kā`, the suffix `ḷo` is added, and there is optional lengthening of `u`.

Khī-khaye, mi-pakkhepe, pī-tappane, cu-cavane, mā-māne, vī vā-gamane, kā gā-sadde, etehi ḷo hoti, ukārassa vā dīgho ca. Khīyatīti khelo=lālā. Mīyati pakkhipīyatīti meḷā=masi. Piṇetīti peḷā=bhājanaviseso. Cavatīti cūḷā=sikhā. Coḷo=pilotiko. Mīyati parimīyatīti māḷo=ekakūṭasaṅgahito anekakoṇavanto paṭissayaviseso. Vāti gacchatīti vāḷo=caṇḍamigo. Kāyati pharusaṃ vadatīti kāḷo=kaṇho, vīmhi kāḷī=kaṇhā.

From the root `khī` in the sense of wasting away; `mi` in the sense of throwing; `pī` in the sense of pleasing; `cu` in the sense of moving; `mā` in the sense of measuring; `vī` or `vā` in the sense of going; `kā` or `gā` in the sense of making a sound. From these, the suffix `ḷo` is added, and there is optional lengthening of the vowel `u`. It wastes away (`khīyati`), thus `khelo` = saliva. It is thrown (`mīyati`), thus `meḷā` = ink. It pleases (`piṇeti`), thus `peḷā` = a type of vessel. It moves (`cavati`), thus `cūḷā` = a crest, and `coḷo` = a cloth. It is measured (`mīyati`), thus `māḷo` = a type of building with a single pinnacle and many corners. It goes (`vāti`), thus `vāḷo` = a fierce beast. It speaks (`kāyati`) harshly, thus `kāḷo` = black; in the feminine, `kāḷī` = a dark woman.

226. Guto ḷaka ca.

226. From the root `gu`, the suffixes `ḷaka` and `ḷo` are added.

Gu-saddetīmasmā [M 0.0291] ḷaka hoti ḷo ca. Gavati pavattati etenāti guḷo=ucchuvikāro. Goḷo=lakuṇḍako.

From this root `gu` in the sense of making a sound, the suffix `ḷaka` is added, and also `ḷo`. It sounds (`gavati`) or proceeds (`pavattati`) by means of this, thus `guḷo` = molasses, a product of sugarcane. `Goḷo` = a ball or lump.

227. Paṅguḷādayo.

227. `Paṅguḷa` and so on.

Paṅguḷaādayo ḷaka antā nipaccante. Khañja-gativekalle, paṅguādeso, akhañji gativekallamāpajjīti paṅgaḷo=pīṭhasappī. Karotismā ḷassa khaña, kibbisaṃ karotīti kakkhaḷo=kurūro. Kukatissa kuka, kukyati pāpakārīhi ādīyatīti kukkuḷaṃ=saṅku saṃkiṇṇo sobbho. Kukkuḷo=thusaggī. Maṃkissa uka, bindu lopo ca, maṃketi vanaṃ maṇḍetīti makuḷo=avikasitakusumaṃ.

Words such as `paṅguḷa` are irregularly formed ending in `ḷaka`. From the root `khañj` in the sense of a defective gait, with `paṅgu` as a substitute: he limped (`akhañji`) or attained a defective gait (`gativekallamāpajji`), thus `paṅgaḷo` = a cripple who moves on a stool. From the root `kar`, with `ḷa` becoming `kha`: he does (`karoti`) wrong (`kibbisaṃ`), thus `kakkhaḷo` = cruel. From `kuka`, `ku` is added: it is taken up (`kukyati`) by evildoers, thus `kukkuḷaṃ` = a stake, a crowded pit. `Kukkuḷo` = a fire of hot ashes. From `maṃk`, `uka` is the suffix, and there is elision of the nasal point: it adorns (`maṃketi`) the forest, thus `makuḷo` = an unopened flower bud.

228. Pāto ḷi.

228. From the root `pā`, the suffix `ḷi` is added.

Pātismā ḷi hoti. Atthaṃ pāti rakkhatīti pāḷi=tanti.

From the root `pā`, the suffix `ḷi` is added. It protects (`pāti rakkhati`) the meaning (`atthaṃ`), thus `pāḷi` = the canonical text (`tanti`).

229. Vīto ḷu.

229. From the root `vī`, the suffix `ḷu` is added.

Vītismā ḷu hoti. Veti pavattatīti veḷu=veṇu.

From the root `vī`, the suffix `ḷu` is added. It goes (`veti`) or proceeds (`pavattati`), thus `veḷu` = bamboo (`veṇu`).

(Iti avaggapaccayavidhānaṃ).

(Thus ends the section on non-varga suffixes).

Iti moggallāne byākaraṇe vuttiyaṃ

Thus in the Vutti on the Moggallāna Grammar,

Ṇvādikaṇḍo sattamo.

the seventh chapter, the Ṇvādi section, is concluded.

Suttaṃ dhātu gaṇo ṇvādi, nāmaliṅgānusāsanaṃ;

Yassa tiṭṭhati jīvhagge, sa byākaraṇakesarī.

The Sutta, Dhātu, Gaṇa, Ṇvādi, and the Nāmaliṅgānusāsana—he on the tip of whose tongue this abides is a lion among grammarians.

Samattā cāyaṃ moggallānavutti

And this Vutti of Moggallāna is completed

Sattahi bhāṇavārehi.

in seven recitation sections.

1.

1.

Yassa [M 0.0292] rañño pabhāvena, bhāvitattayamākulaṃ;

Anākulaṃ duladdhīhi, pāpabhikkhūhi sabbaso.

By the power of which king, the threefold canon, which had been thrown into confusion by evil monks with wrong views, was made completely free from confusion.

2.

2.

Laṅkāya munirājassa, sāsanaṃ sādhu saṇṭhikaṃ;

Puṇṇacandasamāyogā, vāridhīva vivaddhate.

In Laṅkā, the Dispensation of the King of Sages is well established; it flourishes like the ocean in conjunction with the full moon.

3.

3.

Parakkamabhuje tasmiṃ, saddhābuddhiguṇodite;

Manuvaṃsaddhajākāre, laṅkādīpaṃ pasāsati.

While that Parakkamabhuja, endowed with the qualities of faith and wisdom, a banner of the Manu dynasty, rules the island of Laṅkā.

4.

4.

Moggallānena therena, dhīmatā sucivuttinā;

Racitaṃ yaṃ suviññeyya-masandiddha’manākulaṃ.

By the wise Elder Moggallāna of pure conduct was this composed, which is easily intelligible, unambiguous, and clear.

5.

5.

Asesavisayabyāpi, jinabyappatha nissayaṃ;

Saddhasattha’manāyāsa-sādhiyaṃ buddhivaddhanaṃ.

Pervading all subject matter, based on the discourse of the Conqueror, it is a treatise on grammar that is mastered without difficulty and enhances wisdom.

6.

6.

Tassa vutti samāsena, vipulatthapakāsanī;

Racitā puna teneva, sāsanujjotakārināti.

Its commentary, which concisely reveals the extensive meaning, was again composed by that same illuminator of the Dispensation.

Moggallānabyākaraṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Grammar of Moggallāna is concluded.
